div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.

Unjustifiable Jeremiads. I well remember how, not long before the outbreak of war, Mr. Hugh Stokes, writing in the " Art Chronicle,v dogmatically asserted that for unadulterated, blatant, and garish vulgarity, no age could equal our own. About the same time, another pessimist went one better than that. In the course of an address at the Central Y.M.C.A., Mr. T. W. Russell, M.P., teclared that there was more luxurious idleness than there had ever been in the his- tory of this country. Surely in the mean- time these eminent authorities have seen occasion to modify their opinions and revise their gloomy estimates. Anyhow, that same Y.M.C.A. has a very different 'story to tell now.

Something Up His Sleeve. "Is Mickey in condition?" asked an acquaintance of the mother of a brawny Irish recruit. "Is it in condition?" returned Mrs. Doolan proudly. "He's as foine as silk, as fit as a fiddle, an' ready for annything. Moi Mickey's the great boy. He's got something up his sleeve that'll astonish them Jarnrans." "Sure, an' phwat's that, Mrs_ Doolan?" "It's his ar-r-m!"

Concerning Thrift. Under some such significant headline as "Save and bank" (I write from memory at a holiday resort and cannot verify my allusions) "The Examiner" had a timely editorial on this subject the other week. Said a well- known speaker at a public meeting in which I was interested, " Great lessons of thrift may be evolved from a period of industrial depres- sion " ; but those who would hear of this virtue and learn the way of attainment need only sit at the feet of the canny Scot, whose dominant characteristic had passing notice in this column a few weeks ago. The saving habit is systematically and contemptuously derided by the common or garden Socialist tub-thumper, and his intense dislike of that which most of us consider wise and commend- able in the worker is understandable. It strikes me as worth while just to glance at this old Saxon word "thrift," derived as it is from the verb "to thrive "—that is to prosper through industry. Economy has been defined as the law of adaptation of means to ends in the management of one's affairs; but thrift .is not just that—it comprehends pre- cautionary measures calculated to ensure a margin of capital above and beyond the needs of a given period. The importance of habitu- ally spending less than one's earnings has been taught from early times; and Mr. Micawbees favourite precept on this point was better than his example. I recently re- ferred to the extreme frugality of the average Scot, reserving my illustrations and examples. Before passing to these, I may just note that among the Romans thrift was represented mainly by the substantive " frugalitas," which meant originally the capacity of bear- ing fruit. The frugal Roman was the citizen who bore fruit in the sense of acquiring pro- perty. A Handful of Chestnuts.

One of my favourite little anecdotes is to the effect that a stranger asked a fellow- traveller for a match. The other, a Scot, slowly produced his box, carefully took out one lucifer, and parted with it reluctantly. Then his fellow passenger discovered with dis- may that he had no tobacco, and, with a sig- nificant glance at the Scotsman's pipe, avowed his deficiency. " Ah," exclaimed the eager Scot, brightening visibly, "then yell no' be wantin' that match !"

And the following is like unto it: A Glas- gow merchant famous for his stinginess came into his office one morning and found a young ...clerk writing a letter in rather a flourishing hand. "My man," he observed, " dinna mak' the tails o' yer g's an' y's quite sae lang. I want the ink the last the quarter oot." Then there is the foul libel which says that when an Englishman leaves a railway carriage he looks round to see if he has left anything, but a Scotsman looks round to see if anyone else has left anything; and the equally atrocious one about the three friends on tour in Scotland—a native of that country, a visitor from the Emerald Isle, and a mere Sassenach. On the last day they decided to take something back to their wives. The Englishman bought a piece of Scottish plaid, the Irishman took a teapot with a Scottish motto on it, and the Scotsman took home a couple of spoons with G.N.R. stamped on them. A Scot of Peebles said to his friend Mac Andrew, "Mac, I hear ye have fallen in love wi' bonny. Kate McAllister." "Wed, Sanders," Mac replied, " I wis near—verra near—doein' it, but the bit lassie had nae siller, so I said to maself, 'Mac, be a mon.' And I wis a mon, and floe I jist pass her by." Canny? Yes, indeed. Take one more: Sandy (entering a nursery garden) : "Have ye a nice cucumber?" Gardener: "Yes, here is , one; that will be 9d." Sandy: "Too much. Have ye no' one for 3d. ?" Gardener (showing him a small one growing) : "You can have this for 3d." Sandy: "All right, here's the 3d., but don't cut it off—l'll be calling for it in a fortnicht."

Concerning the Collection. I set out with some remarks on thrift; and thereby hangs a tale—another of 'em. It was the morning of the " Sawbeth," and as Sandy was on his way home from kirk he was -over- -taken by the minister. "Eh," said he, "that was a powerful discourse on ' Thrift ' yit3 preached this morning." The minister smiled benignly. " A'm glad ye were able to profit by it," was his gratified reply. " Pro- fit!" exclaimed Sandy. "Why, mon, I would ha' put ma saxpence into the plate wi'out a thought kit for yer providential words. They saved me fourpence there and then." Finally, brethren: A street preacher in a Scottish town called a passing policeman and complained of being annoyed by a certain portion of his audi- ence. He asked t() have the el4etiouable lizi'MMlA removed. "Wed; yO so," said the officer, thoughtfully, "it would be deefficult for me tae spot them. But I'll tell ye what I'd dae if I were you." "What 9" eagerly asked the preacher. " Just gang roun' wi' th' hat!" Well, well; these are times of extreme anxiety, and one may be glad of anything cal- culated to relieve the strain, therefore I dare say our Caledonian neighbours will not mind taking a sort of turn at the good work. Our Soldiers.

The diversion is but momentary, of course; one's thoughts_ imniediately fly back to. the war and its associations. And sooth to say, as Offenbach's vivacious if somewhat fickle "Grand Duchess" used to sing to us before musical comedy shouldered irretriyably into Continued in Next Column.

div.head: FRANCE AND GERMANY.
div.p: FRANCE AND GERMANY.
"The Great Thought" Of France That Preceded "The Day" Of Germany.

div.head: NAPOLEON, 1815; WILLIAM, 1915.
div.p: NAPOLEON, 1815; WILLIAM, 1915.
By C. E.

It is remarkable how history repeats itself. Is there anything new under the sun? going back a hundred years to the first decade of the last century, we find in Europe a striking parallel to its present condition with this difference: instead of Germany, as now, seek- ing to establish its conquests and over-lord- ship over its neighbours, this role was played by France. From the literature of the times we learn that it was a favourable speculation among politicians that a powerful European State might easily arrive at universal dominion. France, from the situation and extent of her ' empire, the fertility of her soil, the number of her population, and her excellence in arms, arts and science, seemed of all nations the best adapted for the achievement of, such a purpose.

World Domination. Here was a nation with a great military genius at its head aiming at world power. Instead of, as now, "Deutschland über Alles," it was France that claimed the posi- tion of overlordship; instead of drinking to "The Day.," the favourite toast of the Parisians was "La Grande Pensee," the great thought of world domination. In this same literature we find that our attitude towards France, and the general situation then existing, affords a remarkable similarity to present conditions in connection with Germany. No doubt the ambition of Napoleon was largely responsible for the part played by France one hundred years ago, and his military genius was the main factor in its temporary success. /But just as now in con- nection with Germany, it is a mistake to put the Whole blame of the present war upon the German Emperor, so it is an error to put the whole of the blame for the French Wars upon the Corsican. France was the greatest war power in Europe; she stood easily first in Western Europe in military development, and she found in Napoleon just the man to ex- press, as well as to exploit, her national am- bition. One old writer, in speaking of France, says : There fin France] is a dreadful energy, and a portentous talent and activity. The ends and the means of that Government are alike cruel and unhallowed; but the skill with which they are adapted to each other, the vigour with which they are pur- sued and the contrivance with which they are arranged for a course of unexhaustible exertion, are calculated to inspire at once admiration and alarm. This is exactly what we are now saying about Germany. The following, if read in our daily Press, would be taken to refer to Ger- many, but it was written over a hundred years ago about France:— And it is from this constitution, com- bined with the code of the conscription, with the despotic regulations on the Press —and with the vast establishment of spies and intriguers—that the gigantic power, which is overturning Europe, derives its

form, and recruits its strength. Vigour and rapidity are its characteristics; and, despotic as itS constitution undoubtedly is, it is, of all the despotisms that history has described, the most active, energetic , and compact.. . . All is bone nn e muscle; there is no sluggish smoothness, no sleek im- becility; every nerve is braced to its firmest tension.

Conscription Fosters War. The military system of France was largely copied from that of Rome. The individual's interest in both was entirely subservient to the interest of the State. The State became the idol and the tyrant, and individual freedom was cruelly crushed for the sake of the accomplishment of the national ambition. Conscription upon which the military power mainly rested, was very similar to that in force in the Roman Empire. Conscription was introduced into France in 1798, and since then it has gradually spread to the other European countries, and has ever fostered war. Its introduction was attributed to Carnot, who founded his plan upon that of the Roman Republic which made every citizen

div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.-

limbo the older form of opera bouffe, "1 dote on the military." I have all along sympa- thised with and in no small degree shared the affection for the soldier's tunic popularly sup- posed to be the peculiar weakness of the young and susceptible domestic slavey. My sincere regard for Mr. Thomas Atkin i dates from a remote period, and has, of course been inten- sified by the tremendous events of the last few months. Some 40 years ago, in a Yorkshire town in which I then lived, it was proposed to establish a military'depot. When War Office representatives began to inquire about a suit- able site for barracks, certain vigilant towns- folk, jealous for the morals of the community, held a protest meeting. They dotibtless acted on genuine conviction, but what the alarmed leaders of that agitation were constrained to say from a public platform would now be de- nounced as gross caricature and groundless calumny. To put the case in a nutshell: there was in those days a pretty general impression that the soldiers were drawn from a lower and altogether more ignorant and debased class than is nowadays the case, and that, what- ever their fighting qualities, they were by no means models of virtue in the modern sense of that good old word, temperance being prac- tically outside the military vocabulary. Con- trast that with popular opinion of the wonder- ful armies we now have in the field, largely composed as they are of total abstainers and men trained in our Sunday schools. I had hoped to enlarge here, but—assuredly, victory will crown the efforts of these splendid war- riors. A Note on Lcoturinga

Even so comparatively lately as a quarto' I of a century or so ago, the public lecture— which has been variously defined as " Concen- trated Knowledge" and "Science arrayed in its holiday • dress "—was a marvellously attractive and successful institution; hut in districts of which. I have recent experience its popularity has decidedly. waned. Among the lecturers who in the earlier half of my profes- sional career included what I may term my area in their itinerary were oratorical giants not a few—men gifted with the power of rous- ing the enthusiasm and playing at will upon the emotions of large audiences ;- but whether the peculiar style which they affected would interest the present generation as it delighted their fathers 'May be doubted. Some of my contemporaries are disposed to pessimism on account of 'this seemly indifference to what they were themselves accustomed to regard and to describe as intellectual feasts. They ap- pear.to imagine that so far as platform deliver- ances other than political are concerned, the rising race is like unto the tramp who pleaded that, he was at the point of death from star- vation, and, _being offered a "tieket-for a Sub- stantial dinner, sorrowfully declined it on being told that sevekal speeches would follow, and crawled wearily into a silent timberyard to die. Things are, by no means s? bad as that would appear 'to imply; still, whatever ' the explanation—And whether we 00 well to be sorry or not—lecttirin,c,r is no longer what it was. . . • -

div.head: PARKER.
div.p: PARKER.

liable for service. In the employment of these conscripts France showed a wantonness of despotism which would have disgraced the worst period of Rome's degeneracy, and has only been equalled, possibly surpassed, by Germany in the present war. France raised a conscript army of 700,000 men, greater than any which Rome ever maintained in the meri- dian of her power. This army would now Ile considered small, but at the time no army could be compared with it in numbers, and it was a menace to every European nation—in- deed to the whole combined. France, then, as Germany now, was considered to be en- gaged in a conspiracy against mankind. Strong in brute force, she was secure of im- punity and careless to censure, discarded the usual prevarications of tyranny, and rested her pretensions and her rights alone on the power of the sword. Under Napoleon she rent asunder the ties that bound Europe in a commonwealth of nations, and stifled every advance in freedom wherever her power ex- tended. Freedom was on her lips, but sub- jugation and lust of conquest in her heart. Napoleon's Conquests.

As the war proceeded, the greater part of what is now the German Empire, Northern Italy, and almost the whole of Spain, came under the dominion of France. In a word, almost the whole of Western Europe was sub- ject to her domination. In her conquests France, in addition to living on the countries she invaded, extorted from these large con- tributions for the pay and equipment of her troops, just as to-day Germany is "bleeding" Belgium and Northern France "white." Napoleon ruined the finances and devastated the countries he subjugated, in order that the hope of future resistance might be more com- pletely extinguished. When any discontent or signs of insurrection was manifested at home in France the leaders were made to join the army, just as now the protesting German Socialists are sent to the Front. Not alone in military matters, but, as now, the con- queror strove to extend his " Kultur " over the world. The Napoleon Code and the lan- guage of its authors are established in the Courts of Westphalia, where the Governnients and civil employments were administered almost exclusively by Frenchmen. Clerks were drafted from the Post Offices of Paris to conduct similar establishments in Hamburg and Danzig. As a writer of the times says : There is not at this moment through the whole Continent a Press exempt from the supervision of his police, nor an asylum in which an obnoxious person could find safety. . . . The ascendancy of the military spirit has crushed and subjugated all literature, and had degenerated the bar and the pulpit. The sentiments towards our own country betrayed itself in every word and jesture, and exerts an influence more like that of passion than of the ordinary calculations of interest and national antipathy. England's Resistance. _England was the one country unconquered

where freedom in any sense, remained alive. But England was comparatively weak; her population was only 15,000,000, against 40,000,000 in France: As- a writer of the period says: "Every other monument of European liberty has perished. That ancient fabric which has been raised by the wisdom and virtue of our forefathers still stands, but it stands alone, and it stands among ruins." This seems a little extravagant because so far the island home was free from invasion and was mistress of the seas, but little had been done by England to check the conquering ad- vance of Napoleon's troops in Europe. In Spain alone Wellington held in check a sec- tion of Napoleon's forces. Naturally the common danger induced the other European countries to forget for a time their differences and to unite to overthrow this arrogant power, and first at Leipsig, then at Waterloo, Napoleon's ambitions were brought to the dust, and France, for her own good, and that of Europe, was compelled to make pace. Strange that Europe has again to go thrauizn the same agony as that of one hundred years ago.

div.head: WAR DISTRESS.
div.p: WAR DISTRESS.
A Large And Useful Field For Personal Service.

The conference on War Relief and Personal Service held in London last week proved a great SUCCfss, and more than justified the Guilds of Help and Charity Organisation Society which promoted the idea. About 00 delegates assembled at the Caxton Hall, and the Soldiers' and Sailors' Families' Association and the Soldiers' and Sailors' Help Society were well represented. Mr. C. E. Parker and Mr. W, J. Rowland went from Warrington. The earlier • papers were devoted to the' methods employed for dealing with distress after the war began. The Countess Ferrers spoke of the work of the Soldiers' and Sailors' Families' Association in London.

Scarborough's distress work was carried out by a special committee, the buckbone of which was the Council of Social Welfare, a society which was a recent amalgamation of a Guild of Hell) with a Charity Organisation Society. One local difficulty was the fact that so many Qf the people of Scarborough depend upon letting lodgings as a subsidiary meahs of live- lihood, and therefore pay larger rents than would be needed for their own families. Ports- mouth, the greatest war port in the world," had a huge problem to face, but the service people rose splendidly to the occasion and rendered fine service.

It is clear that in many cases the distress work was carried out by Guilds of Help or Charity Organisation Societies. Mr. C. E. B. Russell, well known as a social worker in Manchester and now at the Home Mee, opened a useful discussion on the dis- charged soldier and sailor, making many prac- tical suggestions based on experience shortly after the South African War.

Quite a statesmanlike paper on the future of the Local Representative Committees was read by Mr. D'Aeth, of Liverpool, who spoke at the last annual meeting of the Warrington Guild. Councillor Eleanor Rathbone, of the Liverpool Soldiers' and Sailors' Families' Association, spoke very'. sensibly on the problem of the widow and orphan. .Mr. Woollcombe, secretary of the Cavendish Association, read -a paper on "The Development of. Personal Service," in which he itleaded for adequate training and far' greater cohesion among social workers. Certain facts clearly emerged from the con- ference, viz., that many new workers had entered the field in a great national crisis, and had done excellent service. It still remains true that those who in the past had ,rendered organised civic service formed the nucleus of the army of helpers when war broke out. The danger just now was that many ' hew organisations might be started by enthusiastic people without experience, and a good deal of inefficiency and wastefulness might result.

div.p: CHAT and GOSSIP.
By MARJORIE.
London's Season.

Nearly all the great houses in the West End of London are open, but there is little or no entertaining, and quiet seclusion contrasts strangely with the brilliant seasons of the past. The morning canter in the Row and the morn- ing stroll in the Park, are indulged in by both soldiers and civilians, and of course by many women. There will be no rush to the Conti- nent, or elsewhere abroad this year; con- sequently our seaside and other resorts will benefit from the absence of this competition. The riverside haunts are already filling up, and there is an unusual demand for .houses in the Thames valley, which is supposed to be safe from Zeppelin attacks, but there will be no Henley this year.
The Kaiser-i-Hind Medal for Lady Willingdon.

Queen Victoria instituted among other medals that of the Kaiser-i-Hind, for distinguished ser- vice in India. The names of very few women figure in lists of honour, but Lady Willingdon, a daughter of Lord Brassey, and the wife of the Governor of Bombay, enjoyed the proud dis- tinction of finding hers beside those of the dis- tinguished men, whom the King has delighted to honour. For her ceaseless activities for the amelioration of the, native community, Lady Willingdon has received and well-merited the Kaiser-i-Hind Medal. Unfortunately the un- certainty of the fate of their, eldest son causes Lord and Lady Willingdon the most cruel anxiety. That he was wounded in the war last year, is all that can be discovered concerning him.

Women Students in the University of Benares. An experiment is being tried in Benares, which may have, if generally followed through- out India, far-reaching influences in the educa- tion of native men and women. The Govern- ment College of that famous city has been raised to the dignity of a University, to which, under certain conditions women are to be admitted. So far the Government schools of India provide no religious education, but the University of Benares will include theological as well as scientific and technical instruction in its curriculum. The study of Sanscrit and all that is best in the Ilindoo literature, culture and religion of the past, will be encouraged. It is proposed to provide Mohammedans also with a college, on similar lines, and should these two prove a success, others like them will be established in the near future. Women Hairdressers.

Thirty years, ago, some "lady barbers" set up, in the "hairdressing and shaving," in Lon- don. That was a time when "what to do with our daughters" was more of a problem than it is now, but nevertheless the scheme did not prosper, and soon died out. It is, however, obviously a business within the seope of women's activities, and they are again taking it up, owing to the war. There is a scarcity of barbers, due rather to so many being enemy aliens, than to their having enlisted in the British Army. The man of British birth looks down on the barber, as he does on the waiter, and he mostly leaves such occupations to foreigners. Possibly women will now obtain a

div.head: HOME NOTES.
div.p: HOME NOTES.
Profitable Recipes and Useful Suggestions.
Ham Toast.

Two tablespoonfuls grated ham, three eggs, three tablespoonfuls of milk, cayenne, loz. but- ter. Beat the eggs with the milk, add the pepper and grated ham; melt the butter in a saucepan, stir in the egg and ham mixture, stir till quite thick, pile on buttered toast and serve very hot. Cheese Fondu. Beat four eggs until well mixed and light, season with salt and a pinch of cayenne; add four tablespoonfuls of milk and pour into a hot buttered frying pan; add three tablespoonfuls of grated cheese, stir rapidly until smooth, and pour at once over hot buttered slices of entire wheat bread.

Savoury Rice. 'Boililb. rice in two pints of milk and water till soft. (If skim milk is used a little drip- ping or chopped suet should be added.) Grate ilb. of dry cheese, and stir into the rice with pepper and salt. Or it may be put in a, pie- dish in layers with cheese, and some bits of dripping on top, and browned in the oven. Macaroni can be used in the same way. To Economise.

Silk collars are much worn on cotton blouses. It is therefore an economy to make the collars separate from the blouse, arranging them so that they can be fixed with press studs. By doing this you can have one or two different colours and styles of collar for the one blouse, and give it a different appearance by the- addi- tion of a collar of iarious .designs. _

It is quite a popular idea to sew buttons or " bobs " to the end of a sash. If the latter, they are made by cutting circles of silk of the same colour as the sash, gathering them round and then filling with wadding or cottonwool, drawing up, and patting into a rounded shape.

If your last year's cotion dresses are too faded to be used as gowns, remove the collar and sleeves, cut the armholes larger, stitch up the fastenings at the front, and cut the dress right down at centre back, making this neat, and you have a useful "slip-on" apron which can be bleached white, or dyed a dark colour, as pre- ferred.—" Maud," in "Farm and Home."

CHILDREN OF ALL AGES are cordially invited to join this Corner if they read it regularly. Application for membership, stating name, address and age, should be made to "UNCLE NED, 'Examiner' Office, Bewsey- street, Warrington." Every girl or boy, whose name is in the Big Book, is entitled to enter the competitions held every week, to the winners of which useful book-prizes are sent.
WHO WOULD YOU LIKE TO BE IF YOU 'WEREN'T YOURSELF?
MT DEAR CHILDREN,-

Who would you like to be if you weren't yourself? I suppose everyone of us could answer that question without stoppling to think, be- cause we each ,have our heroes—and we should all like to be what • our heroes are like; shouldn't we? Well, that is the subject for our essay-Competition this week—" Who I should like to be if I - was not myself." Only write a few lines, please, and send them in by Monday.

div.head: NEW MEMBERS.
div.p: NEW MEMBERS.

I have been, very pleased to receive the following capital letter " 72, Scott-street, • Warrington, Ju.ne 156, 1915. Dear Uncle Ned,—l do not khow how to thank you for the lovely pre I received ' quite safe this morning. My playmate, who saw what I had won, wishes to become a member so that he. will be entitled to enter - the competitions held every week. :His name . is .-,Thomas Ashton, anti his address is 76, Scott-street. He was 12 on January Bth, 1915. , "Again thanking you for the present,- I must close, hoping you will soon be holding another drawing competition.—l remain, your loving nephew, ERNEST POTTER." • I am very tlad that you have brought along your friend to join our Corner, Ernest; and hope all my other nephews and nieces will do the

permanent footing in the busineSs, at least in some departments, as is the case in America, where no woman would think of having her hair dressed, except by a woman hairdresser. Misleading Short Skirts. The short skirts when worn by women in their second youth, are altogether misleading; a slim, active figure looks twenty when followed, but double that age, when met face to face. Small checks are very much worn in silks, and these make some of the prettiest of this year's silk frocks, with semi-high collars, little vest, and sometimes sleeves of fine clear muslin. Black and white checks come first in favour, then blue and white. In fact every shade of blue is popular this summer, the stronger tints should, however, be left to the youthful; as the softer blue-grey shades prove more becoming to women who have passed their prime. The corsages of dresses of this type are most simply made, and often finished with a Marie Antoinette fichu of soft white muslin. The crossover pointed bodice is a novelty that bids fair to attain some degree of popularity. White undersleeves are very much in evidence, as are also complete sleeves of some filmy fabric, which make for coolness and comfort in hot weather. The Newest Negliges. The war is responsible for many innovations and changes in the wardrobe. For instance the rest gown, and morning wrapper take a much more prominent position than formerly, whilst the restaurant frock may be styled a product of the war, for it was scarcely known this time last year, and is quite a newcomer. Paris has I always specialised in negliges of every descrip- tion, for Frenchwomen wear them at home, at ' all times of the day. The• best designs there- fore come from Paris, and as these are faith- fully copied by the good houses here, the result is that London can show delightful ready-made rest gowns, at lower prices than those of the French. A most effective model tea gown, in soft white satin was 'beautifully lraped in Greek fashion, and finished at the hem with the key pattern embroidered in gold. Very pictur- esaue are the rest gowns i,n taffetas chiffon with dainty Marie Antoinette fichus of fine hem- stitched net. Fancy voile in the most delicate colourings makes ideal wrappers, but of a less expensive kind. The New Coiffure.

The change in the silhouette has necessitated as drastic an alteration in the coiffure, and extreme neatness, even perhaps primness, is the chief characteristic of this season's hair- dressing. The clear line of the brew, so long hidden, is again conspicuous, for the hair is frequently turned off the face, only a stray curl or two breaking the monotony. The parting at the side, however; has not disappeared. The neat coiffure is commendable, but it does not suit all faces, for it &mends exceptional good looks, and a very pretty profile. The loose style softens hard outlines, and as the coiffure is exceedingly important individual seeds should be preferred to a slavish adoption of an un- becoming style, simply because it happens to be the latest fashion. Sometimes the hair is drawn tightly back, and simply tucked away behind the head. Since the war broke out no ornaments have been worn in the hair by day, and merely one comb for evening. But very beautiful jet ornaments, such as flexible bows, and butterflies, have lately appeared, and these make suitable ornaments when a black, or black and white evening toilette is donned.

div.head: HINTS ON HEALTH.
div.p: HINTS ON HEALTH.
Useful Information In Popular Language.
Worry is one of the most fruitful causes of consumption. Care of the Teeth.
It is somewhat rare to find anaongst civilised people an adult with a normal number of sound teeth. This is especially true of the rising generation.

- The care of the teeth: includes not only a supply of proper nutriment, but also cleanli- ness. The mineral matter present in teeth is practically identical with that of bone but more abundant and is composed largely of calcium carbonate and calcium phosphate. Calcium is very deficient in some articles of diet, as in the flesh of adult animals usually consumed for food. White bread has in it much less mineral than wholemeal bread containing the bran of the wheat. Milk and the cereal foods are rich in calcium salts, or lime. It would seem that those subsisting largely on meat and white bread do not give to the teeth the nutriment 130 necessary to keep them in good repair. Carnivorous animals, it is true, have good teeth, but invariably they eat not only the flesh, hut also the bones. Again, most people eat their food in a soft form, avoiding the things which require mastication. This takes away from the teeth work which is necessary in order to keep them healthy. Any organ of the body which is not in use loses; to a large extent, its ability for work and tends to waste away. An active working muscle receives about double the blood supply of a resting muscle. May this not also be true of the teeth and gums? The Scotch •Highlander used to live largely on hard oat-cake and some of the Scandinavian nations who used hard unfermented breads were noted for their fine, healthy teeth.. Old men of seventy or eighty years often possessed a full set of teeth in a sound condition.

It, is a good plan to wash the teeth morning and evening with pure water and at the same time use a little mild soap or French chalk. After each meal any particles of food which re- main between the teeth should be removed.

It is well to visit a qualified dentist in order to have the teeth inspected for possible cavities, which should receive immediate attention, otherwise the teeth will soon become useless and rapidly decay.—Dr. Bell in "Good Health."

div.head: LEARNING TO RIDE.
div.p: LEARNING TO RIDE.
:Queries and correspondence should be addressed to "The Hub," do The Editor. Replies can- not be sent by post and all queries will be answered in our columns.)

It is many years ago since I came across the folding bicycle—it was in France I saw it first —but I never thought that they would come into use in this country. The folding cycle was invented by a Frenchman, Captain Gerard, and these machines have been in use with the French Army for many years. They have now been adopted by the British Army, and con- siderable numbers are being manufactured in this country. Only 11 minutes is needed to fold the bicycle up and strap it on the soldier's shoulders. They are most useful in the Belgian dunes, where cycling is not always possible over the• loose sandhills.

FORK LAMP DANGERS. Although on occasions I have used a fork lamp—l have always deprecated the practice. Only a few days ago I witnessed a very nasty accident, caused entirely by the lamp bracket slipping down the fork, and coming into con- tact with the spokes. There is always a grave danger of this happening. It is difficult to attach the bracket on the tapering fork, though there are two ways which are more or less suc- cessful. A piece of wire fastened to the lamp bracket and the brake clip is ungainly, hut serviceable. If the former becomes loose the noise attracts one's attention immediately. The other method is to fix a brake clip under the lamp bracket. Neither is perfect. The better plan is to carry the lamp on its proper bracket.

div.head: TEACHING ONE TO RIDE.
div.p: TEACHING ONE TO RIDE.

For the first tinte for many years I have just been teaching a friend to ride, and it has occurred to me that a few hints on how to do it may be generally useful. First find a suit- able road for the purpose, preferably one which has a slight gradient. By beginning at the top the learner has little work to do in the way of pedalling. • The seat should be low, so low in fact that the rider can get his or her foot under the pedal when at its lowest. This gives con- fidence, there is not so far to fall if such an event happens. The saddle should be held with the right hand, and the handle bars with the left. As soon as the learner begins to under- stand matters, the grip on the handle bar should be released, and soon after if progress is being made, the hold of the saddle should be released. It should be done gently, so that the learner thinks he or she is still being held. Impress upon the learner that he or she must always turn the bicycle in the direction in which it is falling. Once this has been thoroughly learnt the Whole secret of "balance" has been acquired. After that it is merely a matter of practice. and here the position regard- ing the road gradient should be revised, i.e.. it is better to ride up a slight gradient than down one. In the former case the resistance supplies something to pedal ' against—in the latter the pedals have a tendency to run away with the feet.

div.head: DUTCH FIASCO.
div.p: A DUTCH FIASCO.
A twenty-four hours' I...liability trial, organised by the "Dutch Motor Cyclists' Society" was held in May, under the most trying conditions. The trial was divided into four 'classes :

(A) Motor cycles with sidecars. (B) Three-wheeled cycle cars. (C) Four-wheeled cycle cars with a maxi- mum cylinder camcrty of 1,100 c.c. (weight unlimited). (D) Military men. The start took place in Amsterdam, and the finish was at Utrecht; there were twenty-eight entrants, but the conditions were so bad that only seven finished file course. The story of the trial was simply rain, rain, rain, and the con- dition of the paved roads can better be imagined than described. • Indeed, the trial was practically abandoned.

div.head: RUNNING COSTS.
div.p: RUNNING COSTS.

This question is always of interest to riders of motor cycles, and I have just herd of a very fine achievement by a rider of a 1912 machine. In all he has covered 12,300 miles. The ex- penditure to the date of his letter with statistics shots that he has run 11,312 miles at the rate of .64d. per mile. In 1912 he did 4,000 miles at the cost of .66d. per mile; in 1913 a slightly greater mileage at .47d., and in 1914 rather less at .84 per mile. When it is taken into c:onsideration that this includes petrol and oil, tyres,- belts, engine, lamp sundries, spares, perrhinent fittings, and licenses, it shows what can be done. It is only fair to add, however, that this -ider is able to do quite a little to his machine u.inself. He does not find it necessary to call in an expert on every occasion.

This often means that the driver of a private car •bis to put up with all kinds of abuse on the road. Everyone has a right to the road, Init no one has permission to abuse that right. A private car driver may sound his horn as he likes, but the motor char- a-banc frequently keeps the middle of the road, When one does succeed in passing after a mile or so of trouble—the passengers are derisive. I speak from experience, bitter in the extreme. The Sheffield motorist who prosecuted such a char-a-bane driver was in the right. The defendant was fined £2. May more of us follow, this lead.

div.head: PASSENGER'S COMFORT.
div.p: THE PASSENGER'S COMFORT.

To indicate the great progress that has been piade by motor body builders in the past, the following quotation "from a passenger's point of view" in a motoring contemporary is in- teresting. It sums up in a few words what advance has been made. "Possibly one maY clear the ground a little for future workers by' briefly considering, from the passenger's point of view, the main differences in dimension he- ty.-een the car ten years ago and the car to-daY• Then the cushions of the seats were seventeen or eighteen inches from the floor, horizontal with vertical backs, answering to the standard- measurements of a dining-room chain No the car Seat has a cushion not more than 13 inches from the floor, lower at the back by some three inches,- and the seat back is lowered to an almost reclining angle, corresponding verY nearly to the• proportions of the comfortable armchair. It gives a far more easy position. particularly for long journeys, and one in which rapid acceleration and decelerations are better taken up by the human body- than they were on the old upright seat." There is still, how- ever, a long way to go te make the modern ear perfect. _ • _____

div.head: REAL SPEED.
div.p: REAL SPEED.

Motorists deprived of races on the Continent this year are taking more interest in Aniericall meetings. On May 31st, a 500 mile interna- tional race was held at the Indianapolis speed" way. The speeds maintained were remarkable. After eliminating trials had been held—each car had to do 80 miles per hour—twenty-four cars qualified. Seeing that the _average speed wa9 greater this year than has been attained before. it is surprising that there were no smashes. The track is badly banked and very great care bas to be taken in negotiating corners. The race was an exacting one from start to finish, and there was only some four minutes between the first and second winners. The time taken bY the former was 5 hours 33 minutes 55.5 seconds. This gives an average speed of 89.84 miles Per hour. As `showing the improvement that has taken place in motor cars during recent years a comparison of the records for the past four seasons is instructive. They were as follows: 1911. 74.59 miles per hour; in 1912, 78.7; in 1913, 75.92; in 1914, 82.47.

BRIDGE-STREET FATALITY.
School-Girl Knocked Down And Killed
By A Motor Car.

At the Warrington Police Station on Wednes- day afternoon Mr S. Brighouse, coroner, con- ducted an inquiry into the circumstances at- tending the death of Mary Reardon, aged ten —the daughter of Mr. John Reardon, a general labourer, of 12, Barbauld-street—who died from injuries received in an accident in Bridge- street.

div.head: Ran Right in Front of a Motor Car.
div.p: Ran Right in Front of a Motor Car.

From the evidence it appeared that the child was returning from school on Monday, after- noon, in company with a friend. When in Bridge-street they attempted to cross the road from behind a stationary lorry, and the girl Reardon ran right in front of a motor ear and was run over almost before the driver 'knew what had happened. The girl was taken to the Infirmary, but died shortly after the accident.

div.head: Car Travelling Slowly at the Time.
div.p: Car Travelling Slowly at the Time.

John 11. Kitchener, chauffeur to Mr. Thomas Butterworth, of Lytham, the owner of the car, said he was only travelling at six miles an hour. Albert Patrick, horse-driver, of 166, Welling- ton-road, spoke to witnessing the accident, which, in his opinion, was unavoidable. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," and exonerated the chauffeur from blame.

div.head: " I AM DYING."
div.p: " I AM DYING."
Labourer Complains Of Pain And
Passes Away Suddenly.

At the Warrington Police Station on Wednes- day Mr. S. Brighouse held an inquest on the body of John Atherton, aged 37, a general labourer, of 4, Side Kerfoot-street, who died suddenly on Monday. He was an employe of the United Velvet Cutters' Association at their works in Longford-street. The Association was represented by Mr. T. S. Steel, who said he 'at- tended out of respect to the Court and to give any information required, for though Atherton died in the works, there was no question that his death was not in consequence of his employ- ment.

div.head: Not Required a Doctor for Eleven Years.
div.p: Not Required a Doctor for Eleven Years.
Catherine Atherton said her husband was very healthy, and had not required medical atten- tion for eleven years. On Monday he went to work in his usual health, and returned for his dinner.

div.head: Died Before the Doctor Arrived.
div.p: Died Before the Doctor Arrived.

Samuel Parr, general labourer, 34, Longford- street, an employe of the Velvet Cutters' Asso- ciation's works, said that at 2.45 on Monday afternoon, Atherton came into the workshop and complained of a pain in his stomach. Wit- ness's father, the foreman, told him to sit down and rest, and instructed witness to do his work. Atherton went upstairs and witness followed. When deceased got into the room above he lay down on the floor, and then, rising and walking forward, exclaimed "I am dying." lie was about to fall, when witness got hold of him and laid him down on some rolls of velvet. Doctor McKee was sent for, but on his arrival Ather- ton was dead.
Dr. McKee spoke to making a posf-mortem ex- amination, and said the cause of death was fatty degeneration of the heart. It was a clear case of death from natural causes.
The jury returned a verdict in accordance with the doctor's evidence.

div.head: EXAMINER, SA,TURDAI
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SA,TURDAI
TEACHERS' WAR-TIME PAY DEMONSTRATION SCHOOL.
Committee Make Another Attempt For Better Terms.

At the Education Committee meeting on Monday night the School Management Sub- committee submitted the following resolutions they had passed : " That, from the Ist June, 1915, there be paid to each unmarried teacher (or such other person or persons as he may appoint) who is now serving in, or who may join, His Majesty's Forces, such sums as, with the total Army pay and separation allowances, if any, received from the Government, will make up an amount equal to 10s. per week less than his full salary for the time being, providing always that such sums shall not be less than the minimum sum of 10s. per week referred to in the. Council's resolution of the 6th October, 1914"; and "That Resolutions Nos. C 4219 (b), 4256, 4313 (b), and 4322 be amended accordingly." • Alderman BENNErr thought this proposal con- flicted with the resolution previous.ly passed by the committee. He was under the impression that they agreed that if any teacher went to the 'Front he should not suffer financially as a result of his patriotism. The present resolu- tion appeared to mean that instead of being en- couraged, the teacher who volunteered was fined to the extent of 10s. simply because he was braver perhaps than other teachers, and more anxious than they to do his duty to his country in_ a great emergency. _ •

- Mr: J. JARMAN pointed out that there was no mention in the resolution of whether the teacher had dependents or not. The drawback to the proposal was that, although a man might have paid nothing to the upkeep of the home, his parents were, at the expense of the rates— to which people in poorer 4ircumstances had to contribute—to receive the allowance mentioned.
The -CHAIRMAN suggested that as there seemed to he a difference of opinion on several points it would be as well to have a definite amend- ment so that they could have an expression of opinion.
Alderman BENNETT thereupon moved, and Mr. JARMAN seconded, that the resolutions be re- ferred back.
A WITHDRAWN RESOLUTION.

Mr. UrsoN said Alderman Bennett was cor- rect. A resolution was passed by that auth- ority that the salary of the teacher should be made up, that the difference between his Army allowance should be paid to him. That reso- lution was, withdrawn by the Chairman of that committee when the minutes were before the Town Council so that—he .understood—some general arrangement could be ,made, which should be applicable to all departments of the Corporation.. That was as far as they had got. He could not gather from anyone that the Town Council or any of its committees had made any such arrangements regarding pay- ment to its employes who had gone to the Front, or volunteered, and the matter was ,get- ting very serious. Some of these men had joined the forces eight, nine or ten months ago—and no definite arrangement had been made beyond 10s. or 12s. for single men, and that was all they were getting. He was fully in sympathy with what Alderman Bennett had said, and would vote for the amendment if it meant that they were going to restore the original minute, which was withdrawn by the Chairman: He certainly thought they had erred on the wrong side in the present minute; but they were taking the line of least resistance, being un- able to get the proposal through the Town Connell, so as to get the matter settled in order to give the men a clear understanding as to what the exact position was. The London Education Authority made up the difference both to single and married men, and deducted only the rate of 7s. a week from all men under commissioned rank in addition to separa- tion allowance. One hundred and forty-eight authorities in England did the same—paid the whole difference between the Government allow- ance and the salaries the teachers 'received. A large number of authorities in this neighbour- hood did this—including Lancashire, Cheshire, Manchester, Liverpool, .Bolton, Bury, Burnley, Birkenhead and Chester. Warrington came in with just a small hatidful of authorities who deducted 10s. in addition to the Chivernment allowance, so that they were not erring on the side Of extravagancp. • " Mean in tilt Extreme."

They were going rather the other way, and it did seem to him a petty thing that they should mulct these men because they had joined the forces. Every man who volunteered deserved richly from the rest of us who could not go. (Hear, hear.) He would give every- one of them a handsome pension for life. Some said that after all these men were sacrificing nothing, but "What shall a mangainin exchange for his life?" These men were risking their lives for us, and the plea of the rates was no reason why we should hold our hands from dealing equitably by them. It was mean in the extreme to say that they should receive considerably -less than if they had remained safe and comfortable at home. If Alderman. Bennett's amendment was that the original pro- posal be restored, that the difference between the Government ,allowance and the teachers salary should be made up, he ,would heartily support it. (Hear. hear.)

div.head: COUNCIL GIVEN ANOTHER CHANCE.
div.p: COUNCIL GIVEN ANOTHER CHANCE.

Canon STEVENSON thought the case had been put fairly by Mr. Upson. He supposed the Chairman felt bound to withdraw the original proposal, and the matter was referred back to the School Management Committee. That com- mittee had drawn up the present alternative resolution which, as Mr. Upson said, did not err on tile side of being too liberal. Alderman BENNETT : Canon Stevenson's reply only makes my desire, for amendment stronger. There is no reason why the committee should change its deliberate policy. I agree with all that Mr. Upson has said.
Mr. LONGLAND asked what the position would be if the amendment were carried.
The CHAIRMAN (Mr. Jolley) If carried the resolution will go back for further considera- tion.
Mr. UPSON : We could restore the original resolution at the next meeting. The CHAIRMAN: This resolution is the outcome of our attemptipg to interpret the wishes of the Council.
Councillor CHEWS : I believe there is a small committee appointed from the General Pur- poses Committee to deal with all these ques- tions.

Councillor BizoingunsT said the committee to which Councillor Chrimes referred would; if that amendment • were carried, see what the Education Committee wished. No one worth his salt would begrudge this considera- tion to the teachers.
Mr. UpsoN: Or to anyone else belonging to the Corporation.

Mr. O. WALKER: I wish it could be applidd to the private works. (Laughter.) Thirteen members voted for the amendment, which the Chairman declared carried, without going through the formality of putting "the contrary."

div.head: ATTENDANCE.
div.p: THE ATTENDANCE.

At Monday's Education Committee meeting, Mr. A. J. Jolley occupied the chair, in the absence of Councillor Roberts. There were also present Alderman A. Bennett, Councillors J. Broadhurst, J. Chrinxes, J. Dickenson, J. T. Locker, J. Pemberton, J. Wilkinson; Revs. G. C. Briggs, Father Wilson, Morley Stevenson; Mrs. Holmes, Messrs. C. Sawkins, Burgess, R. T. Fairclough, C. J. Holmes, J. Jarman, J. Long. land, C. E. Parker, E. Plinsfon, J. Upson, G. Walker, and Mr. J. Moore Murray (director).

div.p: A " SELECTED " MEMBER.

div.head: Oakwood-Avenue School To Be Completed.
div.p: Oakwood-Avenue School To Be Completed.
RELIGIOUS ASSURANCES.

The Local Government Board have sanctioned the raising of a loan to complete. the Oakwood- avenue Council School, so that the work which the war threatened to hold up will proceed. At the monthly meeting of the Education Committee on Monday night the School Man- agement Sub-committee submitted for adoption and approval a scheme for the recognition of the school as a demonstration school. They also reported that several teachers had intimated to the Director their willingneis to qualify for work in special , schools, and that the Director would confer With the teachers concerned; and That the Board of Education had approved the committee's proposals for the furnishing of the" school.

div.head: SCHEME FOR DEMONSTRATION SCHOOL.
div.p: THE SCHEME FOR DEMONSTRATION SCHOOL.
The following is the scheme for the recogni- tion of the school as a demonstration school :

I.—The managers of the school shall be the members of the School Management Sub-com- mittee for the time being, and they shall retain all the powers of managers in accordance with the Education Acts and the Code for the time being. 2.—ln appointing teachers, the managers shall consult with the Principal of the Training Col- lege,' and shall have regard to the special fitness of candidates for appointment in this type of school.

3.—The salaries to be paid to the teachers shall be in aqcordance with the Education Cora- mittee'l4 scale of salaries for teachers in force for • the time being. 4.—The number of members of the staff and the equipment shall *be the same as for other schools of similar size in the borough. s.—There shall be formed an Advisory Board, consisting of six rePreselitatives of the staff of the Warrington Training College, six repre- sentatives of the staff of the school, together with the head teacher of each department, the Director of Education and inspector, which shall decide upon the steps to be taken for the purpose of illustrating the most ap- prcived and successful methods of school organisation, discipline and instruction. 6:—The Advisory Board shall not have power to incur any expense. 7.—The Advisory Board shall keep records of their proceedings, which shall be oPen to the inspection of the managers, and no reports of any work or experiments conducted in the school shall be published without the previous consent of the Education \Committee. 8.---No methods of school organisation, disci- pline, and instruction shall be applied in the school which are not capable of application in schools of similar size in the borough. 9.—The school shall not be used as a practising school for the instruction of teachers in teach- ing, but may be used by teachers in training for the purpose of observition. 10.—The Education Committee shall have the right at any time to determine this arrange- ment.
MR. JARMAN ASKS FOR INFORMATION.

Mr. JARMAN pointed out that many new prin- ciples seemed to be involved in the scheme. Up to no they had acknowledged that outside men should also be admitted as school managers. Then the Prineipal of the Training College was to be consulted as to the appointment of the teachers regarding their fitness for the special work required. That looked like giving a veto to the Training College. . There might be no difficulty so long as Canon Stevenson or some- one equally broadminded was .principal. The time might come, however, when that would not apply. 'Was there a possibility that the Ad- visory :Board would arrange for religious train- ing, in which CaSe Nonconformists might be barred from an iippointment? Councillor BROADHURST expressed his sorrow that Mr. Jarman had introduced. the religious question. The Nonconformists were very well represented indeed on that committee and on the School Management Committee. If they took gentlemen like Mr. Upson—he was certain that, with his ability, he was quite able to take tare of the Nonconformists-- Mr. liesox : I am not the Noncenformists' 'representative; I am the teachers' representa- tive.

Councillor 'BROADHURST : "hear, hear." (Laughter.). They were not there to represent any class of people, but to do their duty by the education of the town. He would like to know whether making this into a demonstration school would mean any increase in the rates. Canoll STEVENSON ! No, not at all.

div.head: NO ECCLESIASTICAL ZEPPELINS.
div.p: NO ECCLESIASTICAL ZEPPELINS.

Replying to Mr. Jarman, Canon STEVENSON said he appreciated the friendly tone of that gentleman's criticism, and understood his fears lest .any Council school should be used in any way which was not in accordance with views for which the Council stood; but he could assure Mr. Jarman that there was no intention whatever to .send up an ecclesiastical Zeppelin to drop bombs on Oak- wood-avenue School. (Laughter.) Such an action he would consider most dishonourable, and he would not lend himself to any scheme of that kind. Mr. Jarman referred to the sug- gestion that the school managers were to be the members of the School Management Sub-com- mittee for the time being. The alternative would be to do as in other Council Schools and appoint six or more "managers from different parts of the town. Their idea had been to con- sider the special character of this school, and it was thought the committee contained certain members who were more cognisant of educa- tional detail than a body of gentlemen drawn at random ,from the town. This was not, how- ever, an essential portion of ,the scheme. and if the committee would rather they might select according to the existing. method. He ventured to think the new suggestion was best for the new scheme.

div.head: Wicked Principal of the Future.
div.p: The Wicked Principal of the Future.

Then Mr. Jarman drew attention to the pro- -131011 that in appointing teachers the manhgers shall consult with the Principal of the Train- ing .College. He (the speaker) thanked Mr. Jar- man for his kindly reference to him; but Mr. Jarman feared that some future Principal of the Training College might lay hands. upon those appointments in the interest of some par- ticular body—notably, of course, of the Church. There was no intention of giving the Training College a veto. Nothing had been thought, or proposed, that would for a moment give' the Principal, as Principal, a voice in Making the appointment; but when the management made the appointment they would consult with him in order to get his opinion as to the special fit- ness of candidates for this type of school. He did not think the religious question would ever enter into the matter at all. His own plan for making his voice felt in the appointments in Council Schools—a plan he had always pursued —was never to find out what the religious opinions of the applicants were. (Hear, hear.) Sometimes .knowledge as to those religious opinions came out by accident, but he tried to keep that kind of knowledge in the dark, and lie did not think the difficulty could possibly arise. As to the Advisory Board, the object was simply to allow the parties named to discuss the best methods'of organisation, discipline and in- struction. It did not touch religious teaching in the school in any way—that would • be out- side their province—but merely the teaching of secular subjects. Ho appreciated Mr. Jarman's point of view and in his. place would probably have made the same speech; but he could assure them there was not the slightest intention of introducing the religious question or upsetting the character of the Council School as such. He thought that was sufficiently guarded against by clause 10 in the scheme, which the Education Committee power "to determine" at any time, so that if the wicked Principal of the future— (laughter)—introduced any guile into this matter he could be Very quickly stopped. Warrington Again a Pioneer.

Warrington was one of the first 'towns to do this voluntarily, and he would be sorry if it did not go forward. It would be a great benefit to the Training College, and he thanked Alderman Bennett for having called attention to the bene- fit the College had been to the town. Mr. Jar- man might sleep safely in his bed—in his edu- cational bed he meant—(laughter)—and the Training College would be grateful for their kindness.
The BoLorao was agreed to unanimouzly.

div.head: WIN THE COVETED HONOUR.
div.p: WIN THE COVETED HONOUR.

Among the names published in a supplement to the "London Gazette" on Tuesday night in a despatch from Field-Marshal Sir• John French bringing to the notice of the Secretary for War those whom he recommended for gal- lant and distinguished service in the field, in accordance with the last paragraph of his despatch of April sth last, were the following: 4th BATTALION SOUTH LANCASHIRE - REGIMENT. •Fairclough, Lieutenant-Colonel Crosfield,•Major G. R.

It will be. noted that the honour dates so far back as April, so that the "gallant and dis- tinguished services" do not include what these brave sons of Warrington did last Wednesday. We understand that on that great day the Colonel and the Major led half a battalion each in the charge, and that their example was an inspiration at the Supreme moment in their history. Some hints of this are contained in the letters that have since come from the Front.
COLONEL B. FAIRCLOUGIE Mentioned in Despatches.

div.head: COLONEL FAIRCLOUGH:
div.p: COLONEL FAIRCLOUGH:

Lieutenant-Colonel Brereton Fair°lough, who commands our brave 4th Battalion of the South Lancashires, is the eldest son of Mr. Richard T. Fairclough Barryfield, Latchford. He is 45 years of age, having been born in 1870 —the ,year of the last great German war. Educated .privately and at the Grammar School,- he served an apprenticeship to engin- eering at Dallam Forge, with a view to Under- taking the management of the corn mills of Messrs. James Fairclough. and Sons, Limited, Howley and Bank Quay. He is a director of the firm, general manager, and head of the chemical and engineering departments.

11, has always been fond of drill and physi- cal culture and naturally evinced a great interest- in the Volunteers, which he joined in 1893. The following is his record in the Volunteers and their successors, the Terri- torials :

Appointed. Second-Lieutenant, 16th December, 1893; Lieutenant, 4th May, 1895; Captain, 13th January; 1897; Major, 24th October, 1893; Lieutenant-Colonel, 17th April, 1912. In May, 1912, he succeeded his cousin, Lieutenant-Colonel J. .Dutton Fairclough, as commander of the Battalion.
Colonel Fairelough served in the Boer War as a Volunteer.

Eight years ago to-day he married Miss Ethel Roberts, (laughter of Councillor Henry Roberts, who, with her two children, is staying at "Kingsley," during Colonel\ Fairclough's ab- sence at the war. Mrs. Fairclough is vice- president of -a committee taking a keen intere4 in the welfare of the women-folk of her hus- band's battalion. - '

div.head: " HILL GO" HERO.
div.p: " HILL GO" HERO.
Buried At Thelwall With Full Honours.

The beautifully situated churchyard at Thelwall was the scene on Tuesday afternoon of an impressive military funeral. The mortal remains of Private Arthur Jenkins, of the Ist Cheshire Regiment, who was wounded in action at " Hill 60" and died in Thelwall Heys Hospital, were interred with full honours in the presence of a good number of people anxious to pay a last tribute to self-sacrificing gallantry. The deceased soldier was a Liver_ pool man, and there were a number of rela- titreis in attendance at the graveside. The ser-. vice was conducted by the Rev. Father Talton, of the Murat of Our Lady, Latchford. The late Private' Jenkins, who was 34 years of age and unmarried, was, at the time he .received his wound, attached to the, company of the Ist Cheshire Regiment, commanded by Captain T. L. Frost. had been in the Thel- wall Hospital about three weeks, and won the admiration of all with whom he came into contact by the ,patient fortitude with which he bore sufferings which were recognised to have but one possible ending. The flag-draped coffin was surmounted by some beautiful floral emblems, mostly in red, White and blue. These tributes included a large cross from the staff 4t the hosiiital and others from the committee and the Working Men's Committee. ; The family mourners were followed in the proces- sion to the grave by the Hon. HouSekeeper of the Hospital (Mrs. F. A. Frost) and Mr. Frost; members of the nursing staff, and half-a-dozen comrades from the same ward.

MAJOR GEORGE .CROSFIELD Mentioned in Despatches.

div.head: MAJOR CROSFIELD.
div.p: MAJOR CROSFIELD.

Major George Rowlandson Crosfield, third son of the late Mr. John Crosfield, of Walton Lea, ivas born in 1877 and is 38 years of age. He was educated at Harrow and at Lausanne. At the outbreak of the war he was one of the directors of the firm of Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons, Limited, and was responsible for the technical side of the business.

Major Crosfield—or Captain Crosfield; as he is mostly styled, because he holds the rank of Honorary Captain in the Regular Army, a reward, along with medal and five clasps, for his services during the Boer War—was in com- mand of the Manchester _Squadron of Yeo- manry in South Africa, was invalided home through enteric, and, on recovering, again went out as Officer Commanding a squadron of the 3rd Contingent of Yeomanry. His career in the local Volunteer and Terri- torial Battalion is:— . • .

Appointed Second-Lieutenant, Bth July, 1896; Lieutenant, 2nd July, 1898; •Captain, 31st January, 1900; Major, Ist September, 1912. Major Crosfield is one of the most active Promoters in the country of the National Ser- vice.-League, and his natural aptitude for mili- tary affairs had. even before the war began, made hint a personage of national. importanee. Ile is fond of hunting-, being a fearless rider. He encourages sport and recreation of all kinds, lie was the mainstay of the many social undertakings a Crostield's and in the town—bowling, ambulance, amateur theatricals and • the like having in him a staunch friend. No wonder he is a general favourite. He is a bachelor. •

div.head: FIRST LOCAL MUNITION VOLUNTEER.
div.p: FIRST LOCAL MUNITION VOLUNTEER.
" The Examiner "' Orford
Correspondent.

The first to volunteer at Warrington Town Mill on Thursday for munition _service was Mr. J. (;ibson, of Orford, who besides being engaged at the Vulcan -Foundry, is the Orford corre- spondent for " The Examiner." The certifi- cate, of which he is naturally very proud, is as follows:
G.R. No. 1.
This is to certify that

div.p: JOHN GIBSON
has enrolled as a war munition volunteer on the service of King and country. .
D. LLOYD GEORGE.

div.head: BRONZE CROSS WARRUORS.
div.p: BRONZE CROSS WARRUORS.
Invasion Of Halton By Church Of England Men's Society.

Scarcely had this salient on the Mersey re- covered from its investment by over one hun- dred Sunday school teachers on June sth, than another attack, 'admirably planned and excel- lently executed, took place on Saturday, June 19th. From North, East and West delegates and members of that inner circle of the Church Militant, to wit, the Church of Eng- land's Men's Society, converged on haughty Halton.

The objective was approached in true mili- tary style from varying points of the compass: some detrained at Norton or Halton _railway stations, .others cycled, others again in that ancient aircraft called the Widnes Transporter Bridge, crossed the river and after executing a flanking movement, gained access via Runcorn. The Parish Church was finally entered. by the combined forces of bronze-cross warriors-, and a religious service conducted by the Vicar, heartily rendered. In the course of an impres- sive address, reference was made to members of the C.E.M.S. as men not only occupied upon laying the foundation and superstructure of character, but also incessantly engaged on de- fending both from the assaults of evil, just as the followers of Ezra and Nehemiah in times back laboured with trowel in one haml and weapon in the other, to build again the walls of Zion.

div.head: Appointment of Officers.
div.p: Appointment of Officers.

Tea followed on the Castle :Rill, after which that important business usually conducted at the annual meeting of a Federation, received the attention of all present. The Rev. C. E. Greeitham, vicar of Halton, succeeds Mr. Pier- son as president of the Warrington Federation; Mr. Tegg, secretary of a Widnes Branch, replaces Mr. G. C. Jansway, the latter having been Federation Secvetary since its inception, and only reluctantly retiring so as to put into execution his proffer of services to help. make munitions of war.

Other appointments and matters of peculiar interest to those assembled having been disposed of, various votes of thanks were offered and responded to, after which began a specially con- ducted tour of inspection of the vicinity, in- cluding the Castle, far-famed- , library, and glorious panorama of the surrounding country. As sunset gave place to dusk small groups of enthusiasts might be seen wending towards home, , still eagerly 'discussing matters of supreme interest to them, and strengthened in. the belief that the C.E.M.S. is being used and has untold possibilities for further use in bi.oadening and deepening the moral and spiritual forces that count in a nation's life.

div.head: LORD DERBY WAR HOSPITAL.
div.p: LORD DERBY WAR HOSPITAL.
Accommodation For 2,500
Wounded.
NEW USE FOR ASYLUM.
" The Daily Dispatch " representative in- vited to inspect the Lord Derby War Hospital by which' Winwick Asylum is now known, writes:— .

Lancashire, which has done everything oil the grand scale in this war from the finding of men to the .finding of money, has achieved another triumph of organisation. The great asylum at Winwick, belonging to the Lancashire County Council, has been con- verted into a war hospital capable of accom- modating over 2.500 men. It is 'thus the biggest .fully-equipped military hospital in the kingdom, and forms an important part of a War Office scheme for dealing in the most ex- peditious manner with the great numbers of wounded who may be expected to arrive in Eng- land as our offensive campaign progresses.

The institution will practically perform the functions of a base hospital. Men will be received in large- detachments, and as speedily as possible the hospital will be cleared by dis- tributing the patients among auxiliary and convalescent institutions. . _

The One tremendous thing Which such a visit does is to give a stay-at-home person a glimpse of the renlities of the war. No description ever penned can compete with what one sees, and that is perhaps why the sight of Wounded men is the most powerful recruiting stimulus that exists.

This hospital and its organisation are upon .scale sufficiently imposing to bring home vividly the meaning of our casualty lists. A ,walk through the wards in the ten blocks Of buildings, all connected by covered corri- dors, gives an apparently endless vista of beds. not once to be filled, but again and again—bow often the future alone can tell. it is only five weeks since the institution was taken over, and already there have been a thousand men in at one time. The number is now' about GM.. They include men from all localities, with a nuntber of Canadians and Australians.

div.head: In Constant Readiness.
div.p: In Constant Readiness.

Inside the buildings everything is kept in a state of constant readiness for emergency. Organisation is carried out to the last detail. There are three operating theatres, each with adjacent rooms for surgeons and anresthetics, and each fitted with X-ray apparatus. If at any time the accommodation in the wards should be insufficient for the needs of the moment there are large day rooms which could at once be converted into wards. This elaAticity accomtnodation is one of the valuable things gained in using such an institution as a war 'hospital. -The staff of resident. medical men numbers twenty-one, and the additional services of six doctors in War- rington are available if .ecintred. All the nurses have had special .training, and some have been drafted from Netley. The community is practically self-contained. Fruit and vegetables are grown in the grounds, ,and there is upon the premises a staff of work- men which includes bootmakers and repairers, tailors, -upholsterers, and blacksmiths. There is a laundry capable of dealing with about 60,000 articles a week; electricity for light and power is generated; and the institution has its own water supply puzuped from two deep wells. A railway siding runs to,the'very doors, and it was hoped to be able by this means to unload ambulance trains direct. This, however, has been found impracticable. Comforts Wanted. •

With all these advantages there are a few things lacking—comforts for the men. Th, are not provided by the War Office, and the hospital nrtist rely upon voluntary effort to obtain them. A ladies' committee is being formed in Warrington to help in this way, and an urgent appeal is made to the public. • The wounded soldiers are short 9ti writing paper, stamped postcards and pencils, and they are waiting with longing for pipes, tobacco and cigarettes. These are the things they are tacst ianxious for, though many others are wanted, such as walking sticks, razors, bed jackets, bed socks, and dressing gowns, large slippers, An interesting feature of the management is that though the hospital is qiader. direct War Office control and -regulations, there is an emergency committee composed or the follow- ing members of the County Council, who were on the Winwick Asylum Visiting C-mimittee: Aldermen S. S. Brown (Wigan), J. 'l'. Teggar (Liverpool), T. C. Abbott (Hale), R. L. Burns (Liverpool), E. H. Giles (Liverpool), James Evans (Warrington), and County Councillor J. Mercer (Halewood). The administrator is Lieutenant-Colonel Alexander Simpson, and the deputy adminis- trator Major F. Al. Rodgers.

div.head: Convalescents at Cricket.
div.p: Convalescents at Cricket.

On Wednesday afternoon a cricket team froth Newton-le-Willows, including J. T. Tyldesley and the Brothers Sharp, played a team made up Of wounded soldiers and members of the hospital staff on the excellent playing pitch in the hospital grounds. A New Zealander, in sombrero :and red 'kerchief, zept wicket smartly, and a wounded soldier wit'a a splendid catch at long-on was responsible for putting an end to Tyldesley's innings.

div.head: Match.
div.p: The Match.

An interesting cricket match was played on Wednesday for the 'amusement of the wounded soldiers in the Lord Derby War Hospital. Among those who took part were Jack Sharp, Bert Sharp, and J. T. Tyldesley, the first-named making 77 runs. The teams, comprising twelve players, were Newton-le-Willows and the sol- diers and doctors representing the Lord Derby War Hospital. Scores:—

Newtonlle-Willows : J. Sharp c Smith b Greener 77, H. nylands b Smith 0, J. T. Tyldes- ley c Spicer b Smith -34, B. Sharp b Anderson 13, G. B. Leigh b Anderson 2, J. H. Alderson b Anderson 9; C: Porter 1) Smith 19, F. Flint b Smith 0, IL Walton c Dawson b Smith 7, C. Prescott not out 3, T. Wilkinson mit out 2, extras 8; total (for 9). 171. Lord Derby Hospital : R. Waller e and b Rylands 7, llandforth b Sharp 13, (1. Dawson b ltylands 0, Private Spicer c Sharp b Tyldesley 11, Aliijor Nash b Sharp 5, Smith c Leigh 1) Bylands 0, Private Greener c Leigh b Hylands 2, Private Atkinson b Tyldesley 4, Private Ker- mode not 27, Dr. Anderson b Tyldesley 29, Dr. Twort c Porter b Tyldesley 1, Stevenson b Alder- son 1, extras 8; total (for 11), 108. MALE CHOIR ENTERTAINMENT..

Tho patients of the Lord Derby War hospital were entertained on Sunday afternoon hy the Warrington Male Choral Union, Madame Sara. Sileock, Mr. Bradford Barton, and Mr. A. PeArce. There was a large, enthusiastic and attentive. 'audience. Encores were frequently given, but the time would not • allow of a re- sponse being given in all eases.. - •'
