div.head: Orford Leather Worker Fatally I n jured.
div.p: Orford Leather Worker Fatally I n jured.

At the Warrington Coroner's Court on Wed- nesday afternoon Mr. Coroner Brighouse cell" ducted an inquiry into the circumstances attending the death of Michael Dolan, aged 43, •a belly-roller in the employ of the Orford Tannery Company, who died. in the InfirmarY on Tuesday morning as the result of injurieg received whilst following his employment Oil Friday, May 214.—Mr. T. S. Steel appeared for the relatives and Mr. IL J. Westbrook for the deceased's employers. Thirty-three Years in the Tannery. Evidence of identification was given by the widow, Katliarine Dolan, of Sandy-lane Cot- tage, Orford, who added that she had visited her husband itt the Infirmary daily from the accident to the time of his death, but he never explained to her how he received his injuries. Be had been employed at the •Orford Tannery for thirty-three years. How the Accident Happened. Stephen Dolan, brother of the deceased, alsa employed as a belly-roller at the tannery and . who lives at 29, Melville-street, Warringtol. deposed that at about 5.10 in the evening of Friday, May 21st, the deceased was in the machine-room assisting to put a driving-belt en to the polishing machine. He had put the belt on the machine and was endeavouring to get it on to the pulley-wheel of the main driving shaft, When witness, who was helping, had occasion to turn round. to attend to some- thing else. Witness then heard a scream, and, turning round, saw his brother held fast in the shafting. Witness at once ran and got the engine stopped. In answer to the Coroner, the witness said that a forked rod was provided for the pur- pose of putting belts on to the pulley-wheeig, but the men rarely used them, and it -wag usual to hitch the belts on whilst the shaft was revolving, as it was easier to do so than it was when the pulley-wheel was stationary. Did it of His Own Accord. Replying to questions by Mr. Westbrook, witn*ss said that the machine at which the accident happened had been out of use for about six. weeks. tieing short of raw material front the polishing department and so as not to waste time or money, his brother `f did a bit of polishing on his own, on the old system vogue before, owing to so many men having gone from the Tannery to the Front, the depart- ment was reorganised and girl labour utilised for the particular work in question• His brother nnhooked the driving belt, which had been. hung up and out of use, and started the machine, and whilst he was. getting the belt on to the driving pulley the accident occurred. His brother did not attempt to put the belt on in obedience to instructions. front • anybody, but did it of his own accord, 'without being told.

" Fast in the Shafting." .loh itSkelhorne, a foreman at the Tannery'. living at New Douse Cottages, Orford, spoke to hearing the deceased scream and to seeing ltilo " fast in the shafting." The - deceased caned out "'Chuck' the belt off !" and witness ran tu the main driving belt and knocked it oil, dint': causing the machine to stop. The deceased not told to put the belt on to the pulleY• - was really zeal on his part—a desire to get his work done—that led to the accident. Answering the Coroner. the witness said that it was handier, quicker and easier for the Ine,ll to put the 'belt on to the pulleys with their hands, instead of using the implements Pm" vided. Deceased was a good workman—one of the best.

Mr. Westbrook: What he was doing was heir tog himself to More work, in order to get more pay ? Witness: Yes, sir. No Negligence on the Part of the Firm. Mr. Brothers, the local Factory Act inspector, gave it as his opinion that there had been n° negligence on the part of the firm, whos° reputation was excellent. In summing up, the Coroner said he had learned that the firm had since the accident " boxed off "_ all the shafting and were doing all that suggested itself to them or to 11:M; Inspector to prevent a recurrence of this sa" affair. The jury returned a verdict of " Accidentar, • death," and attached no blame to anyone, a" Mr. Westbrook. expressed the firm's sympatbY with the relatives of the deceased.

div.head: ABSENT WORKMAN. •
div.p: ABSENT WORKMAN. •
A, Mill Stopped Through Lateness Ailil Drink.

At Tuesday's Borough Police Court, before' Councillor H. Roberts (in the ChM!) 311;1. Messrs. C. Jackson Holmes and J. ilyLe` Young, .James Burrows, of 32, Battersby-lane, War.; rmgton, appeared at the instance of .1": employers, who claimed from him it 10S. 'f°l having absented himself without leave, froal his work.

Began Quarrelling. Mr. T. S. Steel, solicitor, of Warringtofl—in. structed by Messrs. H. Greenall and Co. prosecuted. Defendant, he said, was a ball' furnaceman in the scrap forge. He should lifo'n attended work early in the evening of Mondal, June 14th, but did not arrive until seven o'clock in the evening. He was then under till influence of drink, and at once began to quarre, with some of his workmates over the supPlY,_% fuel. Other men were depending upon Ili work, and owing to his late arrival the 11% did not start working until 7 o'clock—and the only (lid so for about an hour. The loss to the: firm on this particular night was £4.; and estimating the loss they had nqt taken account any question of profit, but sine,: charged the minimum cost. div.head: STUDY OF THE CHILD.
div.p: STUDY OF THE CHILD.
Discussed At Orford Hail Prize-Day.
A UNIQUE INSTITUTION.

I wish this study of children was a little clearer in the minds of all of us—as to how far we should go, and what we should do. If we are going to be teachers at all we must be constantly observing the children in our care.

So spoke Mr. J. H. Ward, divisional inspector of schools, at Orford Hall on Saturday after- Moon. The occasion was the annual distribu- tion of prizes, and an excellent attendance in- cluded the Rev. Canon Morley Stevenson (prin- cipal) who presided, the Rev. W. Hendy Cock (vice-principal), . the Venerable Archdeacon Spooner, Mr. Lane Scott (of the College Council and Manchester Education Committee), Pro- ,t.essor Campagnac (Dean of the Faculty of Arts tor Liverpool University), the Rev. W. Thomp- son Derry, the Rev. G. Vale Owen (lecturer), Mr. W. Mason (master of method), and Dr. Bowden (medical officer).

div.head: "YEAR OF PEACEFUL STUDY."
div.p: "YEAR OF PEACEFUL STUDY."

Canon Stevenson,. having extended a hearty welcome to all the friends and past students Present, stated that the college had now been in existence a Sufficiently long time to have Passed what they might call the experimental stage,' and to enable one to say whether the experiment had been successful. As far as his own judgment went, it was. They found them- selves able to ask teachers who had spent some time .in the profession to retire froM active teaching for a year of peaceful study and quiet repose--(laughter)—which was of great physi- cal benefit, affording a change to work of a less trying character; of intellectual benefit, giving time for further study; and of professional benefit, enabling the students to, see 'other schools. It was for the benefit of the highest part of their being, as well. lie never had be- lieved that it Was a good thing to take a teacher and plunge her into the ordinary college, in the middle of her teaching course; but thought that beiiig able to have—as they had in that college alone—a year Mapped out for its own syllabus and examination, the ordinary students being .occupied on their own work with the same end in .view, had proved a very satisfactory ex- periment indeed, lie was glad to say that their numbers had this year increased. The work last • year, shown in the results of the final ex- Istmination, had been very gratifying and quite %(,,tkelnal to expectations. The inspectors, also, had e'x.przery Pleased, and he could not sufficiently suell 8 nis gratitude to those who had given cord. 'Re lal, help in the work of the college. finey .11! to mention that one of the students— 'to th rippin—had gained an essay prize open Th•e Whole rift county, the subject being -ve • That was ,an honour which they ry deeply' appreciated. (Applause.)

EXPERT VERY CHEERFUL. Mr. Ward—having been -introduced by the Chairman as an enthusiast in education who .had an intimate knowledge of all its branches, .?nd having had a hearty reception—congratu- 'ated the committee upon the success of the .'q•ege. • The college, he said, was unique, and _Possessed for the Board of Education a-- special interest; he was very glad to know that the venture promised to be perhaps even more suc- cessful in the future than in the past and Pl:e- -t:Nit It required, and must require, a con- siderable force of character to resolve to give -up a year Of " life " and not only of wage- earning (which must be considere(l) but also of work. However, the students no doubt desired to increase their qualifications with a 'view to earning higher salaries. When he thought of the possibility of this respite, he felt very cheerful about the whole teaching pro- 'fession. Indeed, they were to be envied very intich. People ' engagOd in education in Ainerica had already found the value of "Periodical rests, not for the -purpose of holiday, -)ut for the purpose of study, and that insti- tution some of his number had tried to•intro- Auee into the Board of Education—so far in *vain! (Laughter.)

Professional Sympathy. nut they had this year's holiday, and so far he. could judge it was taken at the right time When they were not 'so much overbored by teaching as to lose the enthusiasm and the benefit. The year was one of great happi- uegs and joy. They were not kept at the grind- stone too much, although working hard. More- Over they had the opportunity of getting sym- "thY and encouragement from other teachers, *tltl that they very much needed. He did find that teachers throughout the country and towns were remarkably aloof from other teachers; and (11;1y the other week had seen a head master '!vilia had never seen inside another schOol durL lug his career! Now they could compare notes, 4!lid get the very satisfactory feeling that these 11,1seouragements, had come to Other people in , same position. Then if they studied there they also gained a proper appreciation of cur- rent ideas in education. They would go back to the schools better able to grasp and understand current discussion that they heard and read 'lbout; and as a whole that side of education Was not thought enough about. even in the ghe.„4?ols. Even the language of educational " i"00 would mean more to them than ever Kiof. to °lnre, and the suggestions ,would be valuable 'e teachers when they understood them._-' - There was no need for him to speak at length :).4.the confidence thus gained, or upon the in- -reased Power of understanding children. ." Comprehension of Ideals. - o°llo result of the year's work should be a curer comprehension of the ideals that. they ;111e no doubt with a view to preserving. It 4ts soruetimes a fashion, especially with. the (iter'nlatter-Of-fact person,. to decry the train- tr received in the colleges—and he thought. tilere were a good many people who expected .t;le visible results of the training to show tirtaselves at nine o'clock on the first morning eY 'went back to school. (Laughter.) They d not But they were there all the same; cl sometimes twenty years after one could see - Plainly the college mark upon them by their

attitude towards their classes and their lessons. At the same time he would advise them not to apply in school what they had learnt In college. It took the form occasionally of special method which was supposed to be final. _Let them not be pedantic (that was advice needed by inspectors as much as teace-ers)—(laughter) —but keep in mind that there were very many ways of approaching the child. When they were face to' face with lessons in class they would have to depend not so much upon verbal advice as upon principles by which they could test any suggestion that was made; they would learn more and more to rely upon themselves.

div.head: Self-Educated Children.
div.p: Self-Educated Children.

The children should be encouraged as far as possible to educate themselves. There were very few to whom it was given to take these studies scientifically—and give them abroad; but all could give themselves that intuitive : knowledge which wes the mark of good teach- ing. It was only constant observation which could give them that.; and very remarkable dis- coveries could be made in a comparatively short time. During the last twenty years, for instance, they had discovered that the child of seven could draw other things beside straight lines, and later on curves—(laughter)--and talk sensibly, and act. He hoped they would make these discoveries. Lastly, when they went back to the schools there were some people who were impatient because "we never have any rest in education." Well, there was some ground for the complaint, and it was not fair to expect a teacher always to be "at it." But he would remind those who made the remark that they had been passing through really revolutionary times; and if they compared the changes that had taken place—not only in teaching but in all branches of society—they would not be discouraged by the comparison. He would not beg the question as to whether it was for better or worse. -What were they to do in the days of all these changes? The only thing was carefully to examine them, find recognise that what might be excellent at ' one time might be very displaced at another time. They must be not unwilling to reconsider their methods, for methods did legitimately de- velop. But they must not run after every new plan. He wished them all success'; that in the teaching of classes and in the understanding of children they might find less and less strain, more and more power. (Hearty applause.)

div.p: ;.,. Is ISTT EVIS -
Y IVI IVI
Watering of Gardens..—By order of the Lymm Urban District Council, the public are warned not to use town water for garden purposes. By so doing they will be prosecuted.

Liberals and Sir Arthur Crosfield..--On behalf of the Lymm Liberal Association, Mr.. Reginald Barker (the secretary) has sent a sincere letter of congratulation to Sir Arthur H.. Crosfield on the great honour conferred by His Majesty.

Private James Gilberts.—Private James Gil- berts, of the Warrington Territorials, who lives at Pierpoint-street, Warrington, and has just been wounded at the Front, is .brother-in-law to Mrs. G. Rixon, Mrs._ S. Owens and. Private Henry Cadman, all of Lymm.

Successful Cookery And Dressmaking,—The results, just issued, of the cookery and. dress- making examinations in connection with the Lancashire and Cheshire Institute, show that all the Lymm evening students have passed success fully, both in the practical and theoretical branches. The ladies responsible for the students' training were, respectively, Miss Harrison and Miss Chappel—who, along with their pupils, are to be heartily congratulated.

Death of Mr. J. Wright.—We regret to record the death of Mr. James Wright, of Oxhays Farm, Lymm—which sad event took place early on Saturday morning, at his residence, from heart trouble and bronchitis. The deceased gentleman was 75 years of age. The funeral took place at the Parish Church on Tuesday afternoon, the Rector officiating. Mr. Wright was a native of High Legh, had lived in the district all his life, and was a farmer. He leaves a widow, four sons and three daughters to mourn their loss.

Lymm Youth Injured At Stockton Heath.— At about a quarter past five on Tuesday morn- ing, Mr. H. Jones. of Newfields, met with a nasty accident at Stockton Heath. We under- stand that he was proceeding with his horse along the towing-path of the Bridgewater Canal when ,the animal turned back towards the stable, jamming Jones against the wall and kicking 'him violently on the jaw. On arrival home the man visited Dr. De Jong, who in- formed him that his jawbone had been broken, whilst his face was also cut; so that it was necessary for him to have stitches put in. Happily he is progressing favourably.

Rev. Penaliggon at Littlemoor.—The Rev. J. Arthur PeuAiggon—late of Lymm and Buck- low Hill—entered on Sunday upon his pastorate of Liftlemoor Congregational Church, and "nothing could have exceeded the warmth" of his welcome at all services. Large congrega- tions. assembled. On Tuesday evening the deacons and deaconesses arranged an "at home" in the schoolroom, and gave their new minister and his wife a most hearty and cordial reception in the midst of a dis- tinguished assembly. The floor of the large and beautiful schoolroom was laid out in drawing- room style, the tables being decorated with flowers. Amongst the speakers was Mrs. George 011erenshaw, of Mere Hall, Knutsford. In the course of his reply, Mr. Penaliggon said the supreme need of this moment, when our great Empire was being tried and tested as by fire. was the need of able leadership. The nation needed to have at it.; head men who were inspired by noble ideals. This was the supreme opportunity of the church. Shortly there is to be held a public recention—in which Mr. Penaliggor's brother ministers of the town will doubtless join. •

div.head: BUSY OLUNTEERS.
div.p: BUSY OLUNTEERS.
Big Efforts For Recruiting In The
Districts.

The Lymm detachment of the Cheshire-Volun- teer Regiment is as busy as ever. On Tuesday evening, after shooting practice, the platoon fell in at the Drill Hall, and marched, via Rush Green and Sandy-lane, to Heatley, accompanied by the •Heatley Scouts' Bugle Band. Here they held a meeting for the Purpose of forming an Oughtrington platoon. - The Rector (the Rev. G. S. Tudor-Evans) opened with a short speech, in which he illus- trated the aims and objects of the movement. Captain G. Williamson also spoke. A rousing address was then delivered by Lieutenant Thomson—who in peace times is a well-known political speaker, and is now inva- lided home from the Front. The Lieutenant narrated many of his recent experiences with striking effect.
The Customary drills have also taken place
To-day's Programme.

This afternoon, after parading at the Drill Hail at 2.45, the detachment will proceed to Broomedge—t,kere to meet the Altrincham Bat- talion. Their will then march round by Booth's Hill to Lymm Cross, thence .to Heatley and back through OUghtrington. Uniform will be worn as usual: •

div.head: OVERWORK AND WORRY DRIVE • A HARD BARGAIN.
div.p: OVERWORK AND WORRY DRIVE • A HARD BARGAIN.

It doesn't pay to defy nature's laws. We all need peace of mind, rest, outdoor exercise and eight hours sleep to keep well. , We must not overeat, nor drink much, unless it be milk or water. They are both good and should be freely used.

Anything bad leads to trouble. Bad habits are no exception. Careless living and overeat- ing are among the worst—they help load the blood with Uric Acid poisons. The kidneys act as safety valves, filtering the blood and Passing off the poisons, but they are bound to weaken under any long continued strain, and once they falter, you feel dull, 'tired and nervous. Your back aches, you lose weight, you have head- aches, dizzy spells and urinary disorders.

The first thing to do is to get back to simple, sensible ,habits. Eat less, sleep more and be careful what you drink. But you must also help the weakened kidneys. div.head: COI ACILLOB ( AA-PEI[I. . AND BELGIANS..
div.p: COI ACILLOB ( AA-PEI[I. . AND BELGIANS..
To the Editor of "The Examiner."
Sir,—Mr. Hendrickx's personal. abuse will not deter me from doing what I consider my duty in a public manner.
Hiding or evading the truth will not help us to eliminate the evil.
Possibly the following extracts will, convince any fair-minded person, and if my public utterance will in the slightest degree reduce the abuse in drinking, I shall be only too happy.
Englishmen and Englishwomen and also the Colonies are doing their duty to the Belgian refugees, and all we ask .is for them to show an appriciation of the same. - C. E. COWPER;
The Chestnuts, LymTn. The Extracts.

The extracts to 'which Councillor Cowper. refers are as 'follows (it will be noticed they refer to West London) : No fewer than six Belgians, none of whom was more than 34 years of age, were brought up at the West London Police Court to-day on charges of drunkenness outside the Refugee Camp at Earl's, Court.

The magistrate made, some strong comments on the fact that these men were not fighting for their own country, and observed that Bel- gium had behaved so splendidly that she ought to have the support of all her sons at this time of distress; but, instead, these men—and he had had many more such before him recently— were skulking in the shelter of this country, getting drunk at the expense of charitable people.

Fines of 10s. and 7s. 6d. were imposed. The drunkenness of the Belgian refugees under maintenance at Earl's Court, in respect of which the West London magistrate has al- ready made indignant comment, was again yesterday the subject of further protests from the same Bench, before whom several Belgians were brought. In sentencing one of them, a big man of 43 years, to 14 days' hard labour, Mr. Fordham said:— *.

"It looks as if we have got the scum of Belgium here. Everyone shows respect for Belgium, and it is sad for me to sit here day after day and see these strong fellows skulking here and living on charity, and getting drunk on the money, when they ought to be fighting for their country. I cannot understand it. Someone in authority ought to inquire into the matter and sort out those who are eligible for the Army, and send them back to Belgium to fight."

div.head: ANGLO-BELGIAN
div.p: ANGLO-BELGIAN
Tells Lytnm Friend About Arm 3 Rough-Riding.

Private G. H. Robinson, of the 23rd Squadron —now at a base camp in France—is an English- man born at Wimbledon. About twenty 'years ago he went out to Belgium and settled there. Subsequently he married a Belgian lady, with ,whom and his two little children he was com- pelled, the beginning of the war, to leave, along with the other refugees, and take refuge in this country. He was a jockey, ail joined the Army Remount. He was then sent to Orms- kirk, and after only about a fortnight was transferred to France. His principal duty is the breaking in of horses; also he is very -use- ful on account of his knowledge of the language. Writing to Mr. F. E. Evans, of The Cross, Lymm, Private Robinson says : " I wrote a letter to you before and left it in my tunic. Tunic got stolen up at railhead. "We expect \to leave here about the end of this month, going up nearer the Front. We shall all be pleased with the change. "I got thrown for the first time the other day. We got a bunch of unbroken Australian

whalers in-. I got on a big black hore.He . went quietly for about ten yards, then he started in. I did a couple of somersaults in the air, and landed flat on my back. But he had to go through it afterwards! A lady could ride him now. . . ."
"I hope everything is going on well in Lymm. For myself, I am keeping good and fit, .but shall not be sorry when the busin9ss is fin- ished. But it's a long way to Tipperary yet, I'm afraid."

div.head: PRIVATE PETER PERCIVAL.
div.p: PRIVATE PETER PERCIVAL.
Ist Cheshire Mon 'Wounded hi 'flu,
Thigh. Mrs. C. A. Percival, of 3, West Hyde, New- fields, received from her husband on Tuesday evening the following letter:—

"No. 1 Canadian -General Hospital, Maples; France, 20/6/15. I daresay you heard about me being wounded. I don't think it is serious;, it is a flesh wound in the thigh. I went under an operation last night, and had the shrapnel taken out; and my leg feels a lot easier now. This is a grand place where we are now; it is about .25 miles from Boulogne. We might shift any time. I will_ write again later on." An addition to this letter, made a little later, ran: "I thought I had told You all, but I have just heard something. • The doctor has just been round, and told me he has not got the shrapnel out of my leg; but he said it would be all right, they would get it out in England. He has booked me for the next boat—it might be to- morrow (Monday) or the next day. Do not trouble; I will write as soon as I am settled doy:n there."
On Wednesday morning a Red Cross card. dated the 21st, said the Private had just arrived at the Colchester Military Hospital.
Worked at Latchford.

Private Percival, whose age is 2, was born at Lymm and educated. at the village school. He then went to work as a fustian cutter for Mr. F. 0. Moston, and after three years proceeded to the Latchford Steel Works, and then as 'a labourer to the Manchester Ship Canal. Here he was when the war broke out, and in August he joined the National Reserve. Six months later he was called up, and has been at the Front with the • Ist Cheshires for nearly three months.
He attends the Parish Church, and has four little boys and one girl. His mother, Mrs. Elizabeth Percival, lives at Cross Brow, Statham.

div.head: LYMM TERRITORIALS.
div.p: LYMM TERRITORIALS.
NEW FURLOUGH SYSTEM STARTED.
The Lymm " Terriers " came out of the trenches ten days ago, after sixteen days in them. They do not yet know when they go in again. ____

-Private Henry Brookes writes on June 19th to his mother at 1, West Hyde We are now out of the trenches for a time, after being in for a whole sixteen days. . . We are looking for- ward to having a furlough soon. I hope it will come off, and then I shall be able to see you all. . ..." ,

Private Percy Clam writes: "It is now Sun- day morning, and very nice. . .• . I don't think we shall be in the trenches much longer. We are keeping in the best of health_ . . . You have had a little bad news round Lymm just lately, and you at home must feel it more than, we do. But do not get downhearted: It is very quiet this morning, and I think about you all at home these nice days. But never mind! It might come to a sudden end; we mue4 live in hopes." Writing later, he says: "it is too hot this• [Monday] morning to walk about. Sunlay dos not make much difference on this jOh;. hat' we keep it up as much as we can. We have a church parade when we are out •sf the trenches."

Corporal Jack 11. Moston writes: "r think the Lymm lads are having very bad lila just at present. We have been in the trenches since ' the let of June, so you can tell we are getting a bit 'fed up with it. Just fancy being ..stuck behind sandbags all this time, with bullets and shells whistling over all the day—so that, you dare not lift your head up for\fear of getting a bit of something in it !" On Thursday word from Private Henry Cadman to his sister, Mrs. G. Rixon, of 'Pepper- street, ran: "We are expecting to have a fur- lough—in fact, it has started this Monday; but by the time we get our turn the war shanld be over. For they are only letting four go at once; so you can tell how long it is going to be for all, to have a turn. I hope I have the luck to come in the first lot when it comes our turn, because it is going to be about two years when the last lot get their turn. But I hope the war will be over then, and that we shall have been home longer than three parts of the time. "We are having some very warm weather -. It would be all right if we were having a week or two at Blackpool. "This last time in the trenches one of our fellows got three years for being asleep on his post in the trenches. It is a very serious job going to sleep on post—well, there have been plenty shot for doing the same thing in other battalions. But we get that sleepy at times that we cannot help ourselves; for we have no sleep at night in the trenches, and we have to take our turns through the day looking out. We get very little sleep in the trenches." Private Joseph Clare writes: "There are a few on furlough out of the battalion. and I think Harold will be coming with the next batch."
now
Private Davies—in peace times, coachman at Dean's Green—is ill with rheumatism and in hospital. His wife has not heard from him for five weeks,

Private Jim Taylor—the first Lymm " Terrier " wounded—writes to his mother from the Clayton Ward, Cnunty Hospital, Lincoln: "I am in the best of health at pre- sent., and have quite recovered from the operation. I am eating my meals snd sitting nn in bed. I have found a fresh friend, froth Manchester: his brother is in the same corn- nom, Fig myself. and has been missing from his home fifteen years. I sow the inquiries for missing friends, and informed the inouirer that he. was at the Front with ouriregiment. So he sent nie sonic' 'fags.'"

div.head: PRIVATE :WILLIAM JACKSON
div.p: PRIVATE :WILLIAM JACKSON
AVounded Collin To Trenches With Carrying-Party.

Another Lymm " Terrier " wounded this week is Private Wm. Jackson, soin of Mr. and Mrs. Wm. Jackson, of 3, Moston-street, New- fields. The news was received first on Thurs- day morning, when the following letter arrived from a &comrade:—

"I am very sorry to have to send you the news of your son, William, being wounded. . We had been carrying timber up to the trenches last night [the 20th], and on our return jour- ney a bullet found its Way into the calf of his left leg. Harry Brookes, our stretcher-bearer, was soon with him—doing all he could. Then he, along with Corporal F. Kay and myself, carried him, On onr backs, to the dressing- station—which, fortunately, was only ,about half a mile away. After he had received atten- tion from the R.A.M.C. we left him; and, be- lieve me, he was very bright, happy and com- fortable. We cheered him up whilst with him, and he was very glad when I told him I would write and inform you. I hope you will not worry. The wound is not serious; he will get the best treatment. in' hospital; and in a very short time he .will be in England. Then you will have him at home. You have every reason.. to be proud of 'him, for he really has . done splendidlyeSpecially. seeing he is; so young. Everything:that has been asked of him he has -done-in a manner that has made him a hero and a great .favourite with us all. Naturally I am sorry to lose him; but I am glad. to know he will soon be with you—and I know you will give him a right royal family welcome. He has earned the excellent name he bears." The letter is signed "Faithfully yours, 11. Clare, Sergeant." . By the same post 'a letter written by Private IT. Brookes was\received. It ran: "Your son has been slightly wounded in the right leg, just below the knee. He is perfectly safe, and the wound is in no way dangerous.. . . . The dressing-station was about a hundred yards away from the spot where he got hit. Every assistance was given; and when we left him at 10.15 he was quite cheerful. We shook hands with him, and bade each other the ,best of luck. We all have often expressed openly, when in conversation, .our sincere desire to some day 'make a fuss of him,' he being the youngest among us out here. . . He has proved to be a brave and cool soldier right through; he was brave even after he had been . hit; and he was very popular with us all. We are sorry to lose him." Yesterday morning a field-card from the Iwounded Private assured those at home that ihe was going on well. Private H. Cadman says: "We were on a

—was his grandfather. Having finished his education at the vilage school, Private W. Jackson went to work for Messrs. William Wright and Son, gold-beaters, Newfields. He was a member of the Congregational Church, and formerly belonged to 7the Lymm Lads' Club.
Of the Territorials he had been a member for about twelve months previous to the out- break of war; and he had been at the Front for four months.

div.head: CORPORAL HENRY BARBER.
div.p: CORPORAL HENRY BARBER.
. Touching Tribure _From Corporal
Stan. llinde.

Mrs. J. Barber, of Rush Green, has this week received among others the following letter:— " 2/sth Battalion, E of C. Essex,—Just a line to tell you how sorry I was to hear about Harry being killed. He was one of my best pals; and I have thought many a time this last week about the happy hours we have spent together at football and at the Lads' Club. And Jack Guest has been killed! Harry and Jack were two of my best lads, and I am very sorry in- deed to hear about their deaths. I was look- ing forward to spending many happy hours with them again. "It grieved .me very much when I could not go out with them, but they would not let me go. They have sent for another hundred men, and my name has gone in again, but I do not know yet whether they will let me go. We are making trenches down here. . . .
"You have my . deepest sympathy in your great loss. lam sure it has been a greal blow. Yours truly, Stan. Ilindes."

div.head: "I CAN'T FACE RATS."
div.p: "I CAN'T FACE RATS."
Amusing Story Of Where " Tommy's " Courage Failed.
Corporal Ben Elliott, of the 2nd Scots Guards, writing from France to his parents at Canter- bury Cottage, Lymm, says :

We are having a hot time of it just now,_as there is a big battle raging. On Monday, the 14th, I was buried twice before breakfast, but I am pleased to tell you that I escaped with just a scar over my left eye. You see, they were shell- ing our trenches.

"But they could not shell Us out. We stuck it like we have always done. I was in charge of a party of men, and some of them had not been in the trenches before. They kept saying to me, 'Do you think we are safe here?' I said, 'Stick it, lads. You are safe as the money in the bank.' And those men did stick it, though I can tell you it was a proper nerve-wrecker. But nevertheless they can't move the Scots Guards; I am just proud to belong to such a smart and plucky corps. They will go any- where, and I have no fear at all.

"Before we went into the trenches we were in a farmhouse billet, where the rats were run- ning over us. One night one of my men went into a field to sleep, so I asked him the follow- ing morning why he did not sleep in the barn. He said, 'Corporal. I will face as many Ger- mans as they like, but I can't face rats.' Well, I had to laugh! We get some funny places to billet in, but we are all as happy as can be when we are giving the Germans the bayonet." • "ONE SHALL BE TAKEN —"

Bombardier W. Elliott, the Corporal's brother, has also had a narrow escape. As Aix fellows and himself were standing talking just after-com- ing out of the firing line a shell burst and every one was killed save himself. , He had to help gather up the pieces, and it was a terrible ex- perience. "There is a very rough • battle rag- ing," he writes, "but his luck is holding just like it. did in the Boer War."

Death of , Mrs. Ives.—Early on Thursday morning the death took place at her home, Oughtrington Bridge, of Mrs. Ives, wife of Mr. Ambrose G. Ives, of the Lyznin Post Office staff. On the outbreak of war Mr. Ives joined the 7th South Lancashire Regiment—with whom he is now stationed in Tidworth. He holds the rank of C.S.M.

Zeppelins, and it dropped about ten bombs at midnight. I believe it killed about five soldiers while they were sleeping, and our billet is only about 150 yards away from where they dropped. We are back at our old place where all the heavy fighting is, and this is also the place where I had my narrow escapes. I might as well tell you we have been in Belgium all along, moving from one place to another; and you must not be a bit surprised to bear of the Germans crying for mercy before this month is out. I don't think this war will last another couple of months, especially now the fine weather is coming on."
It is believed- that Private Shepheard'S battalion was under heavy shell fire at the time of his disappearance.
So recently us Christmas he had returned rom India—where he had been with his regi- ment since September, 1913.

div.head: LIEUT. ALFRED E. WATKIN.
div.p: LIEUT. ALFRED E. WATKIN.

Lieutenant Watkin, of the flrd Royal Welsh Fusiliers, who was recently wounded in France, continues to make good—though necessarily slow—,progress. His doctor states that for some months he will be lame, but not per- mn nently.
Lieutenant Watkin is now at Netley Hospital, where he arrived last Sunday.

div.head: ORFORD.
div.p: ORFORD.
THE DUTY OF THE PEOPLE.
Strong Appeal Made to Men AL The
Village Church.

A special service was held in Orford Church on Sunday evening in response to a request from the Archbishop of York "to point out to the people their duty at this time of trouble." Special music was rendered by the choir. The Irganist, Mr. J. Gibson, played the Russian National Anthem as a voluntary. The choir sang the National Anthem and "Sleepers, Awake!" The Vicar (the Rev. G. Vale Owen) r.onducted the service. The lessons were read )21 Captain Crane and Mr. T. S. Steel.

div.head: Compulsory Service Not Far Oft
div.p: Compulsory Service Not Far Oft

In a short address, delivered in a soldierly manner, Captain Crane made an appeal to everyone to do their very best to help to bring the war to an early and successful conclusion. He gave it as his opinion that compulsion was not far off, and was bound to come, and he asked the young men not to wait to be forced, as they would fare badly. He appealed to mothers, wives and sweethearts, not to hold the young men back, but to urge them to go for- ward end get into khaki. If a man would not come along and do his duty, the best thing would be to shoot him as a coward.

div.p: People Who Live in a Fool's Paradise.

Mr. T. S. Steel made an appeal to everyone to link up and do their utmost in this war for righteousness and freedom. They had, he said. to contend with a nation which was clever and thoroughly prepared. The majority of the people of this country were living in a fool's paradise. They were told of British successes, but the reverses were carefully concealed from them. The war had scarcely come home to them. Certainly prices had risen, but in spite of that, money was more 'plentiful. This war could only be brought to a successful conclusion by everyone assisting with their services and their ,money. They would all have to make sacrifices. Thousands had given up everything to go 'out and fight for their couptry, while the millions were living in security and com- fort at home. This was not a class war. What- ever might be their opinion of the aristocracy. they had given much money and shed much blood in the defence of their country, shoulder to shoulder with the working men. The greatest share of the war was being borne by the working class, and without them Britain would have been defeated.

div.head: PATRIOTISM AND THRIFT. Some Of The Points In The
div.p: PATRIOTISM AND THRIFT. Some Of The Points In The
New War Loan.
By C. E. PARKER.

No Chancellor of the Exchequer was ever faced by a greater financial emergency than was Mr. McKenna. His proposals, formed doubtless on careful expert advice, are worthy of the magnitude of the problem. They are sufficiently attractive to all classes of inves- tors, but they are not extravagantly generous. Without doubt the most interesting part of the scheme is the, facility given to the small investor to participate. Investments from £5 and in multiples up to £2OO can be made through arly Post Office money order office. Amounts over .£2OO must be invested through the Bank of England, Anyone with five shil- lings or more can invest in the Government War Loan. Such investor can take his five shillings' to any Post Office, Trade Union or Friendly Society Office, and possibly to his employer, who, in exchange for the five shil- lings, will give him a receipt or. voucher. He will receive no interest for -the. money unless and until he has. accumulated vouchers to the value of five pounds. When he has vouchers for this amount he will take them to a money order office and receive in exchange a .Stock Certificate in the new War Loan for £5, bear- ing interest at 4.i. per cent. per annum, equal to 4s. 6d. on £5; He will also receive inter- est at the rate of 5 Per cent. per annum on every voucher, i.e., a penny per month on every voucher he has purchased, reckoning from the date of purchase. Further, he will receive—why Ido not know—a bonus of a shilling when he completes his five pounds. If, on, the other hand, he fails to complete his £5 he receives no interest and no bonus, but he can get full value for his vouchers at any money order office. In a word, these vouchers occupy a similar position to Post Office orders. They will not be legal tender. Investment by means of vouchers will be open until , December Ist, and the option may be extended into next year. These vouchers will be ser- viceable. for many purposes where it is at the option of the giver to decide in what form he makes the gift. They might be used in extra payments such. as bonuses, presents, etc. _Parents could start their children's sav- ings by these vouchers, and many other methods will occur to the reader. The 'small' subscriber—that is of £5 and multiples of that sum—has this advantage: that he will have to pay only £4 19s. 4d. for his £5, so that he will get a discount in respect. of each £5 invested, The holder of £5 aid upwards in the War Loan Stock cannot cash • it as in the case of the vouchers,,but on the other hand the Gov- ernment, if it so please, can pay him out at par any time after ten years, and is obliged to pay him out in thirty years, 1945: The holder can, however, sell his stock, for which there will always be a mark-let, and if a market then a market value, and this value may not always be the face value. That is, £5 stock may only be saleable at £4 155., or it may bring £5 ss. It seems more than likely that it will be worth more than par. Surely, a 4-1 per cent. investment with the credit of this country behind it will rise in value. The dividends are to be paid twice a year, June Ist and December Ist, when each holder of War Loan Stock will receive a warrant for the interest, which can be cashed at any money order post office. The Stock Certificate must le shown when the warrant is cashed for the lurpose of identification.

div.head: AN URGENT PATRIOTIC CALL.
div.p: AN URGENT PATRIOTIC CALL.

So much for the business arrangements for. small investors, but underlying these and applicable to the whole lean is an urgent call on the patriotism of the country. We can- not put it better, than did Mr. McKenna : Our requirements are great, and nothing but a great 'appeal to our financial resources, stimulated by a most earnest sense of patriot- ism, will enable us to obtain the money. I would have those who have the means to sub- scribe, and those who can obtain the peans to subscribe, by curtailing part of their cus- tomary expenditure, to remember that every effort they Make now is an 'effort which is not only necessary to enable us to carry on the war, but will bear, great fruit in enabling ,us to maintain .our financial pre-eminence when , the war is Over. ~ - . . He who subscribes now, and saves in order 6 subscribe, Will be able to bear the strain when the war is over. He will be thankful for the effort he has made in this struggle .to help himself, but still dearer to him must be the knowledge that every aid he gives to himself he is multiply- ing .for his country." The i.Eiue is "Victory or Ruin." Every- one must lend his all, to the State. We must all be willing to "" Pay the. price." • Let Warrington do its part to make this loan a huge success. ,

div.head: LOAN,
div.p: THE LOAN,
To Raise Sinews Of War And
Promote Thrift.

" The largest financial transaction the world has ever known," Sit Thonias • Whittaker called the new War Loan Bill on Tuesday in the House of Commons. There has been a rush at Hie banks and post offices of investors and those who wanted fur- ther information. The 'loan has been received with a chorus of approval in every part of the country,- all classes welcoming a scheme which not only raises the sinews of war but inaugurates a great measure of national thrift. • Mr. McKenna, introducing the question of the War- Loan, said that' every element of an- certainty made ,it .unwise and imprudent to fix a limit to the amount of the loan, and the Gov- ernment were not asking. for any definite amount The only limit will be the limit to meet the ex- penditure of the war. Owing to the war, , the nation's expenditure from April 1, 1914, up to Saturday - last exceeded the revenue by £518,000,000, of Which £184,000,000 was attribut- able to the current financial year, which began on April 1. - The 'first War Loan, which was issued in November, at , £95 for £lOO of stock, was for £350,000,000. On Saturday last the Government had about: £80,000,000 in hand out of their, borrowings. The daily 'deficiency in the national revenue is now over £2,225,000, and before long it- will be quite £2,500,000-. • It is these facts,- coupled with the necessity of avoiding the injury which uncertainty as to the future would cause -to the present holders of Government stocks, that make an immediate War Loan highly advisable, if not , absolutely necessary.. The loan is called- the £4 10s. per cent. War Loan, 1925.1945. It. is an issue of stock or bonds, bearing interest' at 41 per cent. per annum, pay- able half-yearly on the Ist June' and the Ist December. The price of issue fixed by H.M. Treasury at £lOO per cent- A full half-year's dividend will be paid on the Ist December, 1915. The stepk is an investment authorised by "The Trustee Act, 1893," and trustees may invest 'therein notwithstanding that the price may at the time of investment exceed the redemption Value of £lOO per cent. Full .particulars as to the loan, conversions, Rm., will be found in an advertisement in to- day's "Examiner." List of applications will be closed on or be: fore Saturday, July 10th.

div.head: FLAG DAY SUCCESS.
div.p: FLAG DAY SUCCESS.

The irsidents of Warrington and district respOnded nobly to the Flag Day appeal made on behalf' of Hit hospital funds of the Allies, no ,less a sum than 092-4 s. 9d. being raised by the sale of the tiny flags. One hardl met a person who had not at least one of the little national emblems pinned to his coat lapel or to her blouse, as the case might be; whilst many that one came across were decorated with anything from a dozen to a score or more. Altogether the energetic young ladies who kindly under- took to sell the flags, managed to dispose of scores of thousands of their ware at prices ranging from a penny apiece to such figure as the purchaser, of his, or her, generosity, cared to give. In addition to the Union Jack, minia- ture replicas of the- Belgian flag were on sale, and in disposing of these a nupaber of the Belgian refugees staying in Warrington were assiduous. The executive committee respon- sible for the arrangements, &twisted of the Mayor and Mayoress (Alderman and Mrs, Peter Peacock), Mesdames Greenall, Johnson, Jcilley and Osborne, and Messrs. J. H. Smethurst and A. T. Hallaway (bon. sec.), who were assisted In the matter of distribution. &c.. by Messrs. Geo. Bihby. Henry Collin. J. Houghton. F. Leitch, H. Morley, T. S. Pemberton, Herbert Smith and T. Whittle.

div.head: DRINK AND POVERTY.
div.p: DRINK AND POVERTY.

Would Wretched Conditions Be Tolerated Without Alcohol ? The question .of drink and poverty was raised by the Rev. W. Harris (of Ashton-in-Maker- field) at an open4ir meeting 'held at the foot of Bewsey-street, last night, under the auspices of the Warrington Citizens' Temperance League. The meeting was the second of a series. Mr. William Wright (of the Rechabites) was in the chair. The Rev. W. Harris pointed out that the annual drink •bill of this country was £500.000,000, It was worse than waste. It would be better if the people of the land dropped , that money to the bottom of the sea than con- ' Untie', spending it as they were now doing. Mr. Philip Snowden had said that it would pay us better to keep the brewers and .the publicans doing nothing than to spend what we are spend- ing on. drink. Alluding to the main object of ' the meeting, which, is to persuade people to follow the King's example and sign the pledge and keep it for the duration of the war, the speaker said that at a. time like the present, it was of great importance to be able to bear stress and strain, and a man who in any way in- capacitated himself was making a danger for his country. What were the judges continually telling us? They told us that 90 per cent. of our national crime was attributable to strong drink. "Do you think," Mr. Harris asked, "that the thousands of people who are living in Warrington under conditions of poverty and squalor would tolerate such conditions except for the drink? Do on think that the horrible slums in which children are brought up without any sense of the beautiful, and little sense of right and wrong worthl,be tolerated if it were not for the drink? I think not!" •

div.head: EXAMINER,
div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, JUNE 26, 1915.
A FIERCE ENCAGEMENT-AND A
VICTORY.
The Warrington Territorials have been in AO their gallant leader; COLONEL FAIR-

CLOUGII, calls a "fierce engagement," and they have come out of the ordeal with victory to their arms and honour on their name. Proud as is the long, the bloody and the glorious record of the South Lancashires, it I will be prouder still in the days to come, for the gallant deeds its Fourth Battalion of Vol- unteers did in Flanders last Wednesday week. In the words of most of those who took part in the fray, and have written home, they did what they were set to do, though the price they paid was a heavy one a price which meant the plunging of Warrington into mourning. It is on this side of, the picture we would first of all wish to dwell. To those who have lost a husband, a father, a brother, a sweetheart, to those who have had dear ones laid aside temporarily, With the knowledge ' that they will, at best, ret.urn to their normal life maimed, or, crippled, or physically im- paireil, we offer our profoundest sympathy. Those relatives and friends, as well as those primarily involved, we know, will , command now and retain for all time the re- spectful, maybe the envious, affection of the town to which we all belong. 4 While the sorrow is new the pain will be bitter, however powerfully the claims of patriotism may ppeal to those called upon to bear personal bereavement and individual sorrow; but the time will come when they will he able to balance their present pride against their past affliction and to see that their sacrifices were worth the making. I
MAJOR CROSFIET.D, writing from the battle
field to the relatives of a fallen private—and doubtless he would write to all the afflicted— said finely:
lie has laid down his life, like so many others of our brave 'Warrington lads, that England May not suffer the same ,fate as Belgium.

All those who fell did this great service to their country. Those who were wbunded in varying degrees of severity bled for the same great cause. The young officer, LIEUTENANT LEONARD 'HENskALL, who will come back to his Church Lads' Brigade work and to his business uainus an arm, will be Sadly handi- capped in many ways; but We fancy that Ow man of the future who can show that he has lost his right arm in such a cause as this will be at a premium. So while we grieve with all the sufferers we envy them their pride of place. More, as a town and as a country we offer them the assurance of remment to the full, so far as it can be Made, wliether -in the way of affection or material help, where that
poor 'service is necessary. The country and the town have undertaken this slight duty in return, and we shall see that that undertak,

jag is honoured. We refer our readers to the aceounts that have come from the Front first hand, and are published in to-day's "Examiner." These simple letters dissipate altogether the many idle, ridiculous and mischievous rumours that were circulated last week. It was stated' that our men had been led into an ambush in the shape of a horseshoe, and had been shot down from all sides. The truth is that they de- liberately went into that horseshoe and levelled out the line by ousting the Germans from their trenches at the point of the bayonet. It was said our men had heedlessly rushed a vacated trench and had been blown up by a previously prepared mine. The truth is that they won the trenches and then, with- stood the tremendous shelling of the enemy, which battered away the barricades and buried many of the occupants. It was said that eer- thin officers were missing, including MAJOR , CROSFIELD. The truth is That, as we have stated, the gallant MAJOR is now engaged writing letters home to console the relatives of his fallen Comrades. And ,so we could go through the whole course of last week's wild talk. The final truth is that the Warrington Territorials, in a brigade composed of the finest troops in the British Army, tackled the Germans at close quarters, resolved before- hand to fight to a finish ; and we were told by their GENERAL, when all was over and their work had been "done," that they had proved that they could /be relied upon in any cenceiv- able situation, and that they had proved that the Fourth South Lancashires could never be broken.

div.head: TERRITORIAL ROLL OF HONOUR.
div.p: TERRITORIAL ROLL OF HONOUR.
FADICUS CHARGE LEADS TO MANY
CASUALTIES.

div.head: HE FIGHT.
div.p: HE FIGHT.
WHAT THE GENERAL SAID OF OUR TERRITORIALS.
"The Battalion Did Splendidly."
YOU HAVE PROVED THAT THE 4th SOUTH LANCS. CAN NEVER BE BROKEN."

The above eloquent tribute was paid to our men by the Brigadier of the Division of which our Battalion forms part, when addressing Colonel Fairclough, Officers, N.C.O.'s and Men of the 4th South Lancashire Regiment," after the action of Wednesday week, in whici they played an heroic and victorious part.
"GLAD YOU WERE THERE."
After the action the Brigadier said

"Colonel .Fairclough, officers, non-commis- sioned officers and Men of the 4th South Lanca- shire Regiment. I have just one or two words to say to you this,morning. I remember about a year ago I used to think I was rather an old soldier. I joined the Army 28 years ago, and have knocked about the world a bit, and I used to think I knew something about war, but I found when I got out here I didn't even know the A B C of "Any man who had been in the trenches a couple of months was better than me. "A week ago I didn't think I had anything left to learn, but I learned a lot of things I didn't know before on Wednesday last. You all remember what happened; in fact, I don't think any ,of us will ever forget the day. It wasn't very pleasant, but I am glad to gay I was there, and glad you were there, for I am sure we all learned some lessons from, it. `lThe first was, We all learned what shelling means. "The second lesson we learned was that the 4th South Lancashires can never be broken, and that all the other regiments of the Brigade can, never be broken. "When you go back into the ttenclies you will know you can depend on them, and they will also know they can depend on you. and -I thank you all very much for teaching me that , lesson. "Thank you. That is all I have to say." The aboye Aire fiat words of the Brigadier General, reported from two different sources, the writer of the longer report remarking, to the friend to whom he sent it, "I am sure the people of Warrington will be proud to know about it, and you might pass it on to the 'Guardian' and ' Examiner.' " Boys Still Full of Fight. "I am in the pink," says the writer, who is in a responsible position, "and so are all the boys, or those that are available. We have had, and are having a h- of a time, but the boys are still full of fight. and buck as ever, and I can promise you that they can and will hold their own. The Hun stops at nothing, but as soon as he finds he is in for it he wants mercy. "We have been knocking 'about here and there since I last wrote, and I am sorry to say our numbers have been very • much reduced; first in one trench, then another, then out for what is called rest. But I think myself the trench is the best rest, although I have not tried it. My department has to do with the A.S.C. . . • The Success and the Price.

"I am going to give you perhaps a little more than is usually allowed, but I do not think there is any harm now the job is over. You have no doubt seen about the success at Well our boys were in it, and it must be taken for granted that a success such as has been obtained is not won witiout loss. Our

casualties, I regret to say, are somewhat heavy —so far as can be ascertained, one officer killed, line wounded; 00 rank and file killed and about 10 wounded:7 The names, 'I have no doubt will forwarded in a few days. You cannot linagine what it is like .unless you are just tlaildY. If anyone should raise the questioh as Why they cannot get names, invite them to "MO out here, and if they can change this BYstem our ' doctor (who, ,by the way. is a trurop—probably yon know him, Pr. Law) will be very' glad of their help, 'providing, they are of ,any use. • "I was not among it myself. but 1 take the 'liberty of quoting yon the General's speech, 'which I coAider is to the point.

div.head: Heldiots Coming to Warrington
div.p: Heldiots Coming to Warrington

-" If you had seen the boys after the fight Your heart would have gone out to them, but with all they had been through they are quite in good spirits. It was fun to see the antics of those who were fortunate enough to secure trophies in the way'of helmets, and I suppose You will see a few in 'Warrington at a very early date. I was not able to get hold ~f one, but live in hopes."

div.head: GRAPHIC DESCRIPTION BY A YOUNG PRIVATE.
div.p: GRAPHIC DESCRIPTION BY A YOUNG PRIVATE.
"WE SI TFERED, BUT WE NA 4) \ .

Private Walter Hindes, 25, Chureh-street, a ,young Territorial of about 20 years of age, who "joined up" on the outbreak Of the war sends .a thrilling description of the action in which the Battalion fought so gallantly and lost\so heavily. Private Hindes, who worked at Dal- lam Forge, fornierly attended St. Mary's School, Buttermarket-street. He was a member of the League of the Cross Club, Bewsey-street, and it was to Father B. Primavesi that he wrote as follows:

"Saturday, June 19th, 1915. "Dear Father Basil,—You must try to excuse Ine not answering your welcome P.C. before I have come‘ through all right. It was a terrible ordeal, .and I shall never forget Wednesday, June 16th, 1915. We went in the .support trenches on the/night of Tuesday, the 15th. In the early hours of Wednesday morn- ing the bombardment started. how terrible it all was to be waiting there while shells were bursting all around us, and feel the earth tremble! About an hour and a half after the bombardment started, the regiment that was in our firing-line charged. Quickly as possible we took their place.

div.head: In the German Trench
div.p: In the German Trench

"Once there, I looked over the parapet and I saw they were in the .German trench. I looked again and I saw them, charging for the second line. Again they were successful. Still the bombardment was going on and the enemy were blowing opr trench to atoms. What a sight it was for one, to see his comrades being buried alive or dashed to pieces! The sights, of a battlefield are never to be forgotten. We had to leave the trench for another, but still the earth was trembling. I saw them bring some prisoners in—some young and some middle-aged. By this time some •of our bat- talion were in the captured trenches, along With other Britisher& They were helping to ,check the connter-attack Which was checked). Germans Repulsed With Loss. "Again the enemy counter-attacked, but they Were repulsed with heavy losses. It got eight o'clock or half-past before our eonapany could get up to the captured trenches. The sights - there were just the same as elsewhere. British and German dead and wounded lay in heaps. I shall never forget. It was just murder—cruel murder. We got relieved about midnight. We had fought hard and well, and, what is more, -we had won!

div.head: Grim Souvenir.
div.p: A Grim Souvenir.

- - -- - "Those of us that have, come through can oonsider ourselves lucky—very lucky. I was lucky because a piece of shrapnel hit my valise, made twelve holes in my towel (the way it was folded), eight holes in my oil-sheet, and buried 'itself in a tin Of bully-beef. I have got the Piece of shrapnel (it will be a:, soutenir). I will now close, giving You my hearty thanks for Your welcome P.C. Remember me to my yiends at the League of the Cross. Let them -!"low that I am as well as ever, and am look- ing forward to the day when I will be back amongst you.--Yours sincerely, W. 1112inE5.".
LIEUTENANT E. L. FROST.
Killed in Action.
Major George Crosfield and the Rev. W. Brace- camp (chaplain to the battalion).
Esteemed by Officers and Men.

The gallant Lieutenant received a bullet wound in the head . and, . without regaining consciousness, passed away half an hour or so later. lie was only 24 years of age. Although he had not been long associated with the War- rington Territorials, h. had Managed to gain the esteem of his brother officers and the affection of the men under him. The early part of his education was imparted at Dover College, from whence he proceeded to Uppingham College, one of the fawns public schools of the country. At 'Uppingliam he distinguished him- self both in the class-room and on the playing fields and, in the latter connection, was, in his time, captain of games, whilst he was also the champion heavy-weight boxer bf the college, and 4 . prominent memiler of the football and hockey teams.

Worked Well and Played Well at Cambridge. • From Uppingharn he proceeded to Trinity College,. Cambridge, where .he enjoyed great popularity amongst a wide circle of gownsmen acquaintances and where,. before "going down" he graduated B.A. with honours in the Sciences Tripos. Whilst it is obvious from this success that he did not neglect the more serious side of the life of his Alma Mater,- neither did he neglect the athletic and recreative side, for he gained signal distinction in more than ,one branch of sport and particularly in rowing— which is the premier • sport at the Cam-side 'Varsity. So excellent an on.rsman. was he— although he only became a ." wet-bob " in his last year—that he narrowly missed inclusion in the Camjiridge crew, which, in his year, did battle against Oxford, and, as it was, ihe was awarded the coveted Trial Eights cap. Ile also got his " half-blue " for shooting, whilst ,he r4resented his University against the -sister University in the annual boxing tourney. Lieutenant Frost was, in addition an enthtsi- astic golfer. and was a member of the War- rington Golf Club.

div.head: STORIES FROM THE TRENCHES.
div.p: STORIES FROM THE TRENCHES.
WITHOUT A SCRATCH.
Battalion Suffered, But Gave The &witty "Mustard;"
Corporal Thos. Wilkinson, an employe of Mr. WinstanleY, plumber, a Territorial who has attended two camps and is now at the Froftt, _ _ _ _

writing to his father, Mr. Thos. Wilkinson, joiner, 7, Dudley-street, Orford-lane, says : " I can only thank God that I am able to write this letter to-day. We have beeni in one of the worst battles of the war, so I am writing to let you know I am all right and none the worse for what we have gone through. ram sorry to say Warrington will be in Mourning when they get to know the number of its brave lads we have lost. We went up fo the trenches at on Tuesday night, June 15th, and. made a charge on the German trenches, and am glad to say got all we went up for—four lines of German trenches. But we paid it deadly price for it. We were under a deadly shell fire for fifteen hours, expecting every minute to be our last.

"We started bombarding about -2.50 on Wed- nesday morning and ceased about 4 a.m. The Germans kept theirs up ull day without. stop- ping. Towards dark our Artillery started again, and fairly got them mustard, I can tell you, blowing all their trenches sky high. I am glad to say I have gone right through with. out a scratch, but I can only thank Him alone that I have been so lucky to pull through.

"We hkld nothing to eat all the time we were fighting, and it was quite a treat to find your parcel and a bit of Warrington cake when we got back to' our billets. "It will be my birthday on Sunday. If we are in the trenches I hope it is the 'last time I shall spend my birthday in them." Private Wilkinson's brother Frank, a Mack- smith at Dallam. is in the R.A.M.C. at Fazakerley, and his brother Herbert, stock- taker at Dallam, is in the same corps in Surrey. TT g is a Church Lads' Brigade boy, and be- longed to St. George's Mission. He was nine- teen last Sunday.

div.head: "SHELLS. SHELLS, AND YET MORE SHELLS ! "
div.p: "SHELLS. SHELLS, AND YET MORE SHELLS ! "
What " Tommy " Wants To Help Him
To Smash The Huns.

Writing to Mr. J. B. Starkey. of 2, Enville- street, St. Mary's-street. Latchford, Private Jack Clarke. of 15, Enville-street. now serving with the Territorials, makes reference to the big fight. "Our brigade," he says. "suffered heavily'. We got what we wanted, viz., three lines of German trenches. We were shelled by the Germans for eighteen hours, all kinds of shells being hurled at s, including the is variety. We took plenty of prisoners. (3.ur artillery was splendid. and gave the enemy a rare taste of their own speciality—the high explosive shell.
"It's Shells We Want," Says "Tommy." _

"Those are the shells we want. Send them along in thousands The Germans shelled us out of our old fire trench with their ' coal- boxes, . but not before we had lost a few men. . . . The enemy did not half bombard our trenches when we were attacking, and men were lying about shattered to pieces or wounded. The people of England seem to thhik that the Germans are getting short of shells, but they would not have thought so if they were over here on that memorable Wednesday. They seem to have plenty. As to the war being over soon, I cannot see how it is going to be over this side of the next twelve months. . . .

Three officers out of my company, including my platoon officer, Second-Lieutenant Henshall, were wounded. .... . I -.do not think much of the German infantry; it is only their artillery that is •puffing them through. Our General told us this morning that the 4th South Lancashires could never.be broken !"

div.head: LANCERS
div.p: LANCERS
MEET "TERRIERS."
Indian-Warringtoniates Letter Of Delight.

Corporal Edward A. Gordon, step-brother of Lance-Coxporal Charles Armstrong, . both of the 17th (Duke of .Cambridge's Own) Lancers, writes from North France to his r. aral t s , at 49, Museum-street: "We have been stationed near the Warrington 'Terriers,' and :lave Lad a glorious time Everyone seemed to know us, and all were glad to see us N.C.O.'s: [Sergeant] Allardice especially I was glad to see, as Ile reminds me of 'dad'; in fact, his . dry humour is a facsimile of 'dad's.' ' "I also met my old teacher from St. Mary's 7--,-Com.-Qtr-Mstr-Sergeant Coakley; Sid Ince, Ford, Joe Walker, Billy Mack from the Post Office, and Bobby Maine. To tell you the truth, I'd, have to give you the battalion roll to let you know the names of those we saw! "We- have been to the old capital of ancient 1 . It. is a mass of ruins. The cathedral and c loth-hall% are absolutely ruined. I won't describe the havoc wrought by the Bodies; it is beyond me."

div.head: "POOR OLD INDIAN CAV."
div.p: "POOR OLD INDIAN CAV."
"AVeren't Fortunate Enough To Cie
A Rub In." Writing from the Front a short time ago Lance-Corporal Charles Armstrong—of the 17t1

Lancers—fold his mother at 49, Museum-street: "There was a big battle round week, which lasted about four days. A certain amount of ground was lost on the first day from a Gtrman attack, but our brave fellows made that good afterwards and crowned themselves with glory. The Canadiaris were most con- spicuous for their gallantry and did splendid work. However, the poor old Indian Cay. weren't fortunate enough to get a rub in. Our luck again! We're itching to get into it, you bet!
"Whet glorious weather we are having here! Plenty of sunshine in a blue sky—something we have hardly known since we left India. I only hope it will keep up. It makes one feel happy to be alive."

div.head: GERMANS WENT MD.
div.p: GERMANS WENT MD.
110 w Lusitania News Affected Sot
Sides At Front.

Rifleman . Stanley Podmore, of the 3rd Rifle Brigade--whose home is at 4, Steel-street, and who was recently wounded—writes to a War- rington gentleman: "It isn't as bad as it used to be out here. We're having some grand weather at present, and it often makes me think of the home I left when I see the orchards in full bloom, and birds singing not a hundred yards from the German trenches The trench we are in is only eighty yards away, so you can guess what kind of a time we have. We don't trouble much about the. bullets; it's French mortars and 'Jack Johnsans ' that make us think a bit. Well, it's no use grumbling; some- one has to do it—although it's dirty kind of work killing a human being. Miles of Cheering.

" What do you think about the bounders sinking the Lusitania, eh? Wasn't it a low- down piece of work., Before we got the news we knew they'd done something, for they cheered themselves hoarse for miles along the line. Then they brought their bands to the trenches, and simply went -mad for about an hour. When our chaps got the news the officers had the job of their lives keeping them in the trenches. There wasn't a manathere but would have gone over the parapet and given them six inches of cold steel, which they richly de- served I" _ _

"They'll Suffer For All This." Lance-Corporal Charles Armstrong, of D Squadron, 17th (Duke of Cambridge's Own) Lancers)—writing from abroad to his mother, Mrs. Gordon,, at 49, Museum-street--says: "I have been reading a lot in the papers of the sinking of the Lusitania and of the feelings of the people at home—being roused almost to madness. What the Gentians think they have gained by it T don't know, but they seem awfully pleased at their smartness, don't they? Ah ! They'll suffer for all this later; you'll see I"

div.head: His Business Career.
div.p: His Business Career.

In 1912 Lieutenant Frost entered upon his all-too-brief business career, becoming actively associated with the firm of Messrs. Peter Stubs, Ltd., file and tool. manufacturers, .Warringtop. of which .firm- his uncle is chairman and' managing .direetor. Early last • summer Lieutenant Frost paid a.visit to France for the dual purpose of aeq airing h knowledge of the Continental trade of the company with which be was associated, and of . perfecting his French, and about seven or eight weeks after his return he Went to can* with the local Territorials—the camp That was .so unexpec- tedly cut short by the declaration of war. Practically ever since he ," came down-" from Oimbridge. Lientennnt Frost had been an officer of. the 4th. South Lancashire& and he had discharged the military duties devolving upon him with zeal and enthusiasm; indeed, as a friend of the family assured our representa- tive.'" be could not have taken greater interest in bio. Territorial work." lie Won the officers' tronhies for rifle and revolver shooting the first awl only time he competed for them. ,

div.head: Two Cousins Mentioned in Dispatches.
div.p: Two Cousins Mentioned in Dispatches.

Lieutenant Frost had : travelled extensively, having accompanied his father on business and pleasure tours to France, Switzerland and America. Another nephew of • Mr. F. Aylmer Frost—Captain T. L. Frost, of the Ist Battalion ,Cheshire Regiment, son of the Mayor of Chester—was recently killed in .action, whilst a third nephew, Lieutenant L. G. Norton, of the ,Durham Light Infantry, has been missing since October - .20th. Both .of these gallant officers achieved the distinction' of -being men- tioned in dispatches. Four other nephews and several additional members of the family are serving with the Forces.. ,

div.head: " Br;ght and Cheery as Ever " in the Thick
div.p: " Br;ght and Cheery as Ever " in the Thick
Of It. •

In his letter to Mr. F. A. Frost telling of the Lieutenant's death, Major Crosfield said:—" I was speaking to him only ten minutes before,' and, though we were then in the thick of it, he was just as bright and cheery as ever. The whole battalion mourns his loss." The • Rev: W. Bra.Cecamp's letter contained the following passages:—.-" When the battalion left to make the charge, he was thoroughly cheery and said to, me 'Good-bye, Padre. We . shall Soon meet again.' Your nephew was.one of the finest charaCters, it has ever been my ' privilege to meet. He was beloved by officers and men alike. His fine physique, his noble character endeared him to everybody. He was one of the noble fellows whose life could not be spared, but he has voluntarily laid it. down in a noble_ cause-,-for God, King and country."

div.head: Entertainment at Winwieli.
div.p: Entertainment at Winwieli.

On Thursday Senor Blanco, ,the noted violinist, gave sevenal selections at an enter- tainment to the patients in the Recreation Hall. at the Lord Derby Hospital at Winwick. The entertainment was arranged by kind per- mission of ithe Warrington Hippodrome manage- ment (manager Mr. Jackson), whose programme included: Overture, Anthems of the Allies (con- ductor Mr. T. H. Hurley), Hippodrome Band; Hal Smithers, the new style comedian; Rex Romaine and Doris Dainwmi, the acme of refinement and Originality; Harold Baker, Lancashire character comedian; De Busse, with his piano-accordion; selection, cornet solo, "If I bad a thousand lives to live," Mr. Allison; Daphne Wynne, the famous dancer; Rich. Taylor, the whistling ventriloquist; Gus Harris. the people's chorus idol.

div.head: KILLED IN DARDANELLES.
div.p: KILLED IN DARDANELLES.
Warringtonian Meets Ilk Fate
Fighting The Turks.

Captain George Webster Owen was shot in the head and killed instantly during the 'recent fighting in the vicinity of the Dardanelles. • Captain Owen, who was 32 years of age, was the fifth son of the late Mr. Thomas Owen and of Mrs. Owen, of the Pollards, renketh, and a brother of Mr. Wm. Owen, of the well-known firm of Messrs. Owen and Sons, grocers and

provision dealers, Sankey-street, Warrington, who lives at 14, Crosfield-street. The Captain was married and resided at Red Croft, Cheadle Hulme, near Manchester,. and prior to volun- teering for active service, was engaged in busi- ness on the Manchester Cotton Exchange, as a member of the firm, of Messrs. Owen, and Booth, cotton brokers, &c. He was educated at the
CAPTAIN G. W. OWEN. Killed in the Dardanelles
Warrington Grammar School, fld subsequently matriculated for Owen: College, Manchester.
Citizen-Soldier Since Youth.

He had been connected with the citizen mili-- tary force---firsf as a Volunteer and latterly as a Territoriai--t-rsce youth, and in 1912 he was given a Lieutenancy in the 10th (Manchester) Battalion of the East Lancs. Division of the Territorial Force, with whom he was serving at the time of his death. He was made Captain on September sth of last year. Five years ago he was married to Miss •Ruth Cocks, a member of a well-known Thrmston family.

div.head: "A Brave and Gallant Soldier."
div.p: "A Brave and Gallant Soldier."

The late Captain sailed with his battalion for Egypt on September 9th, and was subsequently transferred to the region of the Dardanelles, where he saw a considerable amount of fighting before he met his death on June 7th. A letter to the wife of the deceased officer said: "It may be a little consolation to you to know that he was shot and died instantly. . . Ile died, as he lived, a brave and gallant soldier—leading his men!" - _
After leaving school hnd before proceeding to Manchester, Captain Owen was, for a short time, engaged in the chemical laboratory at the Whitecro;s Works.

div.head: LATE PRIVATE S. THOMAS.
div.p: LATE PRIVATE S. THOMAS.
At the Elmwood-avenue Congregational Church on Sunday evening, the Rev. C. P. Pitt (pastor) conducted at memoriali service to the late Private Samuel Thomas, of the 4th South Lancashire Territorials.
