member of "D" Company. He had not been in. France long before he was promoted to ; a promotion *ilia was very popular with his comrades, by whom he was held in high esteem. Before the outbreak of war the Sergeant was employed by Messrs. Armitage and Rigby at the Cockhedß Mills. As a boy he attended the ffeathside School'. He was for some years a member of the Junior :Conservative Club, in Orford-lane. A keen Friendly Society man, he had for-some years been 'a member ..of the Grand United Order of Oddfellows. Besides his widow, he leaves one young child to mourn him. .

div.head: " We Were Blown I nto the Air."
div.p: " We Were Blown I nto the Air."
News of the Sergeant's death first reached the widow through the medium of a lfrief let- ter written by Sergeant Peter Morris, in the
SERGEANT W.. BAILEY. Killed in Action.
oourso of which he said: "It was -something awful, something I shall never forget if I live to be ninety. I was almost buried alive when we were blown into the air."

div.head: KILLED.
div.p: KILLED.
SERGEANT J. C. LIBBITER.
IVeII-known Local Harrier Who Served In Boer "%Var.
Seriseant Joseph , Christopher Libbiter, of -• .1., Hardy-street, is mentioned in several • ttors written. by Territorials to their

• ,speetive homes to say that he has en killed. One says he saw - all during the charge; • and another that he was bit by the.shell Which wounded Private F. S. Per6ival: The: first of these letters reached Warrington on Saturday morning. Moreover, the Sergeant—who has been a regu-. tar writer home—has not written at all this week.

div.head: Seryed Through Boer War.
div.p: Seryed Through Boer War.

Born in Ireland in the Curragh Camp, 27 years ago—his father was a soldier—Sergeant Libbiter.came to live in Warrington at the end of the Boer .War—through which he served. He entered- the employment as a labourer, of Messrs. Crosfield, with whom he remained for fourteen years—till the outbreak of war, when he was called up. Previously he had served k.,is years-with the Territorials, and at Denbigh
SERGEANT J. C. LIBBITER. Killed in Action.

in 1913, the company of which he was in charge, won the Brigade Cup for efficiency during training. In Messrs. Crosheld's sports also be carried off several prizes from time to time. He was a former member of the 'Sankey Harriers, and also belonged to the National Service League-. lie was a devoted member of St. Benedict's Roman Catholic Church.
The Sergeant was single, and the only sup- port of his widowed mother. lie had two sisters, whilst his only brothef is expecting :-hortly to take part in the Dardanelles land
The official casualty list published on Tues- day, contained the Sergeant's name among the killed. . •

div.head: SERGEANT THOMAS GILL. "Died A Soldier's Death, Rallying His
div.p: SERGEANT THOMAS GILL. "Died A Soldier's Death, Rallying His
Men!"

"It is, indeed, with a heavy heart that write to tell you of the death of your husband. He received a rifle bullet through the head when advancing against a withering fire. Death must have been instantaneous. It happened on the 16th June, when we lost a large number of men. Your husbana was a splendid soldier, and an excellent sergeant. He died a soldier's death, facing the foe and rallying his men under extremely difficult circumstances. I
cannot express in words my feelings, but I offer you, on behalf of myself and-every man in the company, our very deep sympathy in the great
WMIIIII=IIIMMIMIIIMMIIII! •
trial that has fallen upon you and your little girl."
Rejoined the Territorials When War' Broke Out.
So wrote Company-Sergeant-Major T. S. Davies to Mrs. Gill, of 52, Forshaw-street, in breaking to her the news of the death of her heroic husband—Sergent Thomas Gill, of the Warrington Territorials.
SERGEANT' THOMAS GILL Killed in Action.

div.head: An Old Friendly Society Man
div.p: An Old Friendly Society Man

The dead Sergeant, who was 28 years of age, had ,been in the Territorials for nine or ten years: At the outbreak Of war he left Messrs. Peter Walker's Brewery, 'Where he had been .employed since leaving the Silver-street School, to rejoin. He was a frequent attender at the Beivsey-road. Wesleyan Church and he member of the Order of Druids, whilst at one time he was connected wi-di the local corps of the St. John Ambulance Brigade. He .had held the rank of sergeant for four or five years and was at ore time secretary to the Battalion Sergeants' mess.

div.head: SERGEANT W. BAILEY.
div.p: SERGEANT W. BAILEY.
Held The South African Medal And At as Proud Of It.

"He was a• brave lad and he .was keen on his work as a 'Terrier.' .He often said after war was declared that he would not -Miss the fighting for anything!" These words were spoken, to an "Examiner" man, of Sergeant William Bailey, by one who had known the gallant warrior well practically the whole of his life.

div.head: Pathetic Reminder of Former Gallantry.
div.p: Pathetic Reminder of Former Gallantry.

Sergeant Bailey, whose name appears in the list of the brave Warringtonians who have given their lives for their country, was a married man and lived at 50 Laira-street, where one of his most cherished possessions— a vellum testimonial appreciative of his pre- vious services to the Empire—hangs on the wall and is proudly exhibited by his grief-stricken widow to the many who call to tender their sympathy with her in her great. bereavement. Promoted After Going On Active Service.

Sergeant Bailey was thirty-two years of age and he first 'donned the King's uniform in the days of the old Volunteers, with whom he 6erved in the 13oer War, .and for service in which be was awarded the coveted ...South
-Afric..an medal. He went to the Front with tho 'l3ez.—.ltomials tebrua-ry last land was A

div.head: CORPORAL S. T. INCE.
div.p: CORPORAL S. T. INCE.
Fine MI-Round Athlete Shot Through
The Heart.

Corporal Sidney Thomas Ince, who fell in the, charge, was a single man, aged ,28, and made his home with his widowed mother, Mrs. Mary Jane Ince, at 3, Tanner's-lane. The dead corporal worked at Messrs. Crosfield's— on the oil plant—and he was one of the best- liked and .most respected employes in the whole of the big works, and many are the tributes of regret that have reached his mother froni officials of the works and fellow-workers. Corporal Ince was a young man of splendid charactei, and he was a well-known worker in connection with St. Paul's Church. As a boy he attended the Sunday School in connec- tion with that church, and subsequently be- came a member of the Bible Class for youths and young men. He was educated at. the Heathside School, and won a scholarship tenable at the MuniciPal Technical Institute for attendance and good conduct at the Heath- side evening continuation school. Eight Years A Territorial.
Corporal Ince had been eight years, in the

Territorials, • having finished one term and nearly completed another. The outbreak of war found him holding the rank of Lance- Corporal, and he was shortly afterwards pro- moted to full corporal, whilst shortly before his untimely end he had been acting in the place of a sergeant who had had to leave the trenches.
"A Brave Soldier, and We Shall Miss Him."

The news of the Corporal's heroic end was conveyed to his mother in a letter written by Sergeant A. Jeffs (No. 1 Platoon, "A" Co.) and received on Tuesday morning. The letter ran: "It is with deep regret that I have to write to inform you that your son was killed in' action at 5.30 a.m. on June 16th. . , . . Sidney was my corporal and he gave. me your address and asked me to write to you if any- thing happened. That was just before we went into action. On behalf of my platoon please allow me to express regret and sym- pathy with you in your great loss. Your son wds a brave soldier and we shall miss him very much. His value to rnf, as a corporal, I cannot find words to describe, and as a soldier and an honest. straightforward man I have never met the like."
CORPORAL S. T. INCE. , Killed in Action.

div.head: His End Was Free From Pain.
div.p: His End Was Free From Pain.

. , A second letter from a brother non. corn.— Corporal T. Jackson—ran: "The fatal bullet penetrated his heart and his end was free from pain. He died a minute,or two after being hit and without regaining consciousness. This must be a great hour of trial for you; I know it is .a great- one for me. . . . May it be some consolation to you to know that he died bravely doing his duty for his King and country. Sidney was my one great, particular nal ':right from the time we mobilised. The Germans got me a short while after, and I am writing this from a base hospital."

div.head: Footballer and Rifle Shot.
div.p: Footballer and Rifle Shot.

The late . Corporal Ince was an all-round athlete. Two seasons ago—when they won the medals—he captained Crosfield's team in the Works' Rugby Football Competition,- and whilst the Territorials were undergoing their training he. acted as captain of his company football team and Also of the company harriers .and shooting team. Under his leadership his company won the cups offered by the officers for both shooting and football. He was well known locally as a splendid gymnast.

"One Hun threw a brick at one of our chaps ' —but it Wes the last brick he will ever throw ! It is very common for the Hun to tell us that he is fed up and to ask us whether we are not the same, but our replylis to rip' a volley at them and to remind them of their gases and 'other things. We are always spoiling each other's meals by .shooting at top sand-bags, whenever we see smoke. It cuts the bag and the dirt flies all over the nice meal. One Germhun shouted across to one of our fellows the oth6r day: 'Go and get. your break- fast, you fool!' A .brick was thrown into our trench and tied to it was a paper -on whia' was written: Tllere'.; not many of us here and we are shifting out of,i.t soon!' . . . . to us. It blew me against the parapet of the trench and covered me with dirt, but did not injure me. _ _ _
It Was a Glorious Death.

"I got up and went to our John to see if I could do anything for him, but it was no use, for a piece of the she'll had hit him in the head. He had no pain, for he was killed instantly. It was a glorious death, for he was doing his duty to his country during one of the heaviest bom- bardments that has over been known. I have lost a. brave brother. He was one of the best, and it is a hard blow to me."

Private Coyne, in his last letter home, referring to the prospect of serious fighting, said: "We shall be going to-night, not knowing whether we shall get back or not, but I have confidence in my God to bring me through." A Signaller and Dispatch Rider.

Private Coyne, who was a single man, was 21 years of age. He was educated at St. Ann's School, and for several years was employed in the wheel shop at the Pearson and Knowles' Coal and Iron Co.'s Works. He joined the Territorials two months before they were, mobolised for war service, and at the Front he htts acted as a signaller and dispatch rider. He attended the Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church, and taught in the Sunday school connected with that church.

He was a keen all-round sportsman, and had played cricket and football or Orford and Bewsey-road teams. He was also a member of the Bewsey-road Church Cycling Club. A younger brother, Walter, is in .training with the 2nd/ 4th Battalion of the South Lancashire Regiment in Kent.

Ragged School Connection.

Aged 22, Drummer E. Marsden was educated at Orford Schools, and on Sundays attended the Ragged School—to the band of which he had belonged from childhood: His .nrst employment was at Orford Tanyard, and after a short stay there entered as a cranedriver the Vulcan Foundry. Here he remained until the outbreak of war—when he was called up with the other "Terriers." He had for four years belonged to "the drums" in that movement.

The Drummer took a great interest in sport, and belonged to S. George's Mission Football Club and the Ragged School Cricket Club. His younger brother is also a drummer in the reserve battalion of the local- Territorials, and is now engaged on recruiting rallies. A brother-in-law also belongs to the Royal .Welsh Fusiliers, and is about to go 6n active service "somewhere abroad."

div.head: PRIVATE ARTHUR EARLEY
div.p: PRIVATE ARTHUR EARLEY
Graphic Last LetterDeseribes The Big
Fight.

Private Arthur Earley was snother of War- rington's brave Territorials to give his life for King and Country. Twenty-two years of age awl single, he made his home, prior to offering himself for active service, with .his mother, and his step-father, Mr. and Mrs. Walter Hart, at 9, Foundry-street. As a boy he attended St. Benedict's School in Orford-lane, and after leaving there he, went to work for the Castle Rubber • Company. • About three years ago, however, he, transferred his services to the St. Helens Cable Company, where he was liked both by his fellow-employes and by his supe- riors, one of whom—Mr. Seymour, the works manager—was the first to sympathetically break the news of his heroic death to his rela- tives. Private Earley—described by a comrade and friend as one of the keenest and smartest soldiers in "the old battalion "—joined the Territorials about five years ago, but left, owing to exigencies of business, at the expira- tion of the three-year-term, only to join again as soon as war broke out and volunteers were called for

div.head: Position In " A Dead!y Wood."
div.p: Position In " A Dead!y Wood."

The last. letter received by the mother from the gallant Territorial w. ptIITP!CI on the 14th inst., and in it he said: "We have taken up a fresh position- and we know about it! You have heard much about the fine town where we are, but it would make you cry to see it!. No one lives in it now, and there must be almost millions of pounds worth of stuff lying about, but it is no use to us! Manchester isn't a patch .on it! From our rest-camp to the firing-line we have to pass through all this ruined beauty, never knowing the number of shells we may have to ' whack ' between us. Once through the town we have the doubtful pleasure of using a pontoon bridge over a cer- tain famous river. . . . . • After a long march over the other side of, the river we land in 'hell. We took up our ef)osition, the other day, in a deadly wood. In this wood the Huns were, in parts, only about 'twenty-five yards from us; indeed, as we looked round, when the 'star-lights' went up, we seethed td be sur- rounded.

div.head: When the "Panto." Started.
div.p: When the "Panto." Started.

"We appeared to be absolutely 'in a horse- shoe.'. As soon as darkness came the 'panto.' started. B-a-a-ng! bang! ba-a-ng!—Cr-a-a-ack ! bang went the trench bombs and the hand gren4es and bullets and other missiles flew from trench to trench, and—oh! it was real hell. It was simply horrible in that wood. • I have never prayed 80 much in my life and I do thank God a thousand times.that I-have now landed out of it once again for another spell of rest. You will' .be all smiling next week —perhaps this week !—when you read the war news. We .ctre all preparing for it—inspecting our rifles, trying our bayonets, &c. I'll tell you no 'more, but I hone we get through it, and then I'll tell you all about it afterward.- In the day-time it is more pleasant than at night, what with `drumming-up' [Le., cooking] and

Aged 45, Private Houghton was employed as a glass-netting-weaver by the hiLeeross Company. lais occupation he had been following for 27 years. .4eviously he attended as a boy the Heathside Schools. , At one time the Private was captain of the Parish Church Football Team when it carried off a cup, and received an inscribed silver metiai from the hands of Mr. Davies, solicitor. He served through the Boer War—he was a member of the first lot of Volunteers to go\ out to South Africa. For his services there he received the medal with five bars, whilst he also attained the rank of Sergeant. •

On August 4th he rejoined the Territorials, and relinquished his raniL of Sergeant in order to go with a comrade. From th 6 Front he has written many letters to his home and friends— by all of whom he was highly respected. , Private Houghton leaves a widow and a (laughter and young son.

Private Wm. Henry Hollowell, who is in- cluded in the list of those who have sacrificed the:i. lives c, o their Country's cause, was a married man and his home was at 2, Jockey- street, off Winwick-road. He was only 26 years of age, and besides a widow, he leaves two young children. A Warringtonian bred and born, he was the son of Mr. and Mrs. Chas. Hollowell, of Dolman's-lane and, as a boy, he attended St. Mary's Roman Catholic School. On leaving school he entered the service of the Corporation as a scavenger, and he had just completed thirteen years' service to the town in that humble, but very important capacity, when the war broke out and he offered his services for the Front. Ile had completed four . . _ _ _ _ _

years in the Territorials before the declaration of war, but when the call for men came he patriotically offered himself, and his services were accepted. He was a keen sportsman and took a player's interest in football, having at

"It is with a very sad heart that I have to inform you that your son Harry was killed in action yesterday. He was doing his bit, hold- ing the trenches during a charge, when a shell came and hit the parapet just in front of where Harry was standing, burying him and half a dozen others. He did not suffer any pain, death being instant. All the boys in No. 10 Platoon are very *much grieved about him, for he was one of the best, and was popular with everybody. Mr. and Mrs. Thomas Sumner, of 15, Robson- street, received on Tuesday morning the follow- ing:letter, dated the 18th "'I am very sorry to inform you of the death of your son George. lie was killed yesterday during the heavy bombardment, having been. hit in the head by a piece of shell. He died almost instantly; and he has been laid to rest on the field of battle, along with many other fallen heroes. George was in my section; and out of nine men 1 have only four left. Please accept my sincerest sympathy. George has been my closest friend out here, and I deeply mourn his loss. The only consolation that I can .offer to you is that' he (lied doing his duty. —Yours truly (PTE.) J. W. MARSH, Section Commander." . _

div.head: PRIVATE- 11. HEACOCK.
div.p: PRIVATE- 11. HEACOCK.
Hit In The Arm And Shoulder, But
Not Seriously.

On Sunday morning Miss Minnie Ileacoek, of 13, Marsh house-lane, learnt that her brother, Private Herbert Ileacock, had been wounded. The news was conveyed through the medium of a field card. On. Thursday came the following letter from .the wounded man, addressed from Ellesmere Cottage llosPital, Salop :—" I am doing all right, .and am in the pink! 1 have got in a good place. "Shall Not Be Long Before I Am Home."

"I was wounded by shrapnel in the right arm and loft shoulder, but the hurt is not very serious. 1 shall not be long before I am at home. it was the hottest place we have been in. Do not trouble about me, I am all right."

div.head: Interested in Football.
div.p: Interested in Football.

Private Heacock, who is 28 years of age, is a single Hidll. He joined the -Territorials at the outbreak of war, and is at present a Member of C Company. He formerly worked at Messrs. Richmond's, and was educated at the 'Hamil- ton-street School. He was a. member of the Warrington Football Club. Three of the wounded " Terrier's " brothers are serving with the Colours. t

PRIVATE HERBERT KNOX. A Crosfield's Wharf-Hand In The Casualty List. Private Herbert Knox, whose home is at 59, Aiken-street,, is included in the list- of those wounded in the desperate and successful assault on the German trenches. He is twenty-two years of age and is a single man and, before the outbreak of war, he resided with his parents and was employed by Messrs. Crasfield's us a wharf hand. As a boy he attended the St. Barnabas' Day School.

div.head: PRIVATE A. 11 ALKER. "II Is War Of Shells," A'riles
div.p: PRIVATE A. 11 ALKER. "II Is War Of Shells," A'riles
AVounded " Terrier."
Private A. Walker, writing to Mr. AVOI), Pad- gate-lane, assistant secretary of the Warrington Adult School, from .the Kent Territorial V.A.D. Hospital, Tonbridge, says _ - . . • .. . _

" Just a line to:Say Chat l'am back in Eng- lund wounded, but not badly—a small wound in the head and a sprained ankle. We had 'ago ' at the Germans. We had a few killed and they lost a lot of men. We captured about 200 of them and two lines of trenches—so we didn't do se had. When I say `we ' I -don't mean the 4th only, of course for there were a lot of regi- ments in. the affair, and I can tell you it was like hell let loose. Over 300 guns going at once between us; but it is a war of shells, and the more we get the sooner the awful war will be over. • Give my best wishes to all at the Friends' Old School. • Hoping to see you soon."

div.head: LINCE-CORPORAI. FL BRADSHAW. Hit In The Head, Hand And Ribs By
div.p: LINCE-CORPORAI. FL BRADSHAW. Hit In The Head, Hand And Ribs By

Shrapnel. Lance-Corporal Robert Bradshaw, whose name figures in the list of wounded, has been four years in the Territorials, and, prior to offering himself for active service, was employed at Messrs. Peter Walker and Sou's brewery. lie is a single man, twenty years of age, and he makes his home with his parents at 30, Orford. lane. As a boy he attended St. Benedict's day school and the Silver-street Wesleyan Sunday school. lie Went to the Front with, the first batch of local "Terriers" to cross the Chan- nel.

On Thursday afternoon his mother received a letter from him, in which he.said : "I am in hospital and ant going on fine. . . . You need not worry yourself about me, for I think I am quite safe. I got hit in the head with shrapnel and also in the. ribs and band. The doctor has got the shrapnel out of my head,-and I feel a lot better for the- operation. . . . I will let you know more when I arrive in England, and I expect that will be in a day or two."

div.head: PRIVATE 11. KITCHEN.
div.p: PRIVATE 11. KITCHEN.
Friend W'rites That The Wound Is
Not Serious.

Private Harold Kitchen, whose home is at 41, Bewsey-road, is included in the list of Terri- torials wounded. Writing to a mutual acquaint- ance to inform him of the fact, Lance-Corporal Arthur Roberts says:—" Like many others he was hit last time we were in the trenches, when we had a rough spell of it. • . . I was one of his pals, both here and at home, and I thought it my place to write and let You know. I cannot tell you exactly how it happened, and I don't think the wound is anything serious; it was the shock that was the worst. As far as T can gather he was struck in the side by a piece of shrapnel. 'I daresay it will not be long before he is in England again. . . . I did not get to know that he had been hit until about ten hours afterwards."

The wounded ma-n, like the writer of the letter—who is now a dispatch rider—was for- merly, for six years, a member of the St. Paul's CompanY of the Church Lads' Brigade; indeed he rose to the rank of Sergeant-Major in that organisation. Some half-dozen other local members of the Brigade are among the wounded.

div.head: LANCE-CORPORAL J. J. HOWL. Hit In The Knee And Is " Quite All Right."
div.p: LANCE-CORPORAL J. J. HOWL. Hit In The Knee And Is " Quite All Right."

Lance-Corporal J. J. howl, whose wife resides at 37, Catharine-street, Bewsey, has been wounded, though not in the big fight, for it was on 'June 7th that he was hit. The news was conveyed to Mrs. Howl in a letter written by Private B. Watson, of B Company, who is acting as servant to one of tne medical officers. " I can assure you. that he is quite all right and that you liave nothing to worry about" writes Private Watson. "He has been hit in the knee. . . . Be received all Possible care from Dr. Law, who takes the greatest pains with all the wounded men who come under him. . . Your husband will leave us to-night (.June 9th), for the clearing station, whence he will be dispatched to the base."

div.head: PRIVATE J. MANNION.
div.p: PRIVATE J. MANNION.
Thouubt He Would Not See Home Again When The Shell Burst.

A letter received .by Mrs. 31annion, at 9, Napier-street, from hospital at Boulogne, con- tained the news that her .son, Private John Ilannion was lying there, recovering from shell wounds in the head and arm. These were received, according to his letter, whilst taking part in the famous charge. "When the shell burst I thought I should not be coming home again" he writes. "it was a large piece which hit the. I am in a very nice hospital here, and I shall not be long before I am home." Private Mannion, who is 19 years of age, for- merly worked at the Paddington Bone Works. He has been in the Territorials three years. Another brother, William, is in training in Kent with tilt) reserve battalion of the Terri- torials. •

div.head: DRUMMER J. LIGHTFOOT.
div.p: DRUMMER J. LIGHTFOOT.
Hit 'Whilst Carrying Wounded
Comrade To Safety.

It appears from a letter writ-ten home by Drummer Joseph Lightfoot that he 'was wounded while carrying a wounded comrade to safety. He had previously been buriAl through the wall of the trench being blown in over him, and he states that it was fifteen minutes before he could be extricated from the fallen earth.

Drummer Lightfoot, who is 20 years of age, is a single man, and makes his home with his parents at 9, Dudley-street., He worked in the nail shop at the Whiteeross Co.'s Works. He was for a long time Scoutmaster Of the White- cross Company of Boy Scouts. ,of joined the Territorials as a bugler when only fourteen years of age, and went to the Front with his. battalion in February.

div.head: PRIVATE H. GLOVER.
div.p: PRIVATE H. GLOVER.
Wounded A Third Time As He NA
AA ail lug For The Stretcher.

On_ Monday morning, Mrs. Glover, ,of For- shaw-street, received the news that her son, Private Harry Glover, was wounded. He him- self wrote the letter conveying the information, and in it he says that he was wounded in three places, having a -slight shrapnel wound in the right leg, a bullet wound in the left leg—both done at the same time—and a wound in the shoulder. The shoulder-wound * was received after he had been lying in the trench from morning till night waiting for the stretcher- bearers to .come, and was caused by a shell bursting right on top of him. In his own words it "made .an ugly mess of my shoulder. I will be in England to-morrow," concluded Private Glover's undated letter.

Educated at. St. Ann's School, Private Glover started work at Messrs. Jackson's pawnshop, in Orford-lane, where he remained until the outbreak of war. Ile played football for the Warrington Thursdays, and. is an all-round athlete.

div.head: I'ItIVA'rE S. MILLETT.
div.p: I'ItIVA'rE S. MILLETT.
Says Hundreds, Of Women And
Children Were Killed

Private S. Alinett was wounded in the head by shrapnel during the big fight on the lUth. News to this effect reached his cousin—with whom he made his home, at 92, drford-lane--- on Tuesday. Later, the injured man wrote a letter to his cousin in which he said that the fight hi which he was: hit was thoi hottest the " Terriers " had been in. Itundreds of women and children, he Said, were killeth and not a whole house was 'left standing in the vicinity.

div.head: " Joined Up" When The War Began.
div.p: " Joined Up" When The War Began.

Private Millett is a single man, 26 years of age. He formerly worked at the Bewsey Wire Ropery. .lie was educated at St. Benedict's School, Orford-lane, and attended the Bewsey- road Wesleyan Church. He was a member .of the Junior Conservative Club in Orford-lane. He joined the Territorials on the outbreak of war, and went to the Front in February.

div.head: PRIVATE ERNES'!' Sllllll.
div.p: PRIVATE ERNES'!' Sllllll.
Orford St. John's Football Play yr Wounded In 'Fhe knee.

Ptivuto Ernest Smith, 21, Norris-street, one of the members et the Orford St. John's Foot- ball Chili, who enlisted almost in a body, nukes the seventt of that patriotic club to iigure in the casualty list. lie was employed at Vichmond's as an apprentice to pattern- moulding. lie is only eighteen years old. Ile Is a good boxer anti gymnast. His brothers, Jelin and Fred, ate also on servicv- Writing to his brother John, . who is with the ammunition column at Birmingham, he

! '1 am feeling well again. lam wounded ! in my right knee, having been struck with a piece of shell. We were told we were in support for a charge at . We had to march about seven miles. ' We started about six o'clock and arrived at 2.30 next morning. The fun then started. We had only been in the trenches five ininutes when the Germans started to shell us like mad, but they did no damage just then. Meg their guns started and you should have heard the noise! Then our brave lath made the charge and we took the trenches and tried to make further head- way, but we could not get any further be- cause the shells were coming in thousands. Yes; all Our chaps weiit through it and a good many must have been hit, &c. Well; there was practically no one left round me at the finish. lam now in a fine hospital, making rapid progress."

div.head: PRIVATE J. MORGAN. Five Territorials Bowled Over By The Second Shell.
div.p: PRIVATE J. MORGAN. Five Territorials Bowled Over By The Second Shell.

Private J. ,Morgan, whose home is at 33, Liverpool-road, was the first to break the news to his parents that he had been wounded. He is 24 years of age, and prior to volunteering for Active service, he was employed at the White- cross CP.'S Works. He has had about six years' continuous service in the Territorials. He received his education at the Wycliffe day school, and he was a regular attendant at the Young Men's Class in connection with the Working Men's Mission in Thewlis-Street. lie is single.

Wounded Man's Praise for Stretcher-Bearer. In a second letter home, dated June 22nd, he says that ho is "-doing fine, and that the pain of his wound is not half so bad as it was. He is not now, he adds, in danger, although at the time or writing the piece of shrapnel which caused his injury had not been extracted. 'Our battalion" he continues, "were told off as One of. the reserves in a elvarge, and we took- up position just behind the firing lane. • We had not been in position very long before shell No. 1 came' over. Shell No. 2 accounted for me and four others. . . . We received very good at- tention at the hands of one of our stretcher- bearers, Private Buttery." In a previous letter the wounded man wrote that owing to the severity of the enemy's fire he. had to lie in the trench about fourteen hours after being hit before he could be removed.

div.head: PRIVATE ALBERT NEWTON.
div.p: PRIVATE ALBERT NEWTON.
Local Swimmer AVounded In Ankle
Ind Shoulder.
Mr. and Mrs. Thomas Newton, of 247, Liver- pool-road.- received on Wednesday the following letter—dated 'the previous Saturday—from their son Albert:—

"I am doing fairly well. . . . There is no need for you to worry; I will soon be all right. I was hit .early on Wednesday morning, the 16th, with a shrapnel bullet—thrpugh my right leg just above the ankle, and I also received a slight wound behind my right shoulder. I shall be in England by the time you get this. I've had a good innings, hut they've bowled me out at last. lamin a nice soft bed, quite `comfy.'" Writing on Thursday from the Royal Infirm- ary, Leicester, Private Newton says : "I am doing champion; my bed is on the verandah— better than the ward. I was wondering how W. Gibson had gone on; be was all right when I got hit. W. Massey was hit at the same time as me; also S. Millett. W. Massey and I were only saying the day before the battle how we had stuck 'together; and we lay in the trench together while they wrapped us up. He was hit in the hip—not very badly. It is glorious here."

div.head: Employe of Messrs. Hesketh.
div.p: Employe of Messrs. Hesketh.

_ Private Newton, who was educated at the Arpley-street School and Sankey Bridges Wes- leyan Sunday school, is in peace times employed as a painter by Messrs. Hesketh. He is a mem- ber of the Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Bible Class, and also an enthusiastic frequenter of the Baths.
He joined the Territorials at the beginning of September, leuviug Warrivstau, bi laT later.

div.head: Old Botelerian Making Excellent
div.p: Old Botelerian Making Excellent

Progress. Lance-Corporal Arthur Stuart Page—who is progressing very favourably indeed in a French hospital—is the son of Mr. H. Stuart Page, of 19, Stanley-street. His age is nineteen. A native of Padgate, the Lance-Corporal received the early .part of his education at the village school, whence he proceeded to the .Clrammar School. Here he remained for four years, afterwards joining the Borough Treasurer's Department. Ile joined the local Territorials twelve months previous to the outbreak of war.

div.head: SNELSON.
div.p: SNELSON.
Florence 31111 s Employe Wounded In
Left Arm.

Private George lerederick Snelson, of 5, Neston-street, sent home on Sunday morning a. field card bearing the news of his wounding in the left arm by shrapnel on the 16th. He now lies in the Boulogne Canadian Hospital.

A 4 a boy, Private Snelson attended -Heath. side School, and St. Peter's Church. He is forty years' of age, and in peace times is employed at the Florence Mills, Howley. He had been at the Front for about three months —having joined the local Terriers" ten months ago.

div.head: MASKELL.
div.p: MASKELL.
Ohl Silver-street Scholar Receives Two Wounds.

_ On Thursday the news arrived at the house of a neighbour that Private Thomas kaskell. of 26, Orford-lane, had been wounded in the right arm and head. The tidings were sent by Lance-Corporal Bradshaw--also of the " Terriers."

Aged 24, Private Maskell is unmarried, and makes his home with his parents. After finishing hi S education at the Silver-street Schools, he entered employment in an adjacent district. He worships at the Bewsey- road Wesleyan Church—the choir of which he is a member. He has also attended the Sun- day school in connection with the church. He had been at the Front since March, and he has a brother serving in the Army.

CORPORAL J. BUTLER. Hit Behind The Shoulder By A Glancing Shot. In a letter to his mother, 'Mrs. Butler, of 100, Lythgoes-lane, Corporal John Butler tells how he was wounded. got hit behind the left shoulder," he writes. "It was just. a glancing shot. . . . I was wounded at about four o'clock on the Wednesday morning. . . We n had 'to stand a awful shelling. . . ." Corporal Butler is 24 years of age, and is a single than. He formerly worked as a Plate- layer on the Cheshire Lines Railway. A brother, Charles, .who is in the Rifle Brigade, is at pres- ent home recovering from wounds. An uncle was, recently killed in action. A second uncle is a prisoner of war in Germany, while a third is in training with the reserve Battalion of War- rington Territorials in Kent.

div.head: IS11"10 "TERRIERS."
div.p: IS11"10 "TERRIERS."
Local Lancer Describes Their Surroundings.

Lance-Corporal Charles M. -Artustrongr.of the (Dtuie of Cambridgen Own) Lancers, who returned from India some 111011t11s ago—writing on June Lau front the Front to Lis mother, Mrs. Gordon, at Cr, Museum-street, buys:— " We have not been in any imminent danger. The enemy's long-range guns have had several • pops ' at the reserves behind, but have never done any damage,,ezicepting to the fields round about.

div.head: Met Many Old Friends.
div.p: Met Many Old Friends.

"Last week ' Teddy ' [Corporal Gordon] and I quite accidentally came across our "Terriers' —who had been camping not more than a mile away irom us ever tilliCe we came up here. The first chap we came across was ono named whom I remembered from the time when I was an 31.1.; hp knew me immediately' too. From 'him we learned where the batta- should say, the two companies— that were not in. the trenches were staying; and oil we went. We asked for Frank Coak- ley, who used to teach ''teddy' at St. Mary's School and who was an 1‘1..1. with us. From Frank we heard all there was to hear of their doings since they came to.Frauce in February.

div.head: Hearts of Gold.
div.p: Hearts of Gold.

• • "There's one thing I must not forget to mention about our "forriers."rhat is: Though they have had things a bit 'rough they are as cheery as ever; not one of them seemed downhearted in the Aust. They .are doing their bit with hearts as good as gold, and are quite determined that. they will do their utmost, with the rest,' to bring this war home to the Kaiser.

"it was surprising how many of them knew Teddy and me, and also how many faces we recognised. It brought home quite near to be among so many of the ' Townies." There was Bob Main, Fred Stephens, young Charlie Taylor—oh! -and many others whose names I had forgotten. Of course it took us a long time to recognise some of the lads, but that. didn't prevent us from feeling quite pleased with our- selves. We walked along with them for about half a mile, when they went up to the trenches again. Then we bade them good luck, and they promised to do their best to help make that hole for us to gallop through. "We had a long talk with Mr. Ingram, the quartermaster, and his -assistant, Q.M.S. Alladice.

div.head: What a Dcvastated Spot!
div.p: What a Dcvastated Spot!

"Whilst we were up forward we certainly took the opportunity of looking round that historical Belgian town --. What a devastated spit it is! What a terrible game the Germans have played with it! In the whole place I don't suppose there is a building that has not been hit. Bricks Lunt mortar strewed the streets; furniture was lying about all over the place. In many of the houses one could plainly see that the late occupants bad attempted to pack up some of their belongings, but had. had to .make a hurried exit—iir order :probably to escape with their lives. We didn't spend much time looking at the ruitieN louses, for what we particularly wanted to see were the Cathedral and the old Cloth Hall. What a sight! Nothing but broken walls and piles of masonry remained of what had once been two splendid pieces of architecture. If the Kaiser were to walk round, no doubt he would con- gratulate his worthy gunners on their splendid. work. It might do some of the strikers and other malcontents a bit of good to see it!"

div.head: "MEN BLOWS TO PIECES ALL
div.p: "MEN BLOWS TO PIECES ALL
ROUND ME."

" Terrier's" Hurried Impressions Of • The Historic Fight. Private Alfred Leicester, whose home is. at 6, Ellen-street, and who, before volunteerinig for active service with the "Terriers," workH at the Bewsey Forge, writes to his wife to say that he is safe, and proceeds: "No doubt you have heard of the terrible battle; I shall remember it to my dying day! Men were being blown to pieces all around me, and how I escaped death God alone knows. Of course, the Germans were getting the same as we :were, and when we got into their trenches we saw what appeared like thousands of dead piled up. Be- fore we took their trenches the beggars kept on mowing us down with machine guns and rifle fire, whilst all the time their big guns were doing their best to blow us to pieces. Germans Cry For Mercy.

"The murderous fire was kept up until We got to their trenches, and then they would not face the bayonet. 'Mercy, English ! ' they cried, and we had to take them prisoners. We have lost about 250 killed and wounded. Life is very uncertain here, and he is a very lucky man who pulls through. . . . It is hell on earth • • • . but I am afraid it will last a long tiniQ yet.".
PRIVATE G. 11. SUMNER. Killed in Action. •

afterwards going to work as a moulder for Messrs. Fletcher, Russell. Here he continued to work until August, when he was called up with the other "Terriers." He had been one of _their number for three years_ previously.
He was also a former member .of the St. Clement's Mission Church Lads' Brigade. He attended that Mission and Sunday school: He was a single man.

div.head: PRIVATE J. H. CARTER.
div.p: PRIVATE J. H. CARTER.
Mainstay Of Parentless Home killed In The Memorable Charge.

Particular pathos attaches to the loss of Private John Henry Carter, whose home was at 9, Admiral-street. Only twenty years of age— he would have been 21 had he lived until next December—he was the main support of his aged grandmother, Mrs. Bond—his mother's mother —and of a younger brother, Albert, who is of school-going age: "He was a•good lad; a right good lad V' his grandmother told an "Examiner" reporter. "-He put his home and his brother and me above everything; he was happy if we were happy and everything was going on all right in the house. He was not. likg lots of other lads; nay, there was not a better lad breathing." The old lady proudly called atten- tion to Me comfortable, tidy • sitting-room in which our representative interviewed her, and, pointing to the numerous bric-a-brac with which it was adorned, said, "Those were his work; he liked to see the hale nice."

div.head: Orphaned When a Boy.
div.p: Orphaned When a Boy.
Private Carter lost his patents when he was a boy, and was brought up by his grandmother, of whom he was intensely fond. He received

Warrington, who is reported kiled, joined the lerritorials eight years ago, though he only attained his twentieth birthday last Christmas. lie was employed 'prior to the outbreak of war, at Walker's Brewery. Aa a bey he attended the National -School. He was a worshipper at Brick-street Church, and a member ui the Rechabites.
" You Have No Need To Be Alarmed" Writes
Comrade.

The following letter from Drummer Joseph Lightfoot tO C.-5.,01. Ryder, who is in camp in England awaiting orders to go to the Front, seems to throw' some doubt on the veracity of the official report as to the young Drummer's fate:—" I am sorry to inform you that your son Jack has been wounded in the back with shrapnel, in four places. You have no need to be alarmed. Ile will pull through all right. Just after he was hit and I had dressed his wounds, we were both buried—another shell hitting the iiarapeti I am slightly wounded." Two Cousins Among The Wounded.
Prutunier Ryder has two cousins in the Territorials, and 'both have been wou4ded. They are Privates Pinsen and Morris.
DRUMMER JOHN RYDER. Reported Killed in Action.
PRIVATE J. 11. CARTER. Killed in Action.
PRIVATE 11. DODD Killed in Action.

div.head: Trusting to be Spared.
div.p: Trusting to be Spared.

So recently as last F,riday morning Private Dodd's last letter was received. It ran: "I am in the best of health at present., I thank God for it; for we are having a warm time of it just now. . . . It is bad to get into the trenches at this *point—for the, firing line i. 4 the shape of a horseshoe, and we have the fire all round us. . . I was glad to hear that you enjoyed your tea at Hill Cliffe. I wish I had been with iyou. But I am trusting to God to spare me to come back to you and the chil- dren We are in the trenches while I am writing this letter; I don't know how long it will be before we get relieved. It would look better of all the men that are anle if they would come here and get shut of this job. . . . What with the mud and the shells and the bullets, it is lively, I can tell you."

div.head: REPORTED KILLED.
div.p: REPORTED KILLED.
DRUMMER JOHN RYDER.
Buried By Exploded Trench Baying AVomul Messed. Drummer John Ryder, son or C.-S.-M. (leo. Ryder and Mrs. Ryder, of 25, Grafton-street,
PRIVATE J. T. TAYLOI?, Reported Killed in Action.

Young Men's Society 'contains his name, and when he went away on September 6th, to under- go his war training, many of his fellow members and friends assembled to give him a fitting send- off. A Popular Young Man.

In peace time Private Taylor lived With his rather and mother at 13, Naylor-street. He was well liked by his employers, neighbours and workmates; in fact, as his mother expressed it, " He has got the best of names—wherever you gto and whoever you ask!" A brother of his— Private William Taylor—is in training with the reserve battalion of the Territorials.

div.head: PRIVATE J. T. TAYLOR. Name In List. Of Dead, Hut Nurse Writes He Is Only .Woun(101.
div.p: PRIVATE J. T. TAYLOR. Name In List. Of Dead, Hut Nurse Writes He Is Only .Woun(101.

The name "Private J. T. Taylor" appears in the list of the honoured dead Territorial vie- titns of the heroic trench-taking episode, in which the local citizen soldiers so distinguished themselves as to win the praise of a Brigadier- General and the undying homage of the people of the town, 'whose name they have covered with So much glory. On Wednesday afternoon, however, there arrived at his home a letter written on his behalf by a nurse, stating that he had been badly wounded in the head. Son of Well-known Footballer.

Private John Thomas Taylor, to give him his full baptismal name, is 24 years of age, and he comes of fighting stock; indeed, his father—Cor- poral Jock Taylor-.--is at present stationed with a section of the South Lancashire Regiment in a well-known South Wales town. Corporal Tay- lor is, by the way, well known to the Warring- ton public as an old and clever footballer, hav- ing in the words of his wife, "played many a

William, they had to take him out of the trenches. He broke down when I spoke to him. .. . We passed a town completely blown to pieces. . , . There are men doing nothing but bury the dead, so you can tell what a grue- some job they have got. Jimmie Ditchford has been wounded in the leg. It has broken it, but it will bring him home to England. Good old England! Tell all .my friends at the Cable Works."

div.head: PRIVATE JOSEPH BOND,
div.p: PRIVATE JOSEPH BOND,
Two Day's After Engagement Reported Doing Well In Hospital.

'Some doubt seems to exist as to the f:ite I hat has befallen Private Joseph Bond, who with his parents at 5, Worrall's-row, Sankey Bridges. Mr. and -Mrs. Bond reeeived during the week-end a field postcard, dated June 18th, from their son, stating that he ins in hospital, doing well and likely to be discharged Shortly. No further news came to hand till Tuesday evening, when Mr. and Mrs. Bond found their son's name in the list of killed published in the evening papers. Private Bond was some two months back reported dead,- and it is hoped that another mistake has been made. Sankey's Goalkeeper.

Twenty-five years of age, Private Bond, who had completed four years as, a Territorial and passed fiat of the regiment, left the service of the Cable Company on the outbreak of war and rejoined the 4th South Lancs. lie kept ;goal for the Sankey Football Club, and won four medals. As a boy, he attended Sankey day and Sunday schools. . .

div.head: Emotion in the Trenches
div.p: Emotion in the Trenches

In his last letter home, Private Bend said: " One of the killed is my pal, W. Newns. Ifis brother was killed a litle while ago. His father is having some luck. - There is another brother out here'. When they told him about
PRIVATE J. BOND. Reported Killed in Action.

div.head: WOUNDED.
div.p: WOUNDED.
WRIGHT.
Took Nearly Two Hours To Dig Him Out After Shell Burst.

Drummer Peter W. Wright is at present in. the Wharncliffe Hospital, .ISheffield, suffering from a severe wound in the right arm received in the big -charge, He is 23 years of age, and he has been a citizen. -soldier upwards of twelve years, joining the old Volunteers when .a boy, and continuing to serve when the Territorial Battalion- was constituted. Ire received his education at the National School, and, prior to going on Active service, was a regular attendant at the Parisi' Church. He made his home with his brother-in-law and sister, Mr. and Mrs. John Hilton, at 64, Scott-street. His father was a keen. Volunteer and was awarded the Long SerL vice Medal'.

div.head: "Pal" Killed Whilst Laughing and Joking.
div.p: "Pal" Killed Whilst Laughing and Joking.

About a fortnight before be was wounded he lost one of hie dearest friends—Bugler Ratcliffe. The pair. were 'laughing and joking together in the trench when a bullet struck the bugler and killed him almost instantly.
Only One of Half a Dozen to be Dug Out Alive!

Mrs. Hilton received a letter from her brother a day or two ago, in which he said that his wound was caused by a species of shell 'which the " Tommies " has(' dubbed " the Kaiser's coal- box." "A coal-box,'" he wi•ote, " dropped into our trench and buried six of us when it ex- ploded., I was the only one of the half-dozen to come out alive, the other five poor chaps being suffocated. As • I lay underneath the soil, I prayed, and my prayer was heard. A chap ziamed Joe Eaton must have beard my cries, for

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 26, 1915.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 26, 1915.
. • :• • • ,"ra, - E TH.... I LLING 7 W DED 4 44, .0 A STORIES. .•
TERRITORIAL ROLL OF HONOUR
WOUNDED.
CONTINUED FROM PAGE 9.
SLIIGEANT A. SKELLIORNE.
Popular 'Warrington Forward Hit By Shell Fragments.

Sergeant Arthur Skelhorne, one.ot the idols of the followers of the doings of the Warrington Rugby F.C., for whonl,he played RS a forward, is included in the list of those who were wounded in the fierce•fight. His Last Aikpearance at Wilderspool.

Sergt. Skelhorne is 28 years of age, and he is the son of Mr. and Mrs. Thomas Skelhorne, of 219, Knutsford-road. As a boy he attended the St. James' day school, subsequently going to work in the grate department at Messrs. Fletcher, Russell and Co.'s works. He .played football in various ,schoolboy combinations, and as a lad showed such alertness and distinction at the game that he eventually came before the notice of the Warrington R.F.C. Committee, who gave him a trial, and were so satisfied with the result of the experiment that throughout_ four or five seasons lie had a regular place, first in the second team and subsequently in the premier thirteen. He made one appearance for his old club during last season, viz., on January 30th, when they played Oldham, and when he scored a brilliant try. He was then home on short furlough, for by that time he had rejoined the Territorials—in which lie had previously completed four years' meritorious service. The popular footballer rejoined the "Terriers" as a private, and was promoted to sergeant whilst the battalion were fitting themselves for their arduous and perilous duties at the front. Whilst taking part in the " Terriers' " gallant rush on the German trenches he was hit by fragments of a bursting shell in the back and shoulder. He was conveyed to hospital and operated upon, the shell fragments being taken out.
"Doing Fine" in a French Hospital.

Writing to his parents from the Ist Canadian Stationary Hospital, Boulogne, under date June 18th, the gallant Sergeant said: "Just a few lines to let you know that I am doing fine up to now and am keeping well. The shell fragments got me in the back and shoulder—about live pieceti in all. All have been got out. My shoulders are not so stiff this morning as they have been, nor are they as painful. I am in a very good bed, and in a healthy place, and am being well looked after and have (Toed food; in fact, I have all the attention I need. It is like being in Paradise, compared with being in the trenches. The sisters are fine, and what I have seen of them and their work up till now makes me realise that no words of mine could really express my gratitude, and that of my comrades, to them for . their kindness. Ido not know -whether or not I shall get to England, but I am hoping to do so as soon as possible." The foregoing letter was received on Monday morning. _

On Saturday morning the Sergeant's family received a brief note from Corporal Skelhorne. the Sergeant's brother, in which be said Ilutt he had seen "Arthur," who had told him to tell those at home not to worry, as his wound was not serious.

div.head: Dreadful Fight.
div.p: A Dreadful Fight.

A brother-in-law of the Brothers SkelLorne, Private Win. Davis—who married Miss Annie Skelhorne, and who is himself also serving with the "Terriers"—has written to his wife to say that the gallant Sergeant's wound is " not had at all." "Frank," he adds, " has just brought me Arthur's parcel over; he says it is no use wasting it. . . This last fight was a dread- ful one, but we won. Of course, I was not there. I am with the transport section, and we were about ten miles away. We have had a lot of fellows wounded, but I have heard that most of the cases are slight; which is a good job !"

div.head: LANCE-CORPL. F. J. PERCIVAL.
div.p: LANCE-CORPL. F. J. PERCIVAL.
One of Six " Terriers " Hit By The
Same Shell.

• News - reached Mrs. Percival at Orford- avenue on Monday, that her son,- Lance- orporal Francis Joseph Percival, of the War- rinFton Territorials, had been wounded in action. • Hopes to Rejoin Regiment in a Few Days.

Writing on June 18th to his mother, he-said: "I am going on fairly well. I suppose that by the time you get this letter you will know that we have had a scrap with the Germans, and some of their shrapnel managed to hit me in the back, but there is no case to alarm your- self; as I. am going on all right. lamin a field hospital at present, but I hope to rejoin my regiment in a few days' time. We started to bombard the Germaji trenches with our big guns, at three o'clock yesterday morning (June 17th). We Got H— From Their Heavy Artillery. "About four o'clock we started to advance upon their trench, which we soon occupied. There were a large number of prisoners taken —old men and young boys! We got h—' from their heavy artillery. I thought I would never get out alive. There were six of us hit by the same shell. We have had n lot of casualties in our lot. We have had a lot of wounded prisoners in here. They were very glad to be taken prisoners. I have lost all my belongings, as I had to leave them in the trench while .I got attended to."
Rejoined the " Terriers" on the Outbreak of War.

Lance-Corporal Percival, whose home is with his wife at 103, Mersey-street, had served in the Territorials before the war, and upon the out- break he rejoined. He was formerly employed at Messrs. Crosfield's works, and he worshipped at St. Mary's 'Roman Catholic Church.

div.head: LANCE-CORPL. WILLIANI GRUND‘'. Hit By A Bullet Whilst Coming Out Of
div.p: LANCE-CORPL. WILLIANI GRUND‘'. Hit By A Bullet Whilst Coming Out Of
lie Trenches.

" I have been wounded, but the wound is not so serious as I expected it would be." In these words Lance-Corporal Wm. Grundy, of the Territorials, conveyed to his father and mother --L-Mr. and Mrs. Grundy, of 87, Laira-street--the news that he had fallen victim to an enemy bullet. The gallant Lance-Corporal is 28 years of age, is single, and he had completed his four years in the Territorials before the war broke out, whereupon he lost no time in rejoining. After leavilig school he went to work at Messrs. Crosfield's boapery, but at the time of "joining Up," was employed by the Cheshire Lines Com- mittee. A keen footballer, he took part in the Works' Competition in more than one season, and was successful in winning a watch and medal.

Force of the Bullet Broken by Pocket Books. "By the time you get this," the Lance- Corporal's letter to his parents went on, "I shall be in England. You need not worry, as lam getting well looked after. The force of the bullet was broken by some books in my pocket. I got hit whilst we were coming out of the trenches. We were further •up the line this time than we had been previously, and it was an awful sight to see the town; there was not a whole place standing in it." A note, dated June 11th, was also received by the anxious parents from the Rev. W. T. Kempster, chaplain, who wrote that the wounded man was well enough to be moved, and was leaving for a hospital lower down the line. The reverend gentleman added: "He is in good heart, and I think there is no cause for over- anxiety."
Lance-Corporal Grundy has a brother and three cousins serving at the Front.

div.head: PRIVATE J. A% . EDDIE.
div.p: PRIVATE J. A% . EDDIE.
Private John William Eddie, of 102, Hardy- street, wrote home on Saturday morning to say he had been wounded. lie is employed at Walker's Brewery.
