div.head: LANCE-CORPORAL ASTLE.
div.p: LANCE-CORPORAL ASTLE.
Came Out Of " The Hie Scrap With A Shrapnel Wound In The Lee.

The first intimation that Lance-Corporal Joe Astle, whose home is at 9, Cobden-street i had been wounded, was contained in a letter written by himself the day after the "Terriers" had performed their great feat at arms. "I am in hospital at present" .he wrote, "having just come out of a big 'scrap.' 1 have a shrapnel wound in my left leg, and I have also hurt my back. Anyway, altogether I am feeling pretty bad. I cannot tell you how Peter or Arthur {two relatives who are also serving] have fared, for I was hit in a different part of the battlefield to that in which they were fighting. However. I know that their company got heavily shelled. " Those In Reserve Always Catch It Pretty

div.head: Hot."
div.p: Hot."

"They were in reserve and those in reserve, or support, always catch it pretty hot. The chances are that I shall not be stopping in the hospital in which I find myself at present, but it is a nice place, and the officers and nurses are very kind; It is a perfect treat ,to be, for a time, where it is quiet." Eight Years a Territorial. .

Lance-Corporal Astle is twenty-four years. of age and is unmarried, and prior to offering for active service, he worked in the export depart- ment at Messrs. Crosfield's Soapery. lie hB3 been eight years in the Territorials, and held his present rank before the outbreak of war. He was educated at St. Ann's School, and he attended St. Peter's Church.

Lance-Corporal Astle has a brother—Private Peter Astle—serving at the Front with the "Terriers," whilst another !rsrother, Private William.. is at present in training with the Reserve Battalion of the 4th South Lancs., on the South-Coast.

div.head: LANCE-CORPORAL PERCY FORD.
div.p: LANCE-CORPORAL PERCY FORD.
" We Gale The Huns Something To Go On With." '

- Lance-Corporal Percy Ford, No. 6 Company, the local Territorials, has been wounded.. The news reaMied his mother at 3, Regent-street, on Sunday morning, when a field card from him ran that he had been wounded and admitted into hospital, was going on well, and hoped to be discharged soon. The (late was the 16th. On Monday morning arrived a letter sent from the South Midland Divisional Clearing Station: "I was hit by a piece of shell in the head, )lut we must thank God that I am living. It was awful; I am afraid we have lost a good many .men. Arthur Earley was killed right. by my side. But I am doing champion, and am being moved from here to Boulogne. I have got an awful head, bUt trust in me to pull through. It was an awful battle, but I think we gave the Huns something to go on with." St. Helens Cable Employe.

The wounded Lance-Corporal, whose age is 24, is an only child, and was born in Regent- street and attended People's College until four- teen years of age. As a compositor he then entered h local printing works. but after seven years joined the St. Helens Cable and Rubber Company. War had only been declared four days when he decided to join the local "Terriers." Pre- viously be bad served four years in Lord Gerard's Yeomanry at Newton. He has since been described as " the life and soul of his sec- tion" by many of his comrades in letters home. He attends the Bold-street Wesleyan Church. In football he also takes a great interest. His father is Bombardier Joseph Ford, who now belongs to the Royal Field Artillery, with which he served through the Boer War.

div.head: EYE STOPPED UP WITH CLAY.
div.p: EYE STOPPED UP WITH CLAY.
Corporal Frank Skelhorne's Experience.

Corporal Prank Skelhorne, brother to Sergt. Arthur Skelhorne, the well-known Warrington footballer (who has been wounded), and himself a player of no mean local repute, met with a slight injury to his eye, presumably somewhere about the same time as his brcther was 'injured. The gallant Corporal made light of the affair; in fact, he wrote that he was not really hurt at all, merely having had his eye stopped up tem- porarily by a lump of clay thrown uP by an exploding shell. His version of what was at first feared by his friends Might prove to hpve been a serious accident is borne out by the fact that his name is not included in the casualty list recently issued. Prior to offering his services to his country, Corporal Skelhorne, who is 21 years of age, was engaged at the Longford Wire Works. Like his brother, be was educated at the St. James' boys' school, and was a football enthusiast, and although he did not attain to the same degree of proficiency in that game as did the Sergeant. he was nevertheless a keen player and a useful man in the front rank. He played in a number of Works Competition games. He was promoted to the rank of Corporal whilst undergoing his war training at Tunbridge Wells.'

div.head: LANCE-CORPORAL S. MONKS.
div.p: LANCE-CORPORAL S. MONKS.
Hurt By Fall Of Earth In The
Trenches.

The news that Lance-Corporal Simeon Monks, of 17' Kean-street, had entered hospital first reached his wife on Sunday morning. In this iV letter the Prate said he had been hurt by a fall of earth in the trench, being for a time buried and afterwards conveyed to hospital.

div.head: Two " Terrier" Brothers.
div.p: Two " Terrier" Brothers.

Second son of Mrs. James Monks, of 5, Wake- field-street, the Private is in peace times a blacksmith with Messrs. Crosfield's (his father was similarly occupied at Hallam Forge). At the beginning of the war he rejoined the Territorials—having previously served his five years in them. His two brothers also belong to the local Territorials.
The Private, who was educated at the Heath- side Schools, at one time belonged to the Con- servative Bowling Club; and also took consider- able interest in boxing—in which he won several prizes.

div.head: LANCE-CORPORAL W. PINSON.
div.p: LANCE-CORPORAL W. PINSON.
Education Office Clerk AVounded In
'thigh.

Lance-Corporal William Pinson sent to his parents—Mr. and Mrs. William Pinson—of 6.3, Chorley-street, a card which arrived on Sunday morning, saying he was in hospital wounded. On Monday a letter from him said he had been wounded by a shell in the thigh, and was going on satisfactorily. He had had two shots before =his_ shoulder and leg being grazed; but the shell caused his casualty. . Speaking of the splendid hospital he is in, he says it is "like Heaven.-"

div.head: Five Years With C.L.B.
div.p: Five Years With C.L.B.
A native of Warrington, the Lance-Corporal is 19 years of age, and was brought up at Heathside Schools. He then entered the Education Office as a clerk, where he remained until the outbreak of war.

Ire then joined the Territorials. Previously he had had five years' service in the St. Paul's Church Lads' Brigade; he belonged to that church. In the brigade he held the rank of Colour-Sergeant. The Lance-Corporal has for some time be- longed to the Municipal Officers' Guild,

div.head: PRIVATE J. J. CLOLGH.
div.p: PRIVATE J. J. CLOLGH.
Hundreds Of Germans Baytmeted In The Charge. _ _
Private J,. J. plough, 30, Scott-street, wounded by shrapnel, writing to his wife, says he was "knocked flat."

" I was," he says, "with the three trenches in five minutes. They brought German prisoners in galore'. They bayoneted many a hundred in the charge. "I am in a beautiful hospital, just near Boulogne. I lost everything when I was in the trench.. We came out of the trench at one o'clock in the morning. We were right in the open, and the Germans were firing at us all the time. We had to run in full view of the -Ger- man trenches, and when..we got about- three 'miles from the trench they started shelling us. I was about twenty yards from a big tree, when a shell hit it and broke it to matchwood."

div.head: PRI\ vrE A. BARKER.
div.p: PRI\ vrE A. BARKER.
Twice-Wounded " Terrier " Hopes To Be Soon In England.

False news drifted throughto Mr. and Mrs. Alfred Barker, of 11, hardy-street, during the week-end to the effect that their son, Private Arthur Barker, had been killed. A telegram arrived stating that he had. been only wounded in the right shoulder. The wound was described as dttngerous, but a.letter that arrived on Mon- day morning, written by the chaplain of the General Hospital, Boulegne, on behalf of the wounded Soldier, re-assured the anxious parents. It stated that he was getting on well and hoped to be in England shortly. Private Barker who is 27 years of age, was employed, prior to the war, at the Whitecross Works., He enlisted early in September, and has now been twice wounded. Some years ago be was associated with the same regiment, of which he is now a member, when it was styled . the Warrington Volunteers. He is a keen foot- baller and played for the .Whitecross Club. Ire has won honours as a billiard player at the Conservative Club. As a .lioy he attended Ham- ilton-street School. •

div.head: PRIVATE T. NICHOLSON.
div.p: PRIVATE T. NICHOLSON.
" We're Now Usinti Iligh Explosives:
Just AVliat 'Was AVanteil."

Writing from the Town Hall, Oxford, under date June 19th, Private Tom Nicholson, of 10, Vere-street, who is married, and who has one little girl, says:—" I shall never forget my 28th birthday, as we went into the trench that night and had it hot. The bombardment lasted for hours, and then the charge came off. We took three .lines of German trenches. It was an awful sight. It was more than words can explain. I got wounded in the right leg, just below the knee, with a piece of shrapnel. . . . Six of us were hit by the same shell. . . .

. . . There are a good few of our fellows hit with shrapnel, but the Germans got it hot. . . . We are now using those high explosive shells, they are just the thing that are wanted, and I tell you they count, too, and no mistake. Our artillery was fine, dropping right in the German trenchgs." Private Nicalson,. who was _employed at Messrs. Crosfield's Soap Works prior to the out- break of war, had previously been in the Terri- torials, but his time had expired, lie was connected with St. Peter's Church.

div.head: PRIVATE ISAIAH HEATH.
div.p: PRIVATE ISAIAH HEATH.
Ohl IA (nits' Footballer Who Joined Al
The Outbreak Of Vi-e'a-r-.

News reached Mrs. 'heath, ofl9, 'l'iJley street, On Saturday, that her husband, Private Isaiah Beath, of the Warrington Territorials, had been wounded in action. Following the field card. there came a letter. from Private Heath—written from .Ratcliffe Hospital, Ox- ford—which read as follows:—" I am getting on as well as can be expected. I got wounded in the right shoulder, but it is not very much, so you have need to upset yourself. lam in the Ratcliffe Hospital, Oxford, and we are having a fine time. . . . 'The people hero are very good to us." .

14iVate Heath, who belongs to A Company, is 28 years of age. At -the outbreak of war he left Messrs. Randall's Tannery,. and joined the Territorials. He played football several times for the team from Messrs. Randall's works, and, as a boy, he attended St. Ann's Church.

div.head: PRIVATE STANLEY COOPER.
div.p: PRIVATE STANLEY COOPER.
Lot A Thumb As A Result Of The Big

Fight. News reached Mrs. Cooper at 48, Orford- avenue, on Saturday, that her son, Private Stanley Cooper, of the Warrington Territorials, had been wounded in action. On Monday there arrived two letters, both written on June 18th. Had to Have a Thumb Taken Off, • One letter was from a nurse at a hospital in Boulogne, and ran as follows: "Your son has asked me to write to let you know that he is in hospital.. He has been wounded in the left hand, and he has been operated upon. He has had to have his thumb taken off, as it was badly smashed. He is. very well in himself, very cheerful', and a gool patient." The other letter was from Private B. Watson, of B Company, who is a medical officer's orderly. "Our Battalion was Right in the Thick of It." "I am sorry to let you know," he wrote, "that your son Stanley has got wounded in the hand, but I can assure you it will be soon all right. We have been in a big engagement, and our battalion was right in the thick of it. I have no doubt that you will see hint in a few days. Dr. Law and I did all in our power for him, but -his right hand is badly shattered. Still he is very fortunate. I am sure it will come as a great .shock to you all at home, but you have the satisfaction of knowing that he did his duty bravely and stood to his post."

div.head: Played for Rylands's Football Club.
div.p: Played for Rylands's Football Club.

Private Cooper is a single man, and is 22 years of age. He was educated at the Heath- side School, and afterwards went :IS a wire. worker at Messrs. Rylands Bros.' works. A keen footballer, he formerly played with the Rylands's team in the St. Helens and District League. At the outbreak of war he rejoined D Company of the Territorials, having before served in them for four years. Another brother in training with a battalion of Territorials at an East Anglican town.

div.head: PRIVATE F. W. LEA.
div.p: PRIVATE F. W. LEA.
Saw Germans Kill Our AVounded On
The Field.

Private Frederick William Lea is lying at Southmede General Hospital, Bristol, suffering from concussion. His father, John Henry Lea, who worked at Dallam Forge, died on the 11th inst., and at the time the son arrived in Eng- land wounded he had not heard of his loss, as the letter with the sad news had gone to Bel- gium as he came home. Private Lea, who is only 20 years of age, and is the oldest child of his widowed mother, living at 40, West-street, worked at Messrs. Richmond's as a moulder, and had been . in the Territorials five years, being a big, well-made boy at fifteen. He is a Longford White Star footballer, a member of the "Garibaldi" Lodge of Oddfellows, and a worshipper at the Gospel Hall. Had to be Dug Out.

Writing on June 19th, Private Lea says "I am not •so well at present. I am suffering from concussion from shell. We went into the trenches on Tuesday night and were in a bayonet charge the next morning. The sights .one saw were awful; what with pieces of bodies and heads flying over, it was something terrible. I got buried by a shell and had to be dug out- I and seven more poor fellows, but four were dead and the other two wounded. • I am expect- ing to he in England to-morrow if all goes well, so don't let this trquble you, as I think I will get over it. "The Germans are surrendering in hundreds; but our fellows had no mercy for them, for we saw them kill three or four of our men who were lying wounded on the battlefield. . . . Good luck to you, and God bless you. Hope to be in Warrington in a couple of weeks from now." Private Lea had a narrow escape some time ago. A bullet hit his boot and tore the leather but fortunately did him no damage.

div.head: PRIVATE TOM KINIBLIN.
div.p: PRIVATE TOM KINIBLIN.
hit Abo‘e The Eye And In The Back,
And Buried Under Debris.
Interesting details are given by Private Tom Kimblin, of 16, Standard-street, Warrington, in

a letter received by his wife on Sunday morn- ing dated June. 17th. Private Kimblin, who before the war, was engaged in the service of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles, Says: "Just a line fo let you know I have been wounded above my eye and in ,my back. I was in the trenches when the Germans shelled us out. We had no chance, because they knocked all the trench in upon us. was buried along with eight com- rades. You need not upset yourself, as I am quite well. I shall never forget the experience if I. live to be a hundred."

div.head: PRIVATE C. 11. ASHTON.
div.p: PRIVATE C. 11. ASHTON.
Former Militiaman Wounded In Head And Shoulder.
Private Charles Henry Ashton, of 31, Cart- wright-street, has been wounded in the head and right shoulder. The news was received by his wife on Saturday morning ii the following letter from him : •

"Got wounded on the 16th—in a charge—in the head and right shoulder. I might come to England in a short time. My wounds are not serious; so don't upset, yourself. Don't send me tobacco or anything till I tell you. . : . I am too ill to write much, but thank God I am for we lost heavily. lam in much pain.'' On Monday morning a letter—not . from the wounded Private himself—reached his home from the No. 2 Canadian General Hospital, Lefreport, which repeated that his wounds were slight, and added that he would soon be moved to another hospital. Penketh and Sankey.

Born in Penketh 45 years ago, Private ,C. IL Ashton was educated at Sankey Schools, and afterwards worked at various places, his latest job prior to going to the Front, being at Cros- field's—where he was, in peace times, a labaurer with the electrical engineers.. 'Previous to his joining the local Territorials in September, he had served for seven years in the Liverpool King's Regiment—in the band of which he acted as a drummer. A Son in the " Terriers."
He has two sons and a daughter. One of his sons is also in the "Terriers." His elder son is a Sergeant in the Church Lads' Brigade.

div.head: PRIVATE JOHN -DILLON.
div.p: PRIVATE JOHN -DILLON.
Suffering Great Pain From Wound In
Throat.

Mrs. Dillon, who is living with her mother, Mrs. Houghton, at 101, Algernon-street, has received news that her husband, Private John Dillon, Of the Warrington Territorials, has been wounded in action. On Monday Mrs. Dillon received the following letter, dated June 18th, which had come from an Australian Con- tingent Hospital at Wimereux, France, and had been signed by a Captain in the Gordon High- landers:—

div.head: " Going on Very Well."
div.p: " Going on Very Well."

" I am writing," ran the letter. "at the request of your husband, Private John Dillon, of the 4th Aunt Lanes. Regiment., who was admitted into the base hospital to-day suffer- ing from a wound in the throat. He is going on very well, although, naturally, lie is having a great deal of pain, but it is already easier than
it was. You may rest assured that ,he is in capable hands, and that he will receive every possible care and attention, both as to his health and his comfort:"

Rejoined " Terriers" When War Broke Out. Private John Dillon had served about six years in the Territorials previous to the out- break of war, When he rejoined, lie was for- merly employed at Randall's .Tannery, Tanner's- lane.

div.head: PNIN ATE J. MULCAHY.
div.p: PNIN ATE J. MULCAHY.
Buried Ali% e Under Sandbags Many
Times.

Private John Mulcahy; who lived. with his 'father, Mr. Maurice Mulcahy, and mother. 37, Orford-street, and worked in the boiler yard at Dallam Forge, joined the 2/4th South Lancs., and then volunteered to go on active service with the First Battalion. lie is 22 years of age; Vis father, who has served in the Army, is now engaged at the Star Kinemo.

In a note from the Australian Boulogne Hospital, Private Mulcahy said. the battalion had been in a move which proved successful, but got hit afterwards. His neck, lie said, was very sore, but there was nothing to be afraid of.
Later, writing from the Howard de Waldron Hospital, Maidstone, Private Mulcahy says he hops to be a little nearer home when he gets a bit better. - Shell Burst Over His Head.

"We had an awful time, I can tell you," he says. "I don't know how Harry Dodd went on. ‘I stopped in the trench two hours after I was hit, carrying men hit worse than myself to a safe place. There were not many safe places. I can tell you. The trench was full of wounded. It was awful, but I must thank .God to be away from it for a bit.. I was very lucky to get off so easily. The shell burst over my .head and a bullet went through the back of my neck. I was buried under sandbags many a time. I didn't think I would get out of it alive. But I am in England once more; that is the main thing to be thankful for."

div.head: PRIVATE JOHN Boom.
div.p: PRIVATE JOHN Boom.
" Germans Tool: To Their Heels 1111(.11 They Saw Us Coming."

Mrs. Booth, of 106, Algernon-street, on Mon- day, received news that her son, Private John Booth, of the Warrington Territorials, had his leg badly crushed by a number of sandbags falling on it. " We Took Three Lines Of Trenches."

Writing under date Juno 18th, he says: "I am in hospital, having been crushed by a trench being blown over on six of us, but it is not serious. We have been in a charge and took three lines of trenches from the Germans. We had a very great many wounded by shells, but there were more of the Germans hurt than there were 61 us. We also took a lot of prisoners. I think it was one of the wbrst battles fought since the war started. . . .
"All my things were buried. . . . I think the Germans are cowards, as they took to their heels and ran when they saw us coming."
The Gallant Charge Described:

In a later letter he said :7—" I write these few lines frau a convalescent camp in Boulogne. I am having a good time, and am feeding like a lord. I was in hospital only two days, and then they sent me here. As I told you before, we were in a charge and we took all the trenches which the Germans occupied. We .were with the retired., owing to a German officer in our uniform telling them to do so. lie was shot, and we were again sent up into the line. We charged, and the Germans ran, with us after them. Thy left helmets, Sic., galore behind them.

div.head: We Took Lots of Prisoners.
div.p: We Took Lots of Prisoners.

"We took lots of prisoners, and many of the enemy were lying about dead on the floor, for our artillery had blown their trench to pieces. Our artillery bombarded their trench for two hours before we charged. The sights which 1 saw, I hope never to see again. After we had taken the trenches, the Germans started to bombard us. It was then that I got buried with the sandbags, all of which were blown in. My hurt is not much, however, and I think myself lucky that I was not killed. We sustained very heavy losses." Attained His Majority in the Trenches.

Private Booth, who belongs to C Company, joined the Territorials in . October. He celebrated his twenty-first birthday in the trenches on the 9th of this month. As a boy he attended the National School, Church-street, and subsequently he was employed by Messrs. Hardiman, printers. He worshipped at St. Clement's Mission Church. Some years ago he played football for the Orford St. John's Club.
PHI\ VIE 'F. It. CERIUM).

div.head: Pearson and Knowles' Employe's Brief
div.p: Pearson and Knowles' Employe's Brief
News.
Of Private Thomas Richard Gerrard's
wounding, the first news reached his wife, at 13, Stevenson-street, on Saturday morning— when she received a field card to say he was in the base hospital wounded, and was going on well.

div.head: Blue Coat School.
div.p: Blue Coat School.
Twenty-nine years of age, Private .Gerrard was educated at the Blue Coat School, and afterwards entered the employment of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles as a bar-weigher. At this he has since remained.
At the end .of August he responded to the call, and has been abroad since February. About seven years ago he was a bugler in the band of the local Volunteers. lie has two little daughters.

div.head: PRIVATE HENRY GRIFFITHS.
div.p: PRIVATE HENRY GRIFFITHS.
Wesleyan AA minded In The Left Foot.

On a Red Cross card sent from the hospital at Bristol—which reached his wife at 28, Stevenson-street on Monday morning—Private Henry Griffiths sent the word that he had been wounded in the left foot. At the, time of writing he had only just reached Bristol. . Aged 35, the Private is, in peace times. eatployed- as a compositor at the " Guardian " Office. In August he joined the "Terriers." Formerly he belonged to the St. Mary's Association Football Club, and attended the Bewsey-road Wesleyan Chapel—to which his wife belongs.
lie has foot. vhildren—three boys and a girl

div.head: PRIX VIE JIM PIKENIX.
div.p: PRIX VIE JIM PIKENIX.
Reeuperating Behind The Firing-Line.

It was on Monday morning that Mrs. Mary A. Phcenix, of 13, Stevenson-Street, received a lengthy letter from her youngest son—Private Jim Phcenix—to say he had been slightly wounded by shell in the back, and was rest- ing behind the line. for a few days to recover. They had had a terrible battle, but had taken four lines of the German trenches, together with two hundred prisoners. His back was only bruised—for the entrenching tool had happily stopped the force of the blow.

div.head: Works at Earlestown.
div.p: Works at Earlestown.

The Private, who is 21 years of age, attended, as a lad, the National schools and' the Elles- mere-street Mission, He first went to work at Messrs. CroSfield's at the boilers, .and latterly at the Vulcan Works, Earlestown—where he is a eranedriver.

In August he was at camp with the "Terriers" —to which he. had belonged for two or three years—when the mobilisation took place; and was called up. He is unmarried, and lives with his mother. He has three brothers-in-law in the local " Terriers " and • another—a Sergeant in the Manchester Regiment—now serving in the Dardanelles.

div.head: PRIVATE TOM WORSLEY.
div.p: PRIVATE TOM WORSLEY.
Wounded km " Beinu Looked After
First-Class."

A week oa,go a field card reached Mrs. Tom Worsley, at 56, Priestley-street from her hus- band, to say be was in hospital wounded in the right jaw, ;111(1 was going on well. A few houn; later a. letter followed: "1 a iii doing line and being looked_ after tirst-class. .. . We don't know for certain where we shall go one day after another. Some of our fellows that are badly wounded are coming over to England. . I hope I shall have the luck to come 0ver...... On Monday morning the Private wrote to say he continued all right, and mentioned that any man who had come out of it with a wound was a lucky chap; it was a treat to be in hospital looked after like they were, and in a nice soft bed. . . ."

div.head: An Oddfellow.
div.p: An Oddfellow.

The wounded Private, whose age is 30, was born in Warrington, and is the eldest son of Mrs. E. Worsley,. of 13, Louis-street. He attended Hamilton-street School, afterwards going to \Volker's Brewery as office boy. Later he became a labourer. The Territorials he joined in August. He belongs to St, Peter's Church, and to the Manchester Unity of Oddfellows. He has one
little (laughter. A brother of his is also in the "Terriers." .

div.head: PRIVATE JESSE SUMNER.
div.p: PRIVATE JESSE SUMNER.
"Look Like Enjo km Myself For A
%Vhile!"

It was on Sunday morning that Mr. and Mrs. Thomas Sunnier, of 15, Robson-street, received the following letter from their eldest son at No. 1 Convalescent Depot, MaThorough, Boulogne: "I -a m glad to say my wound is not very serious—a piece of shell in the back of the knee. No doubt you have read of the charge we were in last Tuesday. . . . in civilisa- tion for a while, and look like enjoying myself for a while. When the shrapnel came into contact with my leg the only thing I saw was home and the kids."
The wounded Private's younger brother is in- cluded amongst this week's list of killed. Another brother is now training with the. War- rington Territorials in the South.

div.head: Paddington United Footballer.
div.p: Paddington United Footballer.

Aged 23, Private J. Sumner was employed as a galvaniser by the Firth Mattress Company, Howley—where he had been for two years. The Previous seven years he had spent at Messrs. llylands' Bros. in the same occupation. lie was unmarried, and attended the Parish Church. For five years he had belonged to the Volunteers; and—like his deceased brother— was a former member of St. Clement's Mission Church Lads' Brigade.

A great footballer, he was an enthusiastic member of the Paddington United Football Club. Previously be acted as secretary for the Fairfield Second Football Club. As a boy he attended lleathside School.

div.head: PRIX ATE J. V. PO1)110RE.
div.p: PRIX ATE J. V. PO1)110RE.
Back And Shoulders Crushed Throu9h
Explosion.

To his parents, Mr. and Mrs. William Pod- more,- of 6, Golborne-street, Private Joseph Vincent Podmore writes on Friday, June 18th: "I have been 'put out of action. lam not wounded in any way, but Suffering pains through getting crushed by the explosion of a shell. You must have no fear for my safety, because I am going on as well as can be ex- pected. I said nothing to anybody when I was Crushed, but kept on with my duty until about nine o'clock at night—when I had to throw my check in, I was suffering that much pain with my back and shoulders;. and the, shock I got was something terrible. • Our regi- ment have caught it fairly, but the people in the old town will be proud of them when they read the report. Cheer up ! I shall be all right -soon. . I am in the hospital at Boulogne, which belongs to the Canadian Ex- peditionary Force, and they will do anything for you."

div.head: Former " Examiner" Employe.
div.p: Former " Examiner" Employe.

Aged 22, Private J. V. Podmore was born in his present home, and received his education at the Wycliffe Schools. After leaving, he entered the services of "The Examiner" Print- ing Works, where he remained for two years, next proceeding to Jones' Printing Works, Liverpool. Here he remained until the outbreak of war. In the meantime he had for four years belonged to the Warrington Territorials, and in Augdst was called up. In February he left for the Front, and "The Examiner" has on several occasions published letters he has sent to local friends. At the Front he has been acting as scout and signaller. The Private is well-known at Bold-street Wesleyan Church, • which he attended 'for several years.

div.head: PRIVATE I. ROBINSON.
div.p: PRIVATE I. ROBINSON.
AVounded In The Right Hand, " But Not Seriously."

News reached Mrs. Wrench on Sunday r-_,rn- ing, at 103, School Brow, that Private Robert Robinson, of B Company of the Watrington Territorials, had been wounded in action. Private Robinson has neither father nor mother, and has lived with Mrs. Wrench nearly all his life. After the postcard had been received on Sunday, there came a letter from the gallant Private himself, an which read as follows: " I am wounded in the right hand, but not seriously. I am in hospital and am going on as well as can be expected. I was in the big fight on June 16th."

Private Robinson Was formerly employed as a labourer at Messrs. Ryland Bros. This work he left in September. As a boy Ile attended the National School, Church-street, and lie regularly worshipped at. the Parish Church.
PIM It lIONKS.
"Like II Let Loose," Hui "We Took The Trenches We W anted."

Private Arthur Monks, who is only 19 years of age and who is brother. to Mrs.. Astle, the wife of Lance-Corporal Astle, of 9, Cobden- street, was another victim in the Territorials' magnificent onslaught on the enemy's trenches. Writing to Mrs. J. Astle, a friend also serv- ing with the Territorials, but who particularly requested that his name should not be given to the reporters, says, in a letter received on 'Monday afternoon:—

div.head: German Prisoners Who Ask For Mercy.
div.p: German Prisoners Who Ask For Mercy.

"- On the 16th we went up, i a reserve. tc. a charge and, I am sorry to tell you, that your Arthur is missing and that our Joe is woandel. We have gone through it something awful thee last twenty-four hours, and I can go on my knees and thank God that I came out of it all right. It was like hell let loose; it was, in- deed, an awful sight. I shall never forget it long as I live; nor shall I forget that we took the trenches we wanted.. At three o'clock on the 16th the bombardment started, the big guns getting to work. They fairly made the earth shake. And then the enemy's 'Jack Johnson's.' started! Shells were falling all around us, and I am afraid there will be a big casualty list. I lost all my pack; it being blown to piels by a shell. I did get a hit with a piece of s rap- nel, but it -did no damage. We took Some prisoners, and they had the cheek to ask for mercy. Keep your heart up."

div.head: _ . ,7_mr PRIVATE DAVID CLAYTON. '
div.p: _ . ,7_mr PRIVATE DAVID CLAYTON. '
Former Volunteer Bandsman
AVounded In Elbow.
Private David Clayton, of 17. thiardian-street, has had part of his left elbow blown away. The news reached his wife on ltonday morning, when she received the following letter:—

div.head: " Our Lads Made a Glorious Charge."
div.p: " Our Lads Made a Glorious Charge."

?No doubt you will have. heard about me being wounded. It is a had wound, but not serious. Do not upset yourself, for I am only too glad to be away from the sound of the guns. Our lildN made a glorious charge on, the lfith inst., but I ant sorry to say that we have been ent up... But we eau say that we were masters of tile situation. Regarding myself, to tell you the truth., 1 :WI very comfortable out here, and the sisters of the hospital, who are Canadians, are worthy of all praise—they o everything possible for us.

div.head: Left Elbow Half Blown Away.
div.p: Left Elbow Half Blown Away.

My *wound is in my left elbow;. in fact the elbow is half blown away. However, .I am glad to say that no sinews or arteries are damaged. I hope that by the time you receive this letter I shall be in the old country, and I do not sup- pose I.shall fight again."

div.head: His Career.
div.p: His Career.

The wounded Private, who is 48 years of age, was born in Warrington, and went to Ifeathside Schools. For upwards of fourteen years he then acted us local insurance agent for the Wes- leyan Cleneral and Royal o-operative Societies respectively. Since then he has worked at Cros- field's, Port Sunlight, and Walker's Brewery for varying periods.

For a-boiit -seventeen years lie belonged to the Volunteer movement, and was in their band for no less than sixteen years. Also .he played in the Wycliffe Baud for several years. lie has four sons and two daughters. On the outbreak of war he rejoined the Terri- torials, and became a stretcher-bearer. He had been at the Front since February, and his last letter home before being wounded ran : We are now about to leave for L where_ we will see some more fighting. My nerves are getting shattered, but keep up your old heart ; I shall return to you. I felt awfully Upset when I. heard of ohr Ernest's [Sergeant Clayton, of the Seaforth Ilighlanders,a nephew of his—whose death we reported a fort-night ago] death; but you can say he died for the freedom and liberty of*the British race. If only the young people had seen what I have seen, they would not flinch one inch, but would come out here. The German can't kill us all, though they have a sporting chance. And I have risked my life too often for them."

div.head: PRIV.VIE E. LITTLE WOOL).
div.p: PRIV.VIE E. LITTLE WOOL).
Accounted For At Least Five Germans Before Beillll ounded.

Private Ernest Littlewood, son of Mr. George Littlewood, and adopted son of Mr. Frank Jolley,- 14, Tilley-street, market porter, has sent home one of the most vivid descriptions of the charge that have come under our notice. He is 25 years of age and single. He is in the netting department of Messrs. Rylands Bros.' Writing presumably from the Boulogne Hos- pital, he says : •
" No doul;t you will have heard of me getting wounded in the head by a shell bursting and blowing the parapet on top of me. I am in a hospital with 700 patients, and we are looked after fine.

div.head: German Brutality to German Boy.
div.p: German Brutality to German Boy.

"I am sorry to say nearly all my company got blown to bits, and I can thank God I am able to write this letter. It was awful while they were digging me out. Shells were dropping all round me. How I got away from that awful hell I don't know. The Germans/got it worse than we did, and we captured three lines of trenches. In one of their trenches I saw a sight that made my blood run cold; they had chained one of their own men, who was badly wounded, to one of their machine guns. lie would not be more than seventeen.. The trenches were full of dead Germans. We fairly let them have can tell you. They tried the cowardly white flag trick with us again, but we were not to be had, and let them have ten rounds rapid, and what .was left of them was not many.

div.head: Warrington Lads Let Them Have It.
div.p: Warrington Lads Let Them Have It.

" It was about four o'clock in the morning of the 16th that I got it in the • nut,' and I can thank God I 'got away as I did. I accounted for five Germans that I know of, so I wiped off an old debt they owed me, didn't I? It was a charge, I can tell you! I know it will be a great blow to, the people of Warrington—won't it? But the Warrington lads fairly let them have it, I can tell you. We made up our minds before the charge to fight to the last. . It has made me a bit deaf, but I think it will be all right soon.

"I hope you won't worry too much about me, and make yourself ill, for you have no need to worry. It is like being in heaven to me to be in a good bed once more and hear the nurses talk English again. • "Everything I had—rifle, bayonet, and all my equipment, and even my hat—got blown to bits, and I have nothing but shoes, punts and Jersey.'.!
MIN ATE W. SAVORY.

div.head: " Practically Buried Alive" By
div.p: " Practically Buried Alive" By

JOill1S011." Private W. Savory, of the Warrington Te toriais, was wounded in the severe righting an,: the 16th inst., and the first intimation to thin' effect to reach his home was contained on a field card addressed to his wife on the 18th. Ile • is now lying in the Rusthall Voluntary Ilos Pita!, Tunbridge Wells, together with a CO rade of the same battalion, Private J. Robin son. " Neuve Chapelle Not In It With Our Charge., In a letter to his sister. Mrs. C. Jarman, to, Forster-street, Private Savory tells the story er the fighting as follows:—" Preparations for the attack were made at '4 o'clock in the morn- - in of the 16th. Being in the supporting trenches, we received orders to advance into the firing trenches, and in so doing I was hit ja the calf, but that was nothing to what WO waiting for us. The Germans seemed to have trained their guns to a-nicety, as shells were dropping within five yards of us, and then, all of a sudden, they sent a 'Jack Johnson' over and hit the parapet of our trench and practi- cally buried seven of us. Private Robinson'6 head was just seen sticking out of the ground. and .he can thank his lucky stars that he Was seen,. as in another minute he would have been done for. I would not wish to witness such a sight again. , We had some soldiers with us who had been in the battle at Neuve Chapelle and they told us that it was not in it with our charge at . I was hit twice again with shrapnel, in the thigh, and I had to be earted off to the dressing station, with Privateilobin' son, to be attended to. We had some wounded Germans in the dressing room, and you would be surprised to see how our men treated thetu, handing them bread and cheese and eigarette3 all round:"

div.head: An Old Soldier Turned Terrier."
div.p: An Old Soldier Turned Terrier."

Private Savory served two or three years with the Ist Royal Scots, after which he joined the local Territorials.. lie had resigned from them, but on the outbreak of war was one of the first to be re-enrolled. He was employed hY the Whiteeross Company, Ltd., and resided at 41, Selby-street.

div.head: PRIVATE lIARRY LEATHER.
div.p: PRIVATE lIARRY LEATHER.
Twice Buried Whilst " 'terriers " Were
Being Shelled.

Private Harry Leather, writing under date June Oth to his sister, Mrs. Holt, of -39' Birchati-street—with whom he lived prior 0 going on active service—says: " I have beer taken to hospital at Rouen and am doing web; I was with the boys in the charge, and I g,°' buried twice as the result of the shell exPT" sions. These experiences gave me a bad shaing l'' up and have left my nerves in a prettY had state, but I am lucky to have escaped with nothing worse. . . . .

div.head: Every Man Deserves the V.C.
div.p: Every Man Deserves the V.C.

Every man who was in that charge deserves the V.C. I don't know how many of our fellows were left, but from what I saw whilst we were making the charge we must bac° suffered heavily. It was awful. . . . The doctor tells me that I shall be all right 18-4 week or two, so it will not be long before I am back with the boys once again. In the meantime I am being well looked after, and the doctor has ordered me chicken and stout for my dinner. . . . We gave the Germans something to be going on with I'll bet they don't want another dose like the one we gave them!! Our lads took the three lots of trenches in about ten minutes. If we were up against the German infantry only, we could end tilt" war in a week, for as soon as they see 0"; fellows coming they put up their hands anu shout for mercy." •

His Third " Close Call." Private Leather is 26 years of age, and "S' up to the outbreak of war, employed at Messrs' llylands Bros.' works—in the netting dePart" meat. Re has now had three narrow ocaPeg from death, the most recent, probably, being the closest call, although on an earlier oectisi°u a bullet lodged in his pack.

div.head: PILINATE W. GLEAVE.
div.p: PILINATE W. GLEAVE.
Comrades At Each Side Killed By A
Shell.

Whilst taking part in the charge I was hit in the left arm by a piece of shrapnel, whilst other pieces caught me in the face. I had to be removed to hospital. . . . It was just hike coming out of hell into paradise!" So write Private W. Gleave, of B Company, to his 'wife, who lives with the one (Iliad of the union at 53, Bostock-street.. Be goes on to say •tbat the charge was easily the most awful experience had ever had, and that he was "a very luck3r chap to escape with so little" injury. " I was sitting down amongst my chums," he writesy "when all of a sudden a German shell burst in the middle of us, killing the two mates who were sat at each side of me. I had the luck to come out wounded, but I was also buried alivo and had to be dug out, after which I helped dress the wounds of those more badly hurt than myself, and did my best to ease their pain. . • - There is no need for you to worry about 'tie. as I am doing well. The sisters in the. hospital see that we do not go short of anything." The letter is dated from "The Australian Hospital, Boulogne Base, 18-6-15." Well-known in Local Bowling C'rcles.

Private Gleave, • who is 23 ;ears of age,. received his ,education at the Orford School and, before the outbreak of war, he iv,"; employed at Roberts' Wireworks at Fearnbead• His favourite recreation was bowling, and be was well-known on many ()I the greens in the Warrington district, particularly that at Fearn: head. His father is serving in the National' Reserye, and an uncle of his was aboard H.M.S.' Ocean when she was sunk in the Dardanelles;/ but happily was among the saved.

div.head: PRIX ATE E YATT.
div.p: PRIX ATE E YATT.
Iteceived Three lloles In l'he Bark In Tlic Great Charge..

Writing to his aunt, Miss A. Bibby, wh!) lives at 22, Steel-street, Warrington, Private Edward Wyatt says he was wounded in the. back during the memorable onslaught on th,7 German trenches. "A piece of a' large silo: caught me in the back," he writes, " made three holes (out of which four pieces ot shrapnel were extracted), but my hurts are,,o to speak, only ' flea-bites ' s compared with, those sustained by some of the other chaps..,' think I shall soon be at the tame again. 31: word, that charge was a hot job! We to' three German trenches and laid out a larg(4, number of their men, as well as taking in'' prisoners. " Tod " Sloan, whose home is 111 Back Crossley-street, is also wounded. . •

div.head: " How the Germans Flew!"
div.p: " How the Germans Flew!"

"flow the Germans flew when our boys Tol after them. They can't stand the bayonet lila' our little speciality—' ten rounds rapid!". - • And now 1 am swanking in a comfortable b''`' in a comfortable VII !MI s hospital. ne dressed in a blue pyjama suit. . . . The Cre,r; mans won't come out and fight and as a result' it is 'all charge, charge on our part!"

div.head: FARM AND GARDEN.
div.p: FARM AND GARDEN.
ENLISTING HARVEST WORKERS.

Sir,—Within the last week the foreman on a farm adjoining mine in Perthshire, who is married and has five children, of which the eldest is eight, has been induced by the recruit- ing agent and the Government allowances to enlist. It is impossible to replace a man in such a responsible position under present circum- stances except by bribing away another farmer's servant. On his judgment the ingathering of the crops in: proper condition largely depends, as well as other work. His enlistment undoubt- edly will mean a reduction in the value of the produce of the farm this year and a reduced area under cultivation next year. I ask what is the good of appeals from the Board of Agri- culture to farmers to increase the area of land under cultivation if the recruiting authorities are permitted to act in this way? From a national point of view the want of organisation of which this incident is an illustration is folly, and if persisted in may be properly described as madness.—Yours faithfully, ERNEST MOON. House of Commons.

div.head: WHEN MILK VARIES IN QUALITY.
div.p: WHEN MILK VARIES IN QUALITY.

Mr. James Sadler (secretary of the Cheshire Milk Producers Association), giving evidence for the defence in the miliK prosecution recently, said there were several causes for the variation in the quality of milk given by cows. The first was the period of laztazion. Gradu- ally, through no causes except natural ones, the cows would proceed to increase the amount of butter fat and non-fatty so _ds. Butter fat almost invariably increased as the cows got nearer drying off and the next calving. For the first few days after a cow had calved the milk was particularly rich. As to the difference in quality at different times he said .tne morn- ing milk was usually a little poorer than the evening supply. Why, was not known. When the milking periods were fairly equal the milk was more equal, in quality. The more the farmer varied them—and un- fortunately he had to vary them to meet the demands of the public—the more difference in quality. Sudden changes of temperature would also affect the quality of milk. Food, ordin- arily speaking, did not affect the quality of the milk except sudden changes of food. A single cow would give from 24 per cent. to 54 per cent. of butter fat on different days. They varied in a most extraordinary way.

div.head: WASTEFUL SLAUGHTER.
div.p: WASTEFUL SLAUGHTER.

A matter which calls for prompt action on the part of the authorities is the slaughter of immature and breeding stock, says "Farm and Home." From all parts come reports of the sale for killing of breeding animals sorely needed to replenish our herds, and last week the Board of Agriculture issued an urgent and almost pathetic appeal to farmers to refrain from dis- posing of such animals to gain a present profit. We endorse the appeal, but an appeal is not enough, and the matter is not so simple as it looks. The Kent farmers at Wye discussed the matter last week, and the necessity for action was urged. It is difficult to obtain general response to an appeal to hold on to stock for which a price above its breeding value is offered by an individual who intends to convert it into meat. Some owners may respond, others prob- ably will not; many, indeed, may even be obliged to sell. It is not, as the speakers at the conference pointed out, a decision which ' should be left to the individual, but one which should be made by an organised body capable of dealing with the question on national lines.' It is probably in the large majority of cases quite an error to put th 6 slaughter of lambs on the same basis as that of calves. The produc- tion of fat lambs is a special business; the lambs are bred for the special purpose of slaughter. They could not in any case lie kept on, for the land would be overstocked, and the difference in the amount of meat produced if they were kept growing would not be considerable. It is true so far as the farms where the specialised in- dustry is carried on are concerned that the pro- duction of fat lamb means as economiCal a use of the food as any other department of meat making, and it is on quite a different footing from the slaughter of calves and of heifers and the sending to market of immature—that is, un- finished Or half-fat—bullocks. A centralised authority alone is able to deal with the intricate question effectively, and we fear that the mere anneal. even though it be received sympa- thetically, will fail to achieve the desired end.

div.head: IN THR GARDEN.
div.p: IN THR GARDEN.

, Ivy growing over the walls of a house renders the structure cool in summer and warm in winter. It also keeps the walls dry. It is, how- ever, very destructive to woodwork, forcing the joints, apart.

div.head: HOEING AMONG GROWING CROPS.
div.p: HOEING AMONG GROWING CROPS.

Now that the weather is so dry and the Various vegetible crops are likely to suffer from drought there is no more useful tool than the hoe, which ought to be in daily use, not only to destroy any weeds, but also to loosen the surface, and thus form, as it were, a' mulch. Select if possible a hot, sunny day to run the hoe through the various crops. When :hoeing do not merely scratch the surface, .but use the draw hoe, working : deeply into the soil and bringing the weeds to the surface. For small seedling weeds lhe Dutch hoe is the best.

div.head: FROST AND POTATOES.
div.p: THE FROST AND POTATOES.

Those who did not draw up the soil to their potatoes will have cause to regret failing to do this, as from many quarters we regret to say reports are to hand that on the morning of May 31st" the potatoes in many parts were quite cvt off by the frost, which will weaken them very much, and lead to a very much reduced crop. Runner beans, though well hardened off before planting, Were also cut off, in many cases not a single plant being left.

div.head: ROSE PESTS.
div.p: ROSE PESTS.

No greater mistake can be made than allow- ing greenfly to overrun the plants before.apply- ing some insecticide to destroy • them. This pest increases very rapidly, the first few 'being responsible for the countless numbers result- ing from a few days' neglect. To-day we examined some vigorous plants of a climbing 7(Y3Q, AO \ore astonished to find that some of the shoots were one mass of greenfly. Steps were at once taken for its destruction by wettifig every ,part of the foliage with quassia extract do soft soap, and we are hoping that by being in time we shall be able to check .the attite.Z. Care will, howevera laekfa that on the re- a ppearene r 91 it:e aphides another application of tla ilMe insecticide shall at once be 'given. good inn is on the morning following the .rippliettiion of the insecticide to thoroughly S'vringe the trees that have been dressed, this -clearing the foliage of any dead insects., Rose maggots, too, are very troublesome; the best way to destroy them ,being to squeeze them between the finger and thumb. A .sure sign that the maggot is present is the curling up of the leaves. k very little practice will enable the grower to distinguish between the leaves in which the maggots are and those whiCh are naturally curled from not being sufficiently
adva need to open Properly.—Wiek, in " Farm and 'Home."

div.head: POULTRY PEN,
div.p: POULTRY PEN,
lIN I s .1,11 l INTERESTING FACTS \ND CHATS FOR AMATEURS.
BITS FOR BEGINNERS.

What to do with those cockerels. By all means market any mismarked cockerels that will not fetch good prices for stock purposes. Thin them down, as your food bill will then be reduced. It is penny wise and pound foolish to sell cockerels for the table if they are not ready. Sort them out into sizes and put a little extra food into them. That little extra will put on any amount of extra flesh and mean a better

price. Whilst care and attention must be devoted to the older stock, the pOultry-keeper must not for- get the younger ones. Eack chicken requires attention. Keep a sharp eye on all just now. At this time of the year the oivner is apt to forget the adult birds that have been on duty for many months. Just look them all over and see if any are in ill-health or a trifle run down, and do the needful.

div.head: DON'T OVERCROWD.
div.p: DON'T OVERCROWD.

The greatest mistake made by the majority of small poultry-keepers is—and many farmers are equally guilty—they keep too many in too small an area. It does not follow says "The Feathered World," that if twelve fowls kept on a limited space leave a profit, double the num- ber will double the profits. According to simple rule of three, it would appear that this should be so, but in practice it will not answer, as many have found to their sorrow, and then condemned poultry-keeping in limited sur- roundings; whereas the fault lay in overcrowd- ing and so causing the ground to become tainted. We have often been told by farmers that fowls do not pays and asked the reason why. In nearly every case two things accounted for the trouble. One was owing to hens being kept too long on one plot of ground, usually housed in a stone building adjacent to the farm- house where fowls had been kept for years, and as fowls rarely wander outside a circuit, they were continually wandering around inside a limited area, the result being the ground had become sour by constant usage, and on which 'it was impossible for them to do well. Yet there were acres of fresh land where fowls had never been.

div.head: WEEK'S WORK IN BRIEF.
div.p: THE WEEK'S WORK IN BRIEF.
Provide shade for the young stock; they will need it. Give the youngsters fresh ground regularly. Keep all drinking vessels clean and always full.

Feed all growing stock at regular hours. • Market all surplus. male birds if ready for the table. Push along any backward chickens. • Don't force-feed the older pullets ; early laying is not advisable.—" The Poultry World."'

div.head: POULTRY PROSPECTS.
div.p: POULTRY PROSPECTS.

Importations of eggs are to be more restricted, and on Sunday last the Swedish Government published a decree forbidding the export of eggs from June 16th to August 16th. This will further stimulate prices for new-laid eggs here probably, and the poor , poultry-keeper may eventually be able to command a paying price for his produce. If the war should unfortun- ately last another year, I .fear the public will be asked to pay record prices for the production of the poultry yard, because if estimates could be made it would be discovered that stocks are greatly down. Many breeders have allowed the breeding season to lapse in a sense, being dis- inclined to run up huge corn bills at inflated prices, and run the risk of produce prices meet- ing their responsibilities. If one is a whole- hearted patriot he has first to live. The outlook, then, is on the side of those breeders who have been possessed of ,exceeding courage, and who have now well-developed flocks of 1915 chickens. Food prices will, I think, continue to fall. Military operations in the passage to Russian corn continue to promise well, and we are also told that there will be something like 2,000,000 tons of wheat available from India. If speculative operations are pre- vented, it is likely that poultry-keepers will be able to breathe easier in the near future.—" The Feathered World:"

div.head: FOOD FOR FOWLS.
div.p: FOOD FOR FOWLS.

With regard to soft-food, it is possible for everyone to economise, to a greater or less extent. by saving, bread crusts and other house scraps, and also by boiling potatoes. turnips and other ,roots. House scraps should be soaked, and mixed with sharps or barley meal into a fairly dry sticky consistency. Potatoes and cooked roofs are more suitable for growing stock than for laying hens, but they are useful in ekeing out soft food made up of biscuit meal and cooked cereal.—" Agricultural Economist and Horticultural Review."

On Saturday teams of twenty players repre- senting the Warrington Liberal Club and the Warrington Caledonian . Association met, in friendly rivalry, on the green of the first named. Some excellent bowling was witnessed, both teams being representative of the best skill available from the -two clubs: A ,number of ladies graced the proceedings with their presence, and they were entertained to tea dur- ing the progress of the games, a little courtesy which they much appreciated.
LIBERALS WIN BOTH DOUBLES AND SINGLES. ,
The Liberals were successful in both the double and single tourneys—in the former by 48 points, and in the latter by C 2 points, a total of 110 points to the good.

POOR BEGINNING FOR OPEN SEASON.

The first week in the open season was not up to the standard owing to the drought. The canals are in a very bad way. They are almost a foot below their usual depth. We know that canals and other waters fish all the better for being a bit low, but this drought is exceptional, especially after the spawning season, when all fish want fresh water to put them in condition. By appearances they seem lazy and sickly for the want of a refresher, and what little rain we have had up to the present is not sufficient to cause any great alteration.

div.head: NORTON.
div.p: NORTON.

Several members were anxious to' try Norton owing to the big match coming off 'there, but they were doomed to disappointment. Fish were entirely off feed, and the conditions were not at all favourable.

div.head: GOWY.
div.p: THE GOWY.

Members had a fair day-at the Gowy amongst the eels, we heard of a couple of Chester anglers taking about 101 b. Coarse fish were entirely off, and beyond a few roach and dace, not up to the usual Gowy standard, nothing further was done. One angler remarked that if twenty cows drank out of the stream all at once they would empty it. We will leave mem- bers to draw their own conclusions.

div.head: HEADQUARTERS.
div.p: HEADQUARTERS.

. The membership at headquarters is improv- ing, and several who are on Government work are being enrolled this year. They have not previously belonged to any society; six juveniles were also enrolled this week. If members will only encourage, the sport amongst our workers who are necessary to stay at home for munitions, ke., I think they would do some good, as the recreation, which is rest- ful, would recuperate the worker for another good week's work.

div.head: BAY HORSE.
div.p: BAY HORSE.

The full complement of members is not yet on the books here, and as the secretary is indis- posed, members should come Up as early as possible to give Mr. Bryers, who is acting in the secretary's place, all the assistance possible to help him out of the difficulty.

div.head: HIPPODROME.
div.p: THE HIPPODROME.

•To all and sundry, we give a hearty recom- mendation to visit the Hippodrome this week. There is a first-rate programme. De Busse gives one of the finest piano-accordion per- formances we have heard. He has a wonderful instrument, and an even more wonderful power over it. His music is entrancing, and fairly takes.the " house "by storm. Daphne Wynne's dancing is delightful; it is artistic, dainty and refined. She introduces "The Dance of •the Allies," and the showers of applause are no more than her performance merits. The instrumental and vocal pot-pourri of Rex Romaine and Doris Dainton is high-- class entertainment and wholly charming. Miss Dainton's violin solo is delicious. 'This turn, too, is immensely popular. The same remark applies to the contribution of Rich. Taylor, whistling ventriloquist, whose efforts at decep- tion .are admirable, and whose imitation of a skylark ascending into the heavens is realistic. Harold Baker, Lancashire character comedian, makes a big "hit," and deserves to. His appearance and mannerisms are a host in them- selves, and with his funny songs he succeeds in making the audience feel immensely tickled; so much so that they part with him with reluctance when the time limit has expired. Gus Harris, chorus comedian, is very successful with his various songs, rendered with plenty of vim, and "gets the Gods" with his song- recitation, "The Gentile and the Jew." Hal Smithers, comedian, raises many a hearty laugh, and the Gaumont Graphic and the excel- lent orchestral selections help to make one feel one has "really had a most delightful evening."
