div.p: LOCAL INTELLIGENCE.
B.A.
Mr. George Woodcock, a Boteler Grammar School old boy, has obtained his B.A. degree at Cambridge.
This Year's Park Festival.

This year's Park Festival in aid of the funds of the Warrington Infirmary has been fixed for Sunday, August 22nd. Members of the choirs which are to take part in the festival are reminded that a combined rehearsal will be held in the Cairo-street School on Tuesday evening next, at eight o'clock. Former Grammar School Student's
Trafalgar Essay. The Education Committee have accepted with thanks, Alderman Bennett's offer again this year.

Councillor Roberts and Licensees. In our report of a licensing prosecution last week we stated that Councillor H. Roberts was chairman of the Bench. It was Mr. W. Roberts who 'presided and made the remarks reported when the Bench decided to dismiss the case.

Volunteers to Visit Lymm. To-day the Altrincham Battalion of the Cheshire Volunteer Regiment, with their band, will visit Lymm. In,connection with the visit a recruiting meeting will be held at the Cross at 5.30 p.m., when Sir Arthur Haworth, Bart., Major Linaker and Lientedant J. D. Thompson will give brief speeches.

div.head: Exhibition.
div.p: Exhibition.

Mr. Geoffrey Gladding, second son of the Rev. T. Gladding—formerly of Padgate Wes- leyan Church, and now of Ashton-under-Lyne has been awarded the Woodiwiss Exhibition at Manchester University, open to first year students taking the Honours Chemistry course. Mr. Gladding is a past .student of Boteler Grammar School.

To-morrow's Band Concert. The Brick-street Mitssion Brass Band will supply the programme at to-morrow afternoon's concert in Bank Park. , They will play: Hymn, "Gratitude," J.: A. Greenwood; march, "The Call to Arms," J. A. Greenwood; overture, "The Caliph of Bagdad," Boieldieu; air Vane, " Hollingside," Balfe ; selection, " Seige of Rochelle," Balfe; sacred song, "The Light of Life," J. G. Veaco ; and "God Save the King." Mr. C. York will be th 4 conductor.

Auction Sale for War Funds. Mr. Herbert Johnson, the well-known local auctioneer, has kindly offered to sell by auction a quantity of household appointments, works of art, jewellery, &c., the proceeds of the sale to be devoted to the Warrington Infirmary, the local Red Cross Hospitals at Raddon Court. Thelw,all and The Oaklands, the local Soldiers' Tobacco Fund,' and to the fund for providing gifts for wounded soldiers in the Warrington district. ,Persons who desire to give articles for inclusion in the sale are requested to forward the same to the Parr Hall. A meeting to make the necessary arrangements is being held in the Town Hall on Monday evening next.

Warrington Motor Ambulance Fund. Up to, and including, June 25th, the total of £577 us. Bd. had been contributed to the War- rington Motor Ambulance Fund, which was therefore still some .t 23 short of the required total. The contributions during the last week amounted to £6l 19s. 9d. A small sale of work, organised by the Guild in aid of the Warrington Motor Ambulance Fund, was held in a field kindly lent by Mr. 11. Gandy, off Wash-lane, on Thursday, and the sum of £lO was raised., which has been handed over to the treasurer of the fund.

"Say Not 'Good-Night." Sunday was the hundred and seventy-second anniversary of the birth of Mrs. Barbauld, our famous Warrington poetess, and, in honour of the occasion, the tablet over the gateway to the site of her residence in Dial-street was wreathed with flowers and bore the following inscription : u ANNIE LETITIA AIKIN (Mrs. BAHBAULD). Born .20th June, 1743. 'And murmuring sounds yet fill the hallowed
air Once vocal to the youthful poet's fame.' She warned us of the Nation's Peril a hundred years ago. Let us heed her warning now !"

Military Wredding. Aft the Parish Church 1:11 Sunday morning, Lance-Corporal Thomas Taylor, of the County Palatine Field Artillery (Lord Derby's Bri- gade) and whose home is at Abroath, Scotland, was married to Miss Doris Lewis, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. W. Lewis, of Dinnington,. Yorks, but who has resided for several years with her grandmother, Mrs. 'Lewis, of Bank-street, War- rington. The ceremony was performed by the Rector (the Rev. Canon Willis), and the best man was Lance-Corporal David Thompson, of the Royal garrison Artillery. Both bride- groom and best man were formerly members of the Warrington Borough Police Force.
Croslield's Saiul to Play for Wounded
Soldiers' Treat:

Crosfield's Band is endeavouring to raise money for, a wounded soldiers' treat, and has arranged to'play a special programme of .music in the Park at 8.15 to-morrow (Sunday) even- ing. The members have voted their fee for the performance towards the fund, and given a fine evening they have high hopes of raising a goodly sum. The band is in first-class form, and has had a fine reception this season in Roch- dale, Stockport, Chester,. Manchester, &c., where huge-audiences have been entertained. -It is estimated that at Rochdale alone, fully ten thousand people were present and nine thousand pro4raniinzss wen! actually printed and disposed of.

div.head: St. Peter's Church Choir Sermons.
div.p: St. Peter's Church Choir Sermons.

The annual choir terinons in connection with t. Peter's Church, were preach I on •::•unday by the Vicar of Stretton, the Rev. the Hon. C. P. Cross. Special music was sung by the choir throughout the dayv In .the morning, they rendered, the anthem "0 Worship the King," the , soloist being Master J. Padmore. In the evening the anthem was "I am Alpha." The soloists were Miss Mabel Percival, Miss Amy Holmes and Mr. H. Sudlow. In the afternoon a special musical service was rendered by the church choir, which had been excellently trained by Mr. E. A. Padmore, the organist and choirmaster. Several friends assisted the choir on this occasion, and the soloists included Miss Tanner, Mr. Dutton and Mr. Sudlow, whilst a duet was given by Miss Nellie Grounds and Miss May Ellis. Two quartets wbre also rendered.

div.head: Fell kilo a Brook in a Fit.
div.p: Fell kilo a Brook in a Fit.

Mr. Coroner Brighouse held an inquest at Warrington on Wednesday on the body of a fifteen-year-old youth named Herbert Martin, the soul of Mrs. Mary Martin, a widow, of 24, Lloyd-street.—The evidence of the mother showed that the deceased had been subject to fits ever since he was four years of age. On June 17th he left home at 6.30 in the morning to visit a married sister at Orford. He returned at about three o'clock in the • afternoon, "covered with mud from head to foot." When his mother asked him how he got into such a condition be said that he had had a fit on the way home and had fallen into a brook. He then seemed to be all right, save that he corn- Plained of feeling cold. He was got to bed and next duy he appeared to be ill and two doctors were sent for, but both were out. On the third day—Saturday—he was worse still, and Dr. Martin was fetched. He examined the lad' and told witness that there was very little chance of his getting better, and he passed away at 5.30 on Sunday evening.—Dr. Martin said that when he was called in to see the deceased he found him suffering from acute pneumonia, from which he died. The fall into, the brook might have been an exciting cause of the complaint.—The jury returned a verdict of "Death from natural causes."

div.head: Church 'War Service.
div.p: Church 'War Service.

At the annual meeting of the Warrington Church Society on Monday, the Rev. Canon Willis (who presided), was re-appointed presi- dent with the Rev. G. Vale Owen as hon. secretary and Mr. C. A. Littler as hon. treasurer The committee was re-elected, with the addition of Mr. W. Milner, Mr. Mockett, Miss Reynolds, Mrs. Guest Gornall, Miss White and Miss Ferriman.

The twenty-third annual report pointed out that the times did not permit of the holding of ordinary public meetings, but members had unique opportunities of doing useful work. Amon.. means of usefulness the committee sug- gested", kcfriespondence with those on active service; tactful and kindly encouragement of those at-home to 'do their duty; cheerfulness at all times; continual private prayer, regular attendance at holy 'communion and public intercession. Members might hold. themselves ready to support very earnestly and energeti- cally any corporate action %deemed advisable as opportunity was presented. The Hon. Treasurer's statement showed that the year began with a balance in hand of £37 12s. 9d. The present balance was £25 15s. 11d., which was allocated, except a few pounds, to the Church House, Church Lads' Brigade, Church of England Men's Society Federation, and other objects.

div.head: Rector's Double Loss.
div.p: Rector's Double Loss.

Last Saturday Canon Willis- lost his second and only surviving sister, Mrs. Georgiana Ger- trude Brown, wife of the Rev. J. Brown, rector of Didcot for the past fifteen years. Mrs. Brown, who was 75 years of age, is the ?ourth sister of 'the Rectc:T's to die in the last two years. On Sunday his sister-in-law, the widow of the late Mr. Henry Rodolph d'Anyers Willis, Halsnead, died in London. The Rector, for whom Much sympathy is felt and expressed, has this week attended bpth funerals.

The Call to Economy. On Monday, at the office of the Guild of Help, a conference was held between represen- .tatives of the Guild, trade unions, friendly societies, Savings Bank, &c. • After a frank interehange of opinions, it was unanimously agreed that it was desirable to carry on a local campaigl to urge the desirability of thrift. A small but representative committee was appointed to give further consideration to the question, and it was suggested that a public meeting might be held. Existing facilities for thrift were discussed, such as the voluntary sections of the friendly societies, insurance against unemployment through trade unions, savings banks, and the special opportunities afforded by employing firms, schools and churches. Two views were exprewd by those present at the conference: (1) That there was an urgent need for personal thrift to meet the trade depression which would follow the war; (2) that however sound the financial position of any individual might ap- pear to be, the call to economy for the sake of the national welfare was one that could not be neglected.

"Warringtonian's Plucky Nephew. Air Mechanic Leonard Newns, son of Mr. Joseph Newns, schoolmaster, Tabley, and nephew of Mr. J. W. Slack, of .Messrs. Rich- mond's, Warrington, has been awarded the D.C.M. for plucky conduct in France. When war broke out Newns was a wireless operator on board a Liverpo6l boat in harbour at New York', but within three weeks of joining the Royal Flying Corps he was in France. His expert kn6wiedge of wireless telegraphy was detected, and he was at once promoted , from mechanic to the wireless telegraphy depart- ment, and thus became the medium of the com- munications from the men "in the clouds" to the officers in chirge of the guns. News has been in some tight corners. , He was' in the trenches when a shell shattered a huge oak 'tree under whose shadow he was. He thought it was time to quit, and a three mile run along the bank of the Yser enSued. When the lull came. he thought of his records and instruments, and of what great advantage they would be if they fell in the hands of the enemy. He was 'warned not to return, but he did so, and secured the tackle, which would have been of immense service to the Germans. He was hard pressed in the battle round Hill 60. and on that occasion destroyed his despatch

div.head: "BUCK UP ! "
div.p: "BUCK UP ! "
Warrington Soldier's thice To %%Torrington Men.

Mrs. Clara Gaffney, 24, Kerfoot-street, Win- wick-road, Warrington, has received a letter from her son, Thomas Gaffney, who is with the Ist Border Regiment in the Dardanelles. Having told his mother that he trusts God to spare him that he may repay her for her kind- ness, the writer says:—

"We are getting along fine, and are quite happy in our mud hilts. „My pal was shot down by my side; but we are making the Turks do the turkey trot quicker than they ever did it before, and they will ,get more yet. They will never take me as long as I have a rifle in my hand and can use it."

div.head: " Delightful " Occupaticn.
div.p: A " Delightful " Occupaticn.
Private Gaffney, thanking his sister for a present, says "We are still knocking the Turks over, and sometimes we have a turn at burying them, which I am sure is very delightful for us.-.

"I am quite pleased to hear what a lot of young men in Warrington are helping in this great war. ram sure if they only knew what we know they would not stop pt 'home. I say 'Buck up, Warrington! and do your share for your children's sake.'"

div.head: 1101 IE FROM THE FRONT.
div.p: 1101 IE FROM THE FRONT.
Bitch. Of " Terrier" Heroes Arrive In Warrington.

Some half-dozen of the Warrington Terri- torials who took part in the recent fighting, and had the good fortune to escape seathless, are at present in Warrington. They arrived quietly at about 4 o'clock yesterday morning, having spent the bigger part of the previowl day in travelling from a South Coast port, which they reached on Wednesday night, after an unin- terrupted and pleasant passage across the Channel. They will proceed to the home head- quarters of their battalion to-morrow night.

div.head: PRIVATE THOMAS BURKE.
div.p: PRIVATE THOMAS BURKE.
Soldier Of Fourteen Years' Service Loses A Leg.

Private Thomas Burke, of the •Ist North Staffordshire Regiment has been wounded, and has had his leg amputated above the knee. News to this effect has reached his wife, Mrs. Burke, of Stephen-street, Manchester-road, Warrington, through the medium of several letters written from hospital in France. , Private Burke, who is 35 years of age, has served in the Army for 14 years. • He fought in the South African War. •

div.head: PRISONER AND WOUNDED.
div.p: PRISONER AND WOUNDED.
Private Carter Says It's "The Fortunes
Of War."

Private James Carter, the King's Own (R.L.) Regiment, writing from Gefangenin Lager, Doeberitz, Germany, to Mr. M. Burke, 3iersey Hotel, Mersey-street, May 25th, says : "I daresay You will be surprised to hear from me, but I received word from home telling me you hadi sent some cigarettes and groceries, which I received quite safe—and I've taken the liberty- of thanking you. "You .may have been wondering what has become of me. lam sorry to say I was wounded through the legs in the retreat from Mons and was taken prisoner in a field hospital. I am now interned in Germany as a prisoner of war, but I am -getting' on all right and knocking about again. I should like to be remembered to Alf. Wood, Jim Burrow, Lee and his chums, or .anyone who remembers me. I am as well as can be expected, and hope you and an the lads are. I am looking forward to being among you again Shortly and would give something to be with you again. Still it's the fortune's of war. and can't be elped. I should like a postcard from you or yone who wishes to send me a few. . • Private Carter, whose wife and Child live at 3, Victoria-street, Warrington, has been in the Army Since 1905. • •
A sure way not to know any too much is to think you do.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

The Mctoring Menace.—Henry Thos. Gwil- Pam, 105, Ellesmere-road, was fined 205., at the Warrington Police Court on Thursday, for driv- ing a motor cycle in Chester-road at a speed dangerous to the public, on the 13th June. Act- ing-Sergeant Edwards said that at 2.15 in the afternoon he saw defendant Coming through the bottle-neck of Chester-road without sounding his horn. A number of people were about, and other cyclists were on the road. He estimated defendant's speed at twelve. or fifteen mils an hour.. Defendant said he was not aware that he was driving to the danger of the public. The Chairman: Don't you think it is dangerous at that Speed. Defendant: I could see my way clear. I had my machine under proper con- trol. The Chairman: We have had one death on that road through people holding the same kind of view as you do. This motor cycle busi- ness is becoming an absOlute menace to the community.—Cyril Charles Cook, of 24, Wilders- pool Causeway, was fined ps. for driving in a manner dangerous to the public.—Walter Hope, a collier, of Atherton, Manchester, was fined 20s. for driving at a dangerous speed. Boys and Telegraphic Insulators.—A, stern .warning to three small boys who one evening not long ago passed the time away very pleas- antly by bombarding the insulators on a certain unoffending telegraph pole at Walton Superior, was delivered by Mr. L: Greening, 'presiding over the Bench at a Juvenile Court held at Stockton Heath on Tuesday. 'Mr. C. J. Holmes was also on the bench.—P.C. Rowlands said that at 8.30 in the evening on the day in question he saw the boys throwing stones at the telegraph poles. near the Bridgewater Canal. He caught them and examined the poles and found that a number of insulators were broken.—The Chair- man, in ordering the payment by the parents of .10s., said they must take it as a warning. If any more boys came before the Bench for a similar offence they would certainly be pun- ished very severely—the maximum penalty was £4O. The country was in need of all the tele- graphic communications available, and was not going to be interfered with by mischievous boys.

div.head: DRIVER JAMES AU UTLEY.
div.p: DRIVER JAMES AU UTLEY.
A Cheery "Tommy "Sends A Cheer 3,

liessalle Home. Driver James Whitley, of the Royal Horse Artillery, son of Mr. James Whitley, Walton- road, writing to his brother, Mr. Joshua Whitley, newsagent, Stockton Heath, says that before long the Germans will be off the French soil altogether. "The French troops," he con- tinues, "are doing excellently Mow and, of course, you don't want telling about our Tommies,' as they are always there' when wanted. It's quite a treat to see our' Tommies ' so bright, cheerful and happy through it all, facing shells, bullets, bombs and gas, and every other method. The Allemen ' have tried to shift them, but all are useless, and well they know it. I know all this because lam amongst them and I am enjoying myself with them; but we keep watching and waiting, and every move we know. I shall be sending you some curios in due course as I get them. I have another piece of 'Jack Johnson,' which is another bit towards your box, which I will make up in a day or so. So keep quiet and calm, as all things come to those who wait.' Driver. Whitley, who went through the Boer War and has the medals an clasps for that campaign, has a brother (Phillip) in the sth Manchesters, serving at the Mediterranean base.

div.head: SUCCESSFUL 'WALKING DAY. "All The Fun Of The Fair" At
div.p: SUCCESSFUL 'WALKING DAY. "All The Fun Of The Fair" At

Wilderspool Park. "Walking Day as usual" said Stockton Heath, and the Fates smiled on their decision and sent a fine day for the big event. The weather yesterday morning was anything but propitious, but by the time the procession was due to start from the church, a complete change had taken plate in the demeanour of the sky, and June had returned in all its sweetness and benignity. The procession, headed by the band of the Blue Coat School, left the Church at two o'clock; and wound its way down the Hight. street. It was a happy sight. There had been disappointment on many a young face in the morning; but now seraphic smiles and looks of eager expectancy combined in a monopoly of expressions. For a section of the partici- pants in the procession, the -term "Walking Day" could hardly be applied with literal truth, the yery young folk riding in state in vehicles of Various kinds, from the lorry to the tiny dog-cart. Just in front of this cavalcade of importance Strode the proudest of the pro- cession, the tots who last year graced the lorries and the dog-carts, but who were now deemed sufficiently grown-up to "pad the hoof" I - with the majority. When the procession had gone the round, tea was taken in the schools and Church Room, whence the youngsters hastened gleefully to Wilderspool,Park; kindly lent for the occasion by Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co. Here were all manner of delights'. A dozen discon- solate donkeys, accompanied by a " baby donk" as it was affectionately all ,d. sullenly awaited riders in one corner- of the spacious .fieid. and made desperate and vicious (but always unsuccessful) efforts to dislodge any human Inirden they might consider too heavy. The "baby 4onk," which, by the way, was mostly ears, was much sought after 'but made friends with Pa one. Plinston's Royal High- Class Ascot Mountain Ponies and Racing Motor Cars was the style and title of another nopular "side-show." We're rather afraid liberties were taken, and that this concern was intimately referred to as "the reound- about." Still, it was holiday time, and one must make excuses. By the way,' the horses were most fierce-looking beasts, chock full of the original Prairie spirit. "The Ariel Flight" sort of overhead-wire slide) was also well patronised, and needless to 'say, the ice cream stall had a host of friends. In addition; there were swings and an Aunt Sally Show, and,: ono way and another, the youngsters spent a real good time.

We should mention that the rear of the .n7.'().- cession—which included the Vicar (the Rey. Jas. Collins) and the Curate (th, Rev. E. W. Clarke), the Wardens (Messrs. T. J. Lee and Xas. Richardson), the School Managers (Messrs. A. Down and Jas. Whitley), Messrs. John Hallows, J. Swinton, W. Mclntyre and A. Broady (church officers). and Mr. P. Rose (marshal), was brought up by the Boy Scouts' Band.

div.head: PAD GATE.
div.p: PAD GATE.

Choir A nniversary.—The nethodist choir anniversary services were held on Sunday last, the preacher being the Rev. E. Bulmer, of Leeds. .The subject of the Morning discourse was "Will Methodism last in the days to come?" the text being taken from Dent. xiv. 2. The preacher pointed out the impoilance of the church being a teaching and evangelical church. If it ceased to evangelise it would perish. The subject of the evening sermon was "The Mission of Methodism," the text being . taken from Genesis xxxiii. 28. The-choir sang the anthems "Sweet is the sunlight" and "Sweet is Thy mercy, Lord" at the morning service, the solo- ists being Arias B. London and Miss- Stewart. At the evening service Sullivan's "0 Gladsome Light !" and Evening Hymns were sung, Mr. G. Walker also rendering "When I survey the Wondrous Cross." At the afternoon service a cantata, entitled "Under the Palms," was ren- dered by an augmented choir of 50 voices, under the 6onductorship of Mr. W. J. Bate. The principal soloists were Miss Mason, Miss Ward, Mrs. L. Bennett, Mr. T. Goostrey and Mr. P. Moon, the quartets being taken by Mrs. W. J. Bate, Miss Appleton, Mr. G. Walker and Mr. W. Seed. Mr. W. H. Ward presided at the organ and Mr. Duckworth occupied the chair. There were good Congregations at all the ser- vices, the collections being in aid of the organ and choir funds.
INFIRMARY WOUNDED CONCERT-R.

Mr. F. M. Darby, organist at the Parish Church, organised two capital concerts for the entertainment of the wounded warriors at the Infirmary. •inese passed off very successfully indeed. The first, given last week, was contributed to by Miss M. Blackburne, Miss Ball and Messrs. J. B. Poole, Fred Fieldhouse, J. Draper, W. Rutter and R. Scarisbrick. Mr. Percy Smith emciently accompanied. On Monday evening a second concert was given by Messrs. Darby, Price, Fieldhouse and Rutter.

div.head: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
div.p: PUBLIC AMUSEMENTS.
FIRST-RATE DRAMA AT THE
ROYAL COURT.

A well-written melodrama of unflagging in- terest 'holds the boards at the Royal Court Theatre this week, and is doing good business. Entitled "The Prodigal Parson, it tells ho' the happiness of a country vicarage is wrecked by the machinations of a villainous schemer; how a pure and gentle wife is cast adrift, and how the Vicar is driven from his home, to drink and to the brink of suicide by a trumped-up charge of murder. The piece is admirably pre- sented by a company headed by Mr. W. V- Garrod, one of the most robust and versatile actors on the contemporary melodrama stage. He plays the part of the sorely tried and muchwronged parson, and does it most effectively, Miss Bertha Kingston rendering him able suP- port iii the role of the vicar's wife, her por- trayal being sympathetic in the extreme. No lover of good, old-fashioned melodrama shcrig miss " The Prodigal Parson."

div.head: " Ripping " Revue Next Week.
div.p: " Ripping " Revue Next Week.

"All Aboard "—that delicious and sparkling revue, reviewed so favourably wherever it has been:--pays a visit next week to the Royal Court, and will worthily maintain the standard of excellence for which the entertainments at this theatre are so well and favourably known. The merry musical melange will be presented by a sprightly company of comedians and dainty soubrettes, assisted by a large London beauty chorus.

div.head: HISTORICAL,. LOVE-DRAMA AT STAR KINEMA.
div.p: HISTORICAL,. LOVE-DRAMA AT STAR KINEMA.

The fact that Mary Pickford is fo." take part in any film is a guarantee ,of that film' excellence • and attractiveness; and " Mistress Nell" is no exception. Indeed, we do not remember_ ever having seen a finer film than that which •occupied place of honour at the Star -Kinema during the first half of this week. For studied detail in every part of the produc- tion and acting this is a superb masterpiece. which will not easily, nor for long; be sur- passed. "Wanted, a • Nurse," a really excruciating comedy, also featured a master of mute-histrionics—Sidney Drew—supported by a well-chosen company. A strong war issue of " Pathes' Animated gazette" illustrated mank branches of Army life—horsemanship, cycling- &c. " Uncle Sam's Phenomenal Achievement

(viz., the Panama Canal)—an extremely valu- able film from the educational point of view -- showed lucidly the method of carrying out 834 use when completed of "the greatest engineer- ing project in history." " Yunnan-fou," Chinese town, yielded a Striking variety of in" terest in the shape of the life and customs of its quaint inhabitants. 'Florence Reed, who plays principal part "The Dancing Girl "—premiere in to-day programme—needs little recommendation to cinema-lovers: , The Kinema management fir° cordially to be congratulated upon such a splendid week's bookings.

div.head: Next Week's Premier Attractions.
div.p: Next Week's Premier Attractions.
The big attraction at the beginning of we will will be. "The Spitfire," whilst at , the week-end a film of intense interest, entitled "The Conspiracy" is expected to prove a great. draw.

KILLED. LIEUT. E. ,LIONEL FROST, • An All-Round Sportsman And A • Popular Officer. The only commissioned officer who lost his life in the brave fight was Lieutenant Edmund Lionel Frost, the son of Dr. Edmund Frost, of Eastbourne, 'and a nephew of Mi. F. .Aylmer Frost; of Grappenhall Hall, near Warrington. The news of the Lieutenant's death was con- veyed to his father in a letter . received on Sunday morning, whilst, the same day, his uncle received sympathetic missives from.

WOUNDED. CAPTAIN EGERTON FAIRCLOUGH. Struck By Shell Fragment When About To Lead A Charge. Captain Egerton Fairclough• was wounded in the memorable charge, but, happily, compara- tively slightly, A, fragment of shell striking him in the mouth and knocking out several of his teeth. A letter, written by a member of the battalion to a friend in Warrington, says that the .Captain was ,struck just as he had scaled the parapet of the trench for the purpose of leading his company in the charge.. Captain Fairclough is thirty years of age,

CAPTAIN A. B. LAI"FON. • Over Ten Years' Service In The Local Territorials. Captain Arthur Bertram Layton is included in the list of wounded in the big fight. He is, in peace times, the 'electrical engineer and departmental manager at Messrs. Crosfield's

and he is he youngest son of Mr. and Mrs. John Fairclough, of the Grange, Latchford. He received his early education at Aston Hall, near Frodsham—under Dr. Carpenter—and sub- sequently proceeded to Harrow': At the time of the outbreak of war he was acting as secretary to Messrs. Chas. Moore and Co., of the Heatley Salt Works. He has been a member of the local Territorials for a number of years. CAPTAIN ALFRED SKINNER. Now Doing Well At Home, After An X-Ray Examination. ' Captain Alfred Skinner, who, as was reported in our last issue, was wounded in the gallant

Soapery, and he resided at 32, Whitefield-road, Stockton Heath, but he is not a native of the town, and his home is in the Isle of Wight. Captain Layton joined the local Territorials as far back as September 17th, 1904, and he is a popular and enthusiastic officer. He is at present in the Royal Military Hospital at Woolwich, where, we learn, he is making satis- factory progress towards recovery. The Captain is unmarried. LIEUT. E. 0. CROSFIELD. Two Bullet Wounds, But Not Serious. Second-Lieutenants Eric Oliver Crosfield is 21 years of age, and is the eldest son of Mr. J. J. and Mrs. Crosfield, Netherdale, Frodsham. He was educated at Shrewsbury, Dresden and Lausanne, Switzerland. He joined the 4th Bat- talion last September, at which time he was en- gaged at Messrs. J. Crosfield and Sons', and went to the Front on the 11th ult. On Sunday a letter was received from him as follows "I was wounded in the foot yesterday morn- ing about 9 a.m., during a charge. I lay in a Shell hole till dusk, when I crawled to one of our communication trenches. Stretcher-bearers were not too plentiful, but I was eventually picked up by one of these of another regiment and taken to their dressing station. I am now

charge, is now recuperating at, his hour,, Fill- top House, Latchford. After receiving attention at a base hospital the wounded Captain was sent over to England and entered the Royal Military Hospital at Woolwich, along with some of the other wounded officers of his battalion. leaving the latter .he entered the service of Messrs. Joseph Crosfield and Sons, and on the outbreak of hostilities was a Second-Lieutenant in the 4th South Lancashire Regiment.
